sections.methods:
We conducted an observational, prospective, cross‐sectional follow‐up study of a cohort of infants hospitalized for RSV bronchiolitis in the Severo Ochoa University Hospital, a public secondary‐care hospital in Madrid, Spain, between September 2023 and June 2025.

The study included children and adolescents with a history of hospital admission for acute viral bronchiolitis, defined by the criteria of McConnochie [], between January 1, 2004 and December 31, 2017 due to a single HRVS infection. These patients were originally enrolled during hospitalization as part of an ongoing clinical‐virological study of severe pediatric respiratory infections, conducted in collaboration with the Influenza and Respiratory Viruses Laboratory at the National Centre of Microbiology (ISCIII) since 1995.

At the time of admission, a sample of nasopharyngeal aspirate was collected for viral identification and HRSV subgroup determination using molecular diagnostic techniques. During the hospital stay, a questionnaire was filled out by a physician providing information on epidemiological and clinical variables. Nasopharyngeal aspirate samples were screened for multiple viruses using molecular techniques; however, only those cases involving RSV monoinfection were included in the present study.

The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Severo Ochoa University Hospital in July 2023 (no specific ethical number available in ethical approval letter) and the study was conducted in accordance with the principles set forth in the Declaration of Helsinki.

Children and adolescents aged 5 to 18 years with a history of admission for bronchiolitis in the Pediatrics Department of the University Severo Ochoa Hospital, between January 1, 2004, to December 31, 2017, caused by a single HRSV‐A or HRSV‐B infection, and whose parents had previously consented to participate in the original etiological study.

Children and adolescents with serious illness that prevents the performance of respiratory function tests, as well as the refusal of parents or children to participate in the study.

Eligible participants were contacted by telephone and were invited to take part in the follow‐up study. For those who agreed, an appointment was scheduled at the hospital. After obtaining informed consent, participants were enrolled. Informed consent was obtained from the parents for children under 12 years of age. For those over 12, informed consent was obtained from both the parents and the minors; the latter was adapted to a minor‐friendly language. Clinical data regarding hospital admission were collected from databases created at the time of admission, including age at admission, sex, personal history of preterm birth, the length of stay, presence and duration of fever, need for and duration of oxygen therapy and the need for admission to a pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), total white blood cell count and C ‐reactive protein level if applicable.

At the time of the follow‐up visit, age was calculated, and weight and height measurements were taken to calculate the corresponding lung function z ‐score values.

During the follow‐up visit, a structured questionnaire was used to gather information on breastfeeding, nursery school, wheezing episodes, related hospital admissions, use of bronchodilators and maintenance medication for asthma [inhaled corticosteroid, combination inhaled corticosteroid/long‐acting beta‐2 agonists (ICS/LABA), leukotriene antagonists], physician‐diagnosed conditions including atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis and food allergies. Additional data were collected on parental smoking habits and family history of allergy, eczema and asthma in first‐degree relatives (parents or siblings), previously diagnosed by a physician.

Patients were encouraged to complete the Spanish‐validated ISAAC questionnaire []. The ISAAC respiratory symptom questionnaire was completed by the patients themselves with their parents’ assistance in the case of older children (> 12 years old), and directly by the parents for the younger ones. This eight‐item questionnaire is widely used in epidemiological studies to assess asthma prevalence. It includes questions on lifetime and recent wheezing episodes (within the last past 12 months), frequency and impact on daily activities (sleep, exercise or speech) and the presence of nocturnal dry cough not associated with infections. Question 2‐ (‘ Have you had wheezing or whistling in the chest in the last 12 months?’) is the one most associated with the presence of current asthma and was used in this study as the primary criterion for defining current asthma prevalence.

Following the interview, participants underwent measurements of exhaled nitric oxide, performance of spirometry and bronchodilator test and skin prick testing for allergic sensitization.

FeNO was measured using the NIOX VERO handheld device. Values < 25 ppb were considered to be normal.

Forced spirometry was performed in accordance with the Spanish Society of Pulmonology and Thoracic Surgery (SEPAR). The parameters recorded were forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 ), FEV 1 /FVC ratio and mean expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of FVC (FEF 25–75 ). Results were interpreted using the reference values provided by The Global Lung Function Initiative (GLI) (2023) available at GLI reference site ( https://www.ers-education.org/guidelines/global-lung-function-initiative/about/ ). Spirometry was considered to be normal when FEV 1 and FVC were ≥ 80%, FEV 1 /FVC > 90% and FEF 25–75 ≥ 65% of their predicted values.

Post‐bronchodilator spirometry was conducted following the administration of 400 μg of inhaled salbutamol. The test was considered positive when an increase of FEV 1 of ≥ 12% over the baseline was observed.

Allergic sensitization was evaluated by skin prick test to common aeroallergens, following the recommendations of the European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (EAACI) []. The following allergens were included: Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, Dermatophagoides farinae, Alternaria alternata, Cladosporium , grass, cypress, olive and plane tree ( Platanus ) pollen, as well as dog, cat and horse dander. Standardized extracts (ABELLO) were used, along with positive (10 mg/mL histamine) and negative (glycerol saline vehicle solution) controls. A test was considered to be positive when the wheal diameter was equal to or greater than that of histamine and at least 3 mm larger than the negative control.

Continuous variables were described using mean and standard deviation. Categorical variables were described using absolute and relative frequencies. To compare qualitative variables, Chi‐squared test or Fisher's exact test was used if the expected frequency was ≤ 5 in at least one cell of the contingency tables. Odds ratio (OR) values and 95% confident intervals (CI) were also calculated. For quantitative variables Student's T test was applied for those with a normal distribution while the Mann–Whitney U test for non‐normally distributed data. A two‐sided value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Risk factors with a p ‐value < 0.10 in the bivariant analysis were entered in a stepwise logistic regression analysis to estimate the independent association among RSV‐A, RSV‐B bronchiolitis and other factors with asthma prevalence.

All statistical analyzes were performed using SPSS software, version 25 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, USA).

According to Sigurs et al. [] 43% of former hospitalized HRSV bronchiolitis with current age of 13 years will present asthma in the past 12 months. We predefined an absolute difference of 15% as clinically meaningful, as such a magnitude would represent a substantial variation in long‐term respiratory morbidity and potentially relevant implications for risk stratification after severe bronchiolitis. Accepting an alpha risk of 0.05 and a beta risk of 0.2 in a two‐sided test, 99 subjects are necessary in the HRSV‐B group and 198 in the HRSV‐A group to find as statistically significant a proportion difference, expected to be of 0.15 in group 1 and 0.3 in group 2.
sections.results:
A database of 470 patients admitted for bronchiolitis with a single RSV infection was available. Of these, 120 could not be contacted due to a change in phone number or because they had moved to a different city. Of the 350 patients informed about the study, 185 agreed to participate as of June 1st, 2025, with a median age 12.44 ± 3.6 years (5–18 years). Of these, 99 were boys (53.5%), and 86 (46.5%) were girls. Regarding the HRSV subgroup, 129 (69.7%) belonged to HRSV‐A infection, while 56 (30.3%) were infected with HRSV‐B. Of the patients who declined to provide informed consent, only one had deceased as a consequence of a bone neoplasm; none of them suffered from severe chronic lung disease.

Hospitalization‐related data during the initial bronchiolitis episode in the first 2 years of life are summarized in Table . No significant differences were observed between HRSV‐A and HRSV‐B groups.

Similarly, no differences were found in personal history of atopy or allergy between the two groups. Regarding family background, maternal atopy was more frequent among children with prior HRSV‐B infection (34.5% vs. 19.5%, p = 0.029; OR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1‐1.5). Conversely, children in the HRSV‐A group more often had pets at home (34.4% vs. 17.9%, p = 0.024; OR: 2.4, 95% CI: 1.1–5.2) (Table ).

Analysis of respiratory outcomes following the bronchiolitis episode revealed no significant differences in the need for new respiratory admissions or requirement of maintenance therapy to control respiratory symptoms (Table ). A high proportion of patients in both groups (according to ISAAC question 1, 80%–85%) experienced RW in early childhood. However, the age of resolution of these episodes was significantly later in the HRSV‐A group (4.7 ± 3.4 vs. 3.6 ± 1.3, p = 0.03).

The prevalence of current asthma at the time of the consultation, as assessed by ISAAC question 2 (‘ Have you had wheezing or whistling in the chest in the last 12 months?’) , did not differ significantly between groups (HRSV‐A 17.2% vs . HRSV‐B 25.5%, p = 0.19) (Table ). A tendency towards a higher prevalence of medical diagnosis of asthma at some point, in HRSV‐B group (question 6, ‘ Have you ever had asthma? ’) than in HRSV‐A group (44% vs. 31%, p = 0.08; OR = 1.4, 95% CI: 0.96–2.2) was detected, although it did not reach statistical significance. The mean age of children with and without current asthma at follow‐up was compared and no significant differences between the two groups were found (12.7 ± 3.2 years vs. 12.4 ± 3.2, p = 0.550). Additionally, age was categorized (< 6 years and ≥ 6 years) to explore whether asthma prevalence differed according to developmental stage. No significant differences in asthma prevalence were observed between these age groups (16.7% in < 6 years vs. 19.8% in ≥ 6 years, p = 0.851).

Regarding severity of asthma, HRSV‐B patients reported more severe respiratory symptoms, particularly speech‐limiting wheezing (ISAAC question 5: ‘ In the past 12 months, has wheezing ever been severe enough to limit your speech to only one or two words at a time between breaths?’ ) (HRSV‐A 1.5% vs. HRSV‐B: 8.9%, p = 0.039; OR: 2.62, 95% CI: (1.3–5.4). HRSV‐B patients also reported more frequent nocturnal dry cough not associated with infections (ISAAC question 8: ‘ In the past 12 months, have you had a dry cough at night, apart from a cough associated with a cold or chest infection? ’) (HRSV‐A: 7.7% vs. HRSV‐B: 16.9%, p = 0.044; OR: 1.78, 95% CI: 1.1–2.9) (Table ).

Additional factors potentially associated with current asthma were evaluated (Table ). In the bivariate analysis, atopic dermatitis ( p = 0.009), food allergy ( p = 0.010), allergic rhinitis ( p = 0.002), and maternal history of atopy ( p = 0.007) asthma ( p = 0.010) showed significant associations with current asthma (Table ).

The factors independently related with a medical diagnosis of current asthma (ISAAC question 2) were maternal atopy ( p = 0.007), food allergy ( p = 0.034) and allergic rhinitis ( p = 0.013) (Table ).

Factors potentially associated with medical diagnosis of asthma at any time were evaluated (Table ). In the bivariate analysis, food allergy ( p = 0.002), allergic rhinitis ( p = 0.001), siblings history of asthma ( p = 0.004), maternal history of atopy ( p = 0.023) and pets at home ( p = 0.02) showed significant associations with asthma at any time (Table ).

The variables independently associated with asthma at any time (ISAAC question 6) were allergic rhinitis ( p = 0.03) and food allergy ( p = 0.016) (Table ). A history of HRSV‐B bronchiolitis showed a tendency, though not statistically significant ( p = 0.057) (Table ).

Factors that related with the presence of nocturnal dry cough in the previous 12 months (ISAAC question 8) were analyzed. In the bivariate analysis, atopic dermatitis ( p = 0.048), allergic rhinitis ( p < 0.001), maternal history of asthma ( p = 0.002) and maternal history of atopy ( p = 0.021) showed significant association nocturnal dry cough (Table ).

The presence of nocturnal cough in the previous 12 months (ISAAC question 8) was independently related to a history of HRSV‐B bronchiolitis ( p = 0.018), allergic rhinitis ( p < 0.001) and a maternal history of asthma ( p = 0.009) and smoking during pregnancy ( p = 0.011) (Table ).

Regarding pulmonary function (spirometry and bronchodilator test), no significant differences could be found (Table ).

Finally, markers of atopic asthma, including exhaled nitric oxide (FENO) and aeroallergen sensitization by skin prick testing, showed no differences between the two groups (Table ).
sections.discussion:
Multiple studies have linked the history of bronchiolitis and viral infection with the subsequent development of asthma or wheezing in childhood and adolescence [, , , , , , ]. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare the medium‐term respiratory evolution in patients with a history of severe bronchiolitis with unique RSV infection requiring hospitalization, comparing the two main RSV antigenic groups A and B. According to our results, the frequency of asthma in the past 12 months was similar in both groups; however, patients with a history of HRSV‐B bronchiolitis exhibited greater respiratory morbidity. Specifically, they reported speech‐limiting respiratory symptoms 2 to 3 times more frequently and experienced nocturnal dry cough at twice the rate observed in the HRSV‐A group. Notably, bronchiolitis caused by HRSV‐B emerged as an independent risk factor for nocturnal dry cough and showed a trend toward a higher prevalence of physician‐diagnosed asthma at any time point.

It is important to highlight that intercritical symptoms, such as dry nocturnal cough, are a key criterion in the classification of asthma severity. Their presence alone is sufficient to categorize asthma as persistent, even in the absence of frequent exacerbations. These findings support the hypothesis that asthma may present greater severity in children and adolescents with a history of HRSV‐B bronchiolitis.

Previous studies have suggested that early‐life viral infections—such as bronchiolitis caused by rhinovirus, HRSV, or viral coinfections—may contribute to the development of severe asthma later in childhood, potentially through variations in the host inflammatory response during the acute phase of illness [, , ]. Recent studies have shown that humoral responses to RSV infection are predominantly strain‐specific, with minimal cross‐neutralization between A and B subgroups, particularly concerning the G protein. In contrast, the F protein elicits more broadly reactive antibodies across subtypes [, ]. Furthermore, differential expressions of cytokines such as TNF‐α, IFN‐γ, IL‐1α, and IL‐1β has been observed in infants infected with specific RSV‐A (e.g., ON1) and RSV‐B (e.g., BA9) genotypes, suggesting subtype‐dependent modulation of innate and inflammatory responses []. In addition, HRSV‐B may induce a weaker interferon‐mediated antiviral response compared to certain HRSV‐A strains, possibly through differential engagement of innate immune receptors such as TLRs, RIG‐I, and NOD2, leading to a more skewed Th2‐type inflammatory profile and prolonged airway inflammation []. Taken together, these immunological differences support the hypothesis that the infecting HRSV subtype may influence long‐term respiratory outcomes.

Interestingly, among infants infected with HRSV‑B—the subgroup in which greater asthma severity was observed in our study—the only significant baseline difference compared to HRSV‑A was a higher frequency of maternal atopy. Maternal atopy, encompassing conditions such as eczema, allergic rhinitis, and asthma, has been independently associated with an increased risk of allergic disease and wheezing disorders in offspring. Evidence suggests that maternal atopic status can influence fetal immune development through mechanisms such as epigenetic modification, skewing of neonatal T‐cell responses toward a Th2 profile []. These observations may suggest that interactions between maternal atopy, host immune predisposition, and viral subtype may influence the long‐term trajectory of respiratory health in affected infants.

A previous study by Sigurs et al. [] which included long‐term follow‐up of patients with a history of HRSV bronchiolitis, reported a higher prevalence of atopic asthma at 18 years of age compared to general population. These individuals also exhibited elevated FENO levels and reduced lung function compared to healthy controls, findings consistent with airway remodeling likely induced by severe early‐life HRSV infection. In our study, we found no significant differences in lung function parameters, including FEV1, FVC, the FEV1/FVC ratio, and FEF 25–75 , between patients with a history of severe HRSV‐A and HRSV‐B bronchiolitis. The mean values of FEV1 and FEV1/FVC were within normal ranges for age in both groups. To our knowledge, this is the first study to specifically compare medium‐term lung function outcomes between the HRSV‐A and HRSV‐B subtypes. It is possible that any potential differences in lung function between the two groups are subtle and would require a larger sample size to achieve statistical significance.

Regarding clinical severity during the admission for bronchiolitis, no significant differences were found in our study between the two main HRSV antigenic groups. The clinical significance of HRSV subtyping, HRSV‐A versus HRSV‐B, in bronchiolitis severity remains a subject of ongoing debate, with evidence pointing in both directions. Several studies have reported that HRSV‐A is associated with more severe clinical outcomes compared to HRSV‐B, particularly some genotypes of HRSV‐A—such as ON1 and GA5—[]. The proposed mechanisms include greater replicative capacity and enhanced induction of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL‐6, IL‐8, TNF‐α), potentially exacerbating the host immune response and airway injury []. However, HRSV‐B has also been shown in some cohorts to induce a comparable or even more sustained inflammatory response, especially in genotypes such as BA9, though this may not always correlate with more severe clinical manifestations [].

A recent meta‐analysis concluded that while HRSV‐A is more frequently detected and may be associated with increased viral load, the evidence supporting consistently greater disease severity is inconclusive and potentially confounded by other factors [].

The principal strength of our study lies in the medium‐term follow‐up of a substantial cohort of patients whose clinical data were prospectively collected during hospitalization for severe bronchiolitis due to a single HRSV infection. This design allowed us to investigate the medium‐term clinical impact of the two major antigenic groups of HRSV—an area that, to our knowledge, has not been previously addressed in medium and long‐term studies.

However, our study also has certain limitations. The sample size was smaller than the initially calculated target, and the number of patients infected with HRSV‐B was notably lower than those with HRSV‐A, reflecting the distribution typically observed in clinical practice. The study was powered to detect an absolute difference of 15% in asthma prevalence between the RSV‐A and RSV‐B groups. Smaller differences might still be clinically relevant; however, the study was not powered to detect effects of this magnitude, and therefore a type II error cannot be excluded. In addition, the study population included a wide pediatric age range (5–18 years). Nonetheless, it is generally accepted that from the age of five, asthma symptoms can be considered well established, distinguishing them from the transient wheezing phenotype often observed in younger children. In fact, we did not find any significant difference between children < than 6 years or ≥ 6years of age regarding the prevalence of current asthma. It should also be acknowledged that the symptom survey was conducted at a single time point; therefore, some degree of recall bias is possible. Patients and their families—especially in the case of older children—may have difficulty accurately recalling details such as the age at the last wheezing episode or the precise number of recurrent wheezing episodes per year. Lastly, the potential for selection bias must be acknowledged given the substantial number of patients who were not enrolled; however, it is worth noting that the primary reasons for non‐participation were logistical, namely residing outside the city or a lack of time to attend the follow‐up visit.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that school‐aged children and adolescents with a history of hospitalization for HRSV‐B bronchiolitis experience poorer respiratory outcomes during childhood and adolescence, including more frequent intercurrent symptoms. Furthermore, HRSV‐B infection emerged as an independent risk factor for limited speech and nocturnal dry cough at school age and during adolescence. According to our results, since a history of HRSV‐ B bronchiolitis appears to be associated with a poorer prognosis, closer monitoring of this patient group—with better medical management of respiratory symptoms during the first years of life—could lead to reduced medium‐term morbidity.

title: Mucin-Inspired Filamentous Sulfated Copolymers Effectively Inhibit Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus (hRSV) Infectivity.
abstract: Virucidal compounds capable of binding to and disrupting viruses represent a promising avenue for antiviral applications. In this study, the development of high molecular weight (≈300 kDa) dendronized polyglycerol-based mucin-inspired amphiphilic statistical copolymers (MIACPs) is reported using the RAFT polymerization technique. These copolymers comprise ≈30% repeat units containing aliphatic C11 carbon chains with terminal carboxylate (MIACP-1) and alkyl (MIACP-2) functionalities, while the remaining ≈70% of the repeat units consist of dendronized polyglycerol sulfates. Structural characterization using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) reveals that MIACPs form single-chain filamentous structures, similar to natural porcine gastric mucin (PGM). These biocompatible MIACPs exhibit strong, sulfate-dependent inhibition of human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV), with exceptionally low IC50 values (C = ≈0.25 µg mL-1). The virucidal activity is assessed using serial dilution experiments, which confirms that MIACPs demonstrate virucidal activity, indicating a very strong binding affinity of the polymers to the hRSV. In contrast, a similar molecular weight homopolymer composed solely of sulfated dendronized repeat units exhibits comparable hRSV inhibition activity but lacks any virucidal effect. Therefore, designing a statistical copolymer with ≈30% virucidal functionality is unique in that it renders the copolymer virucidal without compromising its inhibitory activity.

sections.other:
Human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) is a leading cause of acute lower respiratory tract infections in infants, as well as in elderly individuals and high‐risk adults with chronic lung condition or a compromised immune system. [ , , ] Despite its clinical significance, [ ] there remains a lack of effective vaccines [ ] or widely available antiviral treatments for hRSV, highlighting the urgent need for new treatment options. As a result, the development of broad‐spectrum, potent, and biocompatible antiviral inhibitors remains a critical research priority.

Preventing hRSV infection at its early stages represents an alternative strategy to inhibit viral progression. hRSV initiates infection by interacting with cell surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) or other sulfated proteoglycans. [ , ] Additionally, several membrane proteins have been implicated in facilitating hRSV entry into host cells. [ ] On the viral side, the envelope glycoprotein (G protein) and fusion protein (F protein) mediate attachment to the target cell membrane and promote membrane fusion. [ , ] At the molecular level, the negatively charged sulfate or carboxyl groups of HSPGs or heparin bind to clusters of positively charged basic amino acids within the linear heparin‐binding domain (HBD) of hRSV glycoproteins. [ ] This HSPG‐HBD interaction is a common and critical feature in hRSV‐mediated infection, making it an attractive target for the development of negatively charged antiviral agents.

In this context, heparan sulfate‐mimetic polymers and peptides have emerged as promising inhibitors of hRSV due to their ability to bind viral glycoproteins. [ ] Inspired by these findings, our group explored heparin‐mimetic linear and hyperbranched polyglycerol sulfates, which showed strong potential as antiviral agents owing to their biocompatibility. [ ] These results further motivated us to design functional polyglycerol sulfates with varied molecular weights, architectures, and structural compositions, aiming to broaden the scope of polysulfate‐based inhibitors with enhanced anti‐hRSV activity.

Mucin, a high molecular weight glycoprotein, is a key component of the protective mucus layer. [ ] Inspired by its structure and function, various mucin‐inspired biomaterials have been developed, demonstrating excellent inhibitory activity against a range of pathogens. [ , , , , ] This effectiveness is attributed to their unique characteristics, including high molecular weight, filamentous structure, and strong electronegative charge. Recently, our group developed a series of mucin‐inspired dendronized polyglycerol sulfates with varying molecular weights and found them to be potent inhibitors of sulfate‐binding viruses such as HSV‐1, SARS‐CoV‐2, and their variants. [ , , ] In those studies, polymers with longer filamentous structures and higher overall electronegative charge emerged as the most effective inhibitors. Their antiviral activity was comparable to that of antibodies, [ ] making them among the most promising synthetic inhibitors reported to date. These findings motivated us to investigate functionalized, high molecular weight, filamentous polymeric architectures for the inhibition of hRSV.

Another important consideration is that virus binding mediated by electrostatic interactions may be a reversible process, potentially allowing virus particles to detach from the inhibitors and proceed to infect host cells‐thereby limiting their therapeutic efficacy. This limitation can be addressed by employing inhibitors with virucidal properties that irreversibly deactivate viruses. [ ] This insight further motivated us to enhance the previously developed mucin‐inspired platform by introducing a defined percentage of virucidal functionality, forming the basis for the design of new copolymers. In selecting the virus‐disrupting moieties, alkyl chains with aliphatic C11 carbon lengths have been shown to irreversibly disrupt viral membranes through hydrophobic interactions, [ , , , ] which guided our development of amphiphilic copolymers ( Scheme ).

Amphiphilic polymers often tend to self‐assemble into various aggregated structures. [ , , , , ] However, in our research, we aimed to retain a filamentous morphology instead of promoting other ways of aggregation, in order to leverage the structural advantages of mucin‐like filaments. [ ] Previous studies have reported that other types of aggregation can be minimized by carefully tuning the hydrophilic‐hydrophobic balance of amphiphilic polymers. Notably, systems containing up to ≈30% hydrophobic units have been shown to be very positive in that aspect. [ , , , ] Guided by this, we designed amphiphilic copolymers composed of ≈70% dendronized sulfated groups and ≈30% C11 hydrophobic units (Scheme ). The sulfated groups are intended to inhibit viral binding via electrostatic interactions with positively charged regions on viral surface proteins, while the hydrophobic C11 domains are expected to provide virucidal activity by disrupting the viral membrane.

In this work, we present the synthesis and comprehensive characterization of mucin‐inspired amphiphilic copolymers (MIACPs) incorporating C11 aliphatic chains, along with their homopolymer counterpart (MIP) of similar molecular weight (Scheme 1b). We investigate their morphology in aqueous solution using cryo‐electron tomography (Cryo‐ET) and small‐angle neutron scattering (SANS), assess their biocompatibility, and evaluate their antiviral and virucidal efficacy against hRSV.

The authors declare no conflict of interest.
sections.results:
The chemical structures of the investigated polymers are depicted in Scheme . We report three different dendronized polysulfates with similar molecular weights ( Table ). The first group consists of copolymers (MIACPs) comprising two components: ≈70% repeat units of sulfated dendronized oligoglycerol methacrylate (OGMA), and ≈30% repeat units containing an aliphatic C11 carbon chain terminated with either a carboxylate group ( MIACP‐1 ) or a purely aliphatic group ( MIACP‐2 ). The second is a homopolymer ( MIP ), which lacks any hydrophobic functionality and serves as a control to assess the impact of virucidal groups in MIACPs. Due to their amphiphilic nature, MIACPs carry a risk of particle aggregation. To minimize this, hydrophilic and hydrophobic units were statistically distributed within the copolymer chains. [ ]

For synthesis, we first optimized the polymerization conditions to prepare a relatively high‐molecular‐weight precursor copolymer, P1 (pOGMA‐co‐pNHSMA), on a gram scale (Scheme , Supporting Information). Synthesis and characterization of P1 are provided in the Supporting Information. N‐Hydroxysuccinimide methacrylate (NHSMA) units were selected as pre‐functional groups, which can later be replaced by amine functionalities to install virucidal moieties. [ ] The composition of copolymer P1 was determined by 1 H NMR analysis (Figure , Supporting Information), which confirmed that ≈30% of the repeat units were NHSMA. Considering ≈80% conversion of individual monomers, the molecular weight of P1 was estimated to be 183 kDa, closely matching the size exclusion chromatography (SEC) measurement ( M W = 128 kDa) (Figure , Supporting Information), indicating successful controlled radical copolymerization. The NHS units in P1 were then substituted with either commercially available 11‐amino undecanoic acid or 11‐amino undecane via standard nucleophilic substitution, yielding P2a and P2b , respectively. The disappearance of the NHS peak at δ = 2.88 ppm and the appearance of additional peaks at δ = 1.35–0.85 ppm region (corresponding to ‐CH 2 protons from the aliphatic chain) for P2a and P2b in the 1 H NMR spectrum confirmed successful substitution (Figures and , Supporting Information). The integration of aliphatic protons relative to glycerol units further supported ≈30% incorporation of hydrophobic C11 units.

The acetonide groups of P2a were deprotected to yield P3a which was then sulfated to produce MIACP‐1 (Scheme , Supporting Information). The disappearance of the δ = 1.4–1.35 ppm proton peak in the 1 H NMR spectrum of MIACP‐0 (Figure , Supporting Information) confirmed deprotection. Additionally, the shift in the methylene proton peak adjacent to the sulfate groups in the 1 H NMR spectrum of MIACP‐1 (Figure , Supporting Information), compared to P3a , and confirmed the successful introduction of electronegative sulfate groups.

Elemental analysis of MIACP‐1 (Table ) showed >90% sulfation of the hydroxyl groups in P3a . The molecular weight of MIACP‐1 , estimated from 1 H NMR, was ≈320 kDa, matches with the molecular weight ( M W = 290 kDa) obtained from size exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Figure , Supporting Information) and within the molecular weight range for the large, glycosylated regions of mucin polymers. [ ]

MIACP‐2 was synthesized using similar reaction conditions as described for MIACP‐1 . For that, the acetonide groups of P2b were deprotected to yield P3b ( MIACP‐0 ) which was then sulfated to produce MIACP‐2 (Scheme , Supporting Information). The characterization data are shown in Table and in the Supporting Information (Figures , and , Supporting Information). The investigated homopolymer, MIP , was synthesized using a previously reported protocol from the group, with slight modifications (Scheme , Supporting Information). Characterization data are provided in Table and in the Supporting Information (Figures , Supporting Information).

The overall electronegative charge of sulfated MIACPs and MIP was confirmed by their negative zeta potential values, attributed to the highly sulfated functionalities (Table ). Cryo‐EM was measured to investigate the morphology of MIACPs in aqueous solution. Both MIACP‐1 and MIACP‐2 exhibited elongated filamentous structures ( Figure ). Cryo‐ET was employed to determine the 3D structure and length of the amphiphilic elongated fibers. To eliminate human bias, the fiber length distribution was semi‐automatically analyzed with Fiji [ ] using 3D skeleton analysis [ ] of pre‐processed cryo‐ET volume stacks (illustrated for MIACP‐1 in Figure and in the supporting movie SM‐01). Using this calculation, the average length for MIACP‐1 and MIACP‐2 were 83.1 ± 29.2 nM and 85.3 ± 19.0 nM, which is aligned well with the theoretical average stretched length of ≈150 nM of MIACPs (average number of repeat units = 500), calculated based on the atomic distance in the polymer chain. The observed length distribution of fibers is plausible considering the polydispersity ( Đ = 1.5) in MIACPs .

Interestingly, ≈30% of the hydrophobic functional groups in the case of MIACPs did not affect the overall filamentous morphology of the copolymers. Since aliphatic C11 carbon chains are randomly distributed throughout the polymer backbone, the possibility of aggregation is reduced and filamentous structures are formed.

For comparison, the morphology of commercially available porcine gastric mucin (PGM), was also evaluated. It displayed thread‐like elongated fiber structures (Figure ), suggesting that MIACPs mimic the mucin‐like elongated morphology. [ ]

Small angle neutron scattering (SANS) was further applied to evaluate the morphology of MIACPs . The SANS spectra of the MIACPs with subtracted background (cell and incoherent scattering) are shown in Figure . The spectra can be divided into three regimes. At low q , where large structures are visible, the intensity roughly follows a q −3 power law, which indicates the presence of large‐scale inhomogeneities with sizes > 10 2 nM, i.e., clusters of polymers, as observed frequently in cross‐linked polymer gels [ , ] or in entangled polymer solutions. [ , ] The fact that such domains are seen in SANS, when there were none in cryo‐EM, can be explained by the much higher concentration (20 mg mL −1 for SANS as opposed to 1.0 mg mL −1 for cryo‐EM). The increased concentrations of the SANS measurements were chosen to ensure a sufficiently high scattering intensity. At such high concentrations, the polymers overlap and entangle, giving rise to large‐scale inhomogeneities visible in low‐q. At intermediate q , meaning on a more local scale, the intensity scales roughly as q −1 , as expected for a filamentous structure. Notably, the q −1 region is significantly more pronounced for MIACP‐1 and extends to lower q values. This suggests that the carboxylate moiety at the end of the hydrophobic chain promotes the formation of longer and stiffer fibers. In contrast, for MIACP‐2, one observes a markedly different scattering pattern at mid‐ and low‐q, which indicates the formation of more compacted structures on the length scale of 3‐5 nM. This may be attributed to the presence of the hydrophobic C 11 ‐chains, whereas the MIACP‐1 has a charged group at the end of this chain. At high q , the spectra of MIACP‐1 and MIACP‐2 look identical. On such small length scales, the local structure of the polymer chain is visible. The q −1.8 scaling suggests that the polymer chains are slightly swollen, as expected for a polymer in a good solvent. For a comparison to mucin, we investigated BSM as a representative of commercially available natural mucin, using small‐angle neutron scattering (SANS). The resulting scattering pattern closely resembles that observed for MIACP‐1 . Therefore, SANS data confirmed mucin‐like filamentous morphology for MIACPs .

The cytocompatibility of the MIACPs and MIP was evaluated on A549, HBE, and Vero E6 cell lines at polymer concentrations of up to 1.0 mg mL −1 . The results suggest that MIACPs are biocompatible ( Figure ) in different cell lines and the introduction of C11 aliphatic functionality did not result in significant toxicity compared to the control polymer, MIP . The inherent anticoagulant activity of sulfated polymers generally limits their direct application. [ ] In this context, the MIACPs exhibited negligible anticoagulant activity up to 10 µg mL −1 compared to heparin (Figure ). Our studies further revealed that anticoagulant activity increased with the degree of sulfation, although it remained substantially lower than that of heparin.

We investigated the antiviral activity of MIACPs and MIP against hRSV using an hRSV subtype A long strain containing a GFP reporter gene (hRSV‐GFP). [ ] A549 lung epithelial cells were used to evaluate the anti‐hRSV efficacy ( Figure ). In an infection inhibition assay, the dose‐response curves demonstrated that both MIACPs and MIP inhibited hRSV‐GFP, whereas the non‐sulfated copolymer ( MIACP‐0 ) showed no inhibitory activity (Figure ), confirming the charge‐dependent mechanism of inhibition. [ ]

The similar viral inhibition activities of MIP (IC 50 = 1.57 nM) and MIACP‐1 (IC 50 = 0.83 nM) confirm that ≈70% sulfation is optimal for maximum inhibition, aligning with previously reported degrees of sulfation required for maximal inhibitory activity. In fact, the relatively better inhibition observed for MIACP‐1 compared to MIP is likely due to the presence of ≈30% carboxylate functionality, which may contribute additional inhibitory effects owing to its electronegative nature. A remarkably low half‐maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 = 0.51 nM) highlights the excellent antiviral efficacy of these mucin‐inspired polymers against hRSV. Such low IC 50 values make them among the most potent electronegative inhibitors reported for hRSV. MIACP‐2 also exhibited a low IC 50 value for hRSV‐GFP inhibition (IC 50 = 1.82 nM), reinforcing their potential as effective antiviral agents.

The lower IC 50 of MIACP‐1 compared to MIACP‐2 is likely due to the additional ≈30% carboxylate content in MIACP‐1 . Commercially available porcine gastric mucin (PGM) and bovine submaxillary mucin (BSM) also showed hRSV‐GFP inhibition, but with significantly higher IC 50 values (Figure ). This suggests that the synthetic inhibitors are more effective than commercially available natural mucins in terms of antiviral activity.

MIACPs exhibit strong charge‐dependent interactions with viral glycoproteins, as previously reported for polyglycerol sulfate groups, thereby inhibiting viral infection. [ ] Additionally, the long‐chain polysulfate amphiphilic elongated fibers of MIACPs likely engage in polyvalent interactions, providing sufficient steric shielding that contributes to their excellent inhibitory activity against hRSV. These features mark MIACPs as outstanding viral inhibitors.

We next wanted to investigate the virucidal activity of copolymers MIACPs through a dilution experiment. [ ] In this experiment, hRSV‐GFP (≈2 × 10 4 PFU mL −1 ) was incubated with the desired amount of MIACPs , achieving a final concentration of 100 µg mL −1 (≈IC 90 concentration), for 45 min at 37 °C. The virus‐ MIACPs mixtures were then diluted 1:1000 fold into fresh medium, yielding a MIACPs concentration of 0.1 µg mL −1 ( Figure ). Then the diluted mixtures were applied to A549 cells to quantify the viral titer. At 24 h post‐infection, the viral titre was calculated by counting the number of infected cells per well. If the interaction between virus and MIACPs were reversible (virustatic), the dilution would be expected to promote the disassociation of MIACPs from the virus surface and restore the infectivity towards the control (≈90–100%, Figure ). Conversely, a virucidal activity would have prevented recovery after dilution. No notable recovery of viruses was observed after serial dilution in MIACPs treated groups, indicating that MIACP‐1 and MIACP‐2 are virucidal, confirming their strong binding to hRSV (Figure ). On the other hand, MIP , which lacks the C11 aliphatic group, did not exhibit any virucidal activity (Figure ). This further confirms the importance of the C11 hydrophobic functional groups in conferring virucidal efficacy.

Both the attachment protein G and the homotrimeric fusion protein F mediate viral binding to negatively charged heparan sulfate residues on the host cell surface, [ , ] providing a rationale for the inhibitory effect of the negatively charged polymer structures used in this study. It can be hypothesized that these structures interact with positively charged motifs of the ectodomain (ECD). It has been concluded that the binding of the G protein occurs via a stretch of positively charged amino acids (aa 187‐198: KRIPNKKPGKK; Uniprot P03423 |GLYC_HRSVA) located between two mucin‐like motifs. [ , , ] To date, no motif has yet been identified for the ECD of the F protein. However, as we [ , ] and other groups [ , , ] have shown, analyzing the surface potential of the ECD of viral proteins can provide clues for binding sites. Nevertheless, this requires knowledge of the 3D structure. The ECD of the G protein essentially corresponds to an intrinsically disordered structure, [ ] as we have confirmed by an analysis using Alphafold3 (not shown). This makes it impossible to analyze the surface potential. However, it can be assumed that the flexibility of the structurally disordered ECD enables efficient interaction with negatively charged groups.

In contrast, the 3D structure of the ECD of the F protein has been experimentally elucidated ( Figure ). Recently, we have analyzed the surface potential of the crystal structure of the F ECD (PDB 5UDE). [ ] However, the latter is missing an essential domain (aa 75‐111) of the ECD which contains two stretches of positively charged amino acids. To take this domain into account, we modeled the 3D structure of the complete ECD sequence (Uniprot P03420 |FUS_HRSVA) using Alphafold3. As illustrated in Figure , the 3D structure aligns with the experimentally determined structure. The domain aa 75‐111 is depicted in magenta which could be described as intrinsically disordered structure. The positively charged amino acids of two stretches are shown as blue spheres. The sequence RARR (aa 81‐84) is exposed on the ECD surface, while the second sequence KKRKRR (aa 106‐111) is localized inside the trimer.

Figure shows the surface potential of the ECD. It is evident that there are multiple regions of positive surface potential that have the potential to function as binding sites for negatively charged groups. Notably, the exposed stretch RRAR contributes to a distinct region of positive potential. This sequence exhibits a striking similarity to a Cardin‐Weintraub motif, which has been implicated as a binding motif for heparan sulfate residues. [ , ]
sections.discussion:
In this work, using RAFT polymerization, we developed a series of high molecular weight amphiphilic copolymers ( MIACPs ) composed of ≈70% sulfated dendronized oligoglycerol methacrylate repeat units and ≈30% C11 aliphatic chain repeat units bearing terminal alkyl and carboxylate functionality. We also developed a homopolymer ( MIP ) of similar molecular weight, composed solely of sulfated dendronized methacrylate repeat units, without any C11 aliphatic functionality. The synthesized polymers were well characterized by 1 H NMR, SEC, zeta potential, and elemental analysis. Cryo‐EM of the MIACP s confirmed a single‐chain filamentous structure. SANS corroborated the filamentous structure. The strategic statistical distribution of ≈30% aliphatic chains led to the formation of a single‐chain filamentous structure instead of an aggregated morphology.

MIACPs demonstrated good biocompatibility and less anticoagulant activity, as confirmed by cell viability assays across various cell lines and by anti‐complementary assays, respectively. A plaque‐reduction assay confirmed that MIACPs inhibit hRSV infectivity in a sulfate‐dependent manner, with activity significantly superior to commercially available natural mucins such as PGM and BSM. The excellent inhibitory activity is further supported by the possible interaction of the ECD domain of hRSV with the polymers. The inhibitory activity of MIACPs is comparable to that of MIP , confirming that ≈70% sulfation is optimal for effective virus inhibition. Additionally, MIACPs exhibited virucidal activity, as demonstrated by dilution experiments. In contrast, MIP did not exhibit any virucidity. Therefore, the strategy to develop MIACPs is unique in that they not only destroy the virus through their virucidal functionality, but also maintain strong inhibitory activity, despite having only 70% electronegative functionality. In addition, surface analysis of hRSV F revealed multiple potential MIACPs engagement sites, suggesting a high genetic barrier to resistance mutation, as single‐point substitutions are unlikely to abrogate inhibition. In addition, RSV F is a highly conserved protein, which makes it an ideal target for antiviral and vaccine‐based interventions. [ , ] These findings demonstrate that combining high sulfation and virucidal functionality within a filamentous polymer architecture is an effective strategy for developing potent antiviral materials.

title: The prevalence and role of human respiratory syncytial virus in pediatric respiratory tract infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis of global data.
abstract: BackgroundHuman respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) is a major cause of respiratory tract infections in children worldwide. This study aims to describe the prevalence of hRSV in pediatric patients with respiratory tract infections, clarifying its association with such infections.MethodsWe analyzed studies from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science up to August 15, 2025, focusing on polymerase chain reaction-confirmed cases in children under 18 years. Data from 539 studies (584 datasets) were included. Pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model, with subgroup analyses by region, gender, age group, sampling time, type of respiratory disease, types of patient care, genotypes, and subtypes of hRSV. Odds ratios evaluated the association between hRSV infection and respiratory disease risk.FindingsThe global prevalence among 1,733,341 children was 21.6%, with the highest rates in children aged less than 6 months (33.8%), and inpatients (25.9%). Bronchiolitis showed the highest prevalence (56.9%). Prevalence declined over time, possibly due to the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. hRSV-A (55.7%) was more common than hRSV-B (44.3%). Infection significantly increased respiratory infection risk (odds ratio = 7.0), especially for lower respiratory infections.InterpretationhRSV is a key contributor to pediatric respiratory tract infections, with notable variations by age and region. Prevention strategies, including vaccines and monoclonal antibodies, are urgently needed for high-risk groups.FundingNone.

sections.abstract:
Human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) is a major cause of respiratory tract infections in children worldwide. This study aims to describe the prevalence of hRSV in pediatric patients with respiratory tract infections, clarifying its association with such infections.

We analyzed studies from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science up to August 15, 2025, focusing on polymerase chain reaction-confirmed cases in children under 18 years. Data from 539 studies (584 datasets) were included. Pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model, with subgroup analyses by region, gender, age group, sampling time, type of respiratory disease, types of patient care, genotypes, and subtypes of hRSV. Odds ratios evaluated the association between hRSV infection and respiratory disease risk.

The global prevalence among 1,733,341 children was 21.6%, with the highest rates in children aged less than 6 months (33.8%), and inpatients (25.9%). Bronchiolitis showed the highest prevalence (56.9%). Prevalence declined over time, possibly due to the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. hRSV-A (55.7%) was more common than hRSV-B (44.3%). Infection significantly increased respiratory infection risk (odds ratio = 7.0), especially for lower respiratory infections.

hRSV is a key contributor to pediatric respiratory tract infections, with notable variations by age and region. Prevention strategies, including vaccines and monoclonal antibodies, are urgently needed for high-risk groups.
