sections.other:
The human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the leading causes of acute lower respiratory tract infections (ALRTIs), especially among newborns, young children, immunocompromised patients, and older adults. , , The high incidence of RSV and the severe disease it causes in these groups are a pressing public health challenge, given the considerable global burden of hospitalizations and fatalities. Globally, RSV causes approximately 3.6 million hospitalizations worldwide annually, leading to nearly one hundred thousand deaths each year in children under five years of age. Six decades after its discovery, it is estimated that more than 80% of children under two years of age have been infected with RSV at least once, underscoring the importance of developing practical tools to prevent the associated complications of RSV infection, ranging from mild colds to severe outcomes such as pneumonia, neurocognitive disorders, or even death. , , , , , ,

Several approaches have been explored to prevent and treat RSV, including monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, and antivirals. Our group has developed and previously demonstrated that a recombinant vaccine based on a Mycobacterium bovis Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) expressing the RSV nucleoprotein (rBCG-N-RSV) is safe and immunogenic in mice and elicits a strong Th1-type cellular immune response against RSV that prevents disease, promotes viral clearance, and reduces virus-induced lung injury. , , ,

Importantly, because this vaccine platform is based on live recombinant attenuated BCG, preservation of immune responses against mycobacterial antigens has also been observed. Previous studies from our group demonstrated that vaccination with rBCG-N-RSV induces antibodies against both RSV- and BCG-derived antigens, supporting its potential as a dual-purpose vaccine platform. , ,

Compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is crucial for vaccine development, ensuring quality, safety, and reproducibility through stringent controls at every stage of production. In previous studies, the safety, immunogenicity, and capacity to prevent RSV disease of rBCG-N-RSV manufactured under GMP conditions were evaluated in mice, neonatal calves, and humans, validating its safety, immunogenicity, and protective profiles, initially characterized in laboratory experiments with the precursor non-GMP vaccine. , , , , , Administering a single dose of rBCG-N-RSV GMP with 1×10 5 colony-forming units (CFUs) was safe and provided protective immunity in BALB/c mice challenged with RSV. The vaccine did not cause adverse effects and reduced lung neutrophil infiltration. Additionally, ex vivo stimulation of T cells with RSV-derived antigens results in the secretion of IFN-γ and IL-17, indicating the capacity of rBCG-N-RSV to elicit a specific cellular immune response against the RSV N protein capable of halting viral replication. The vaccine also prevented long-term behavioral impairments caused by RSV infection, as evidenced by normal marble burying behavior observed six months after RSV infection in mice.

In addition, under controlled laboratory conditions and field conditions, the safety, immunogenicity, and capacity to confer protection of rBCG-N-RSV against bovine RSV (bRSV) and Mycobacterium bovis were evaluated in calves from 5 to 21 days of age. These assays were primarily supported by the high sequence similarity (93.3%) of the bRSV nucleoprotein relative to that of humans. In both studies, calves received the first dose subcutaneously (s.c.) in the left neck zone with 1 × 10 6 CFUs of rBCG-N-RSV. Two weeks after the primary vaccination, a booster dose was administered in the right neck zone with the same dose. In calves, the vaccine was found to be safe and well-tolerated, with no systemic or local adverse effects. , Concluding remarks of this study prove that the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine, under controlled conditions, induced a robust immune response mediated by cell proliferation and specific antibody production, including an antigen-specific activation profile in immune cells up to 180 days post-immunization under field conditions.

Furthermore, in 2017, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1 clinical trial ( ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03213405 ) with escalating doses was conducted in healthy volunteers aged 18 to 50 years to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of the GMP rBCG-N-RSV vaccine. This study demonstrated that the vaccine is safe and well-tolerated, inducing serum antibodies specific to BCG (anti-PPD) and the RSV N protein (anti-N-RSV), highlighting the vaccine’s dual role in humans. In addition, serum IgG from vaccinated patients showed increased in vitro RSV-neutralizing activity compared with the BCG-WT group, as measured by a plaque-reduction neutralization assay. These data suggest that immunization with rBCG-N-RSV GMP promotes the production of antibodies with greater neutralizing capacity compared with the wild-type BCG (BCG-WT) group.

Moreover, the vaccine induced IFN-γ and IL-2 production in ex vivo -stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and elevated the number of circulating PBMCs capable of producing perforin and granzyme B.

As outlined earlier, vaccine production under GMP standards requires stringent controls at every stage of manufacturing. These controls ensure safety, quality, reproducibility, and compliance with international regulatory frameworks. , , Despite ongoing development of recombinant BCG-based vaccines, there remains limited evidence on the long-term stability, the evolution of quality control parameters, and the preservation of biological activity of GMP vaccines during extended storage.

In this context, in the current work, we conducted a series of characterization and quality control assays on the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine manufactured under GMP conditions in the US and subsequently evaluated at the Hellenic Pasteur Institute (HPI) in Athens, Greece. This institute, bearing Good Laboratory Practice (GLP), GMP, and International Organization for Standardization (ISO) certifications, specializes in BCG. We measured potency, stability (at both the genomic and protein expression levels), sterility (microbiological safety), bacterial endotoxin, and physicochemical parameters, including humidity, pH, and vial integrity. Finally, in an in vivo assay using BALB/c mice, we assessed the safety profile of the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine and its capacity to protect against RSV infection, comparing this vaccine with unvaccinated mice and mice vaccinated with BCG-WT, which is routinely used as a vaccine against Mycobacterium tuberculosis .

Our data show that all evaluated parameters match the original specifications assessed in 2013 at the time of manufacture, underscoring the stability of the investigational product, the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine, manufactured under GMP conditions. These findings demonstrate that a GMP-manufactured recombinant BCG vaccine can maintain its physicochemical, microbiological, genomic, and immunological properties over time, supporting its feasibility for long-term storage and future clinical translation.

Initial colonies of wild-type BALB/c mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory, and mice were subsequently bred at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile facility. Female and Male mice aged 6–8 weeks were used for all experiments. Animals were housed in standard ventilated cages measuring 1422 × 522 × 1998 mm within a BSL-2 room under specific-pathogen-free conditions, maintained on a 12-h light/dark cycle, with controlled temperature and humidity, and provided with unrestricted access to food and water. The mice received environmental enrichment using autoclaved cardboard cones and absorbent paper. Mice were assigned to experimental groups according to the experimental design. Randomization into different experimental groups was performed once the mice entered the BSL-2 room, without distinction. No formal blinding procedures were used.

HEp-2 cells (American Type Culture Collection, ATCC; CCL-23; RRID: CVCL_1906) were used for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) propagation assays. Cells were cultured in Minimum Essential Medium (MEM) (Gibco; cat#61100-061) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Capricorn Scientific; cat#FBS-HI-12A), 100 U/ml penicillin-streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific; cat ·15140122) at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . HEp-2 cells tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.

RSV Long strain was used for all infection experiments. Recombinant BCG expressing RSV nucleoprotein (rBCG-N-RSV) vaccine produced under Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) standards, and commercial WT BCG vaccine for human use (Serum Institute of India), were used in in vivo assays. All viral and bacterial stocks were routinely tested for lipopolysaccharide and Mycoplasma contamination.

All experimental protocols were designed in accordance with the Sanitary Code of Terrestrial Animals of the World Organization for Animal Health (OIE, 24th Edition, 2015), the Chilean Animal Protection Law No. 20,800, and the ARRIVE guidelines. The animal protocols were reviewed and approved by the Scientific Ethical Committee for Animal and Environmental Care of the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile (Protocol number #210810006).

RNA was isolated and reverse-transcribed into cDNA as previously described. RT-qPCR was used to evaluate RNA copies of the RSV nucleoprotein gene using SYBR green kit and standard curves for qPCR generated using pTOPO-N-RSV or pTOPO-β-actin as templates. The data analyses were expressed as the number of RSV N transcripts per 5 x 10 3 copies of housekeeping gene β-actin. This assay quantifies RSV N transcripts and distinguishes viral genomic RNA.

Cellular infiltration and immune response during infection were measured by flow cytometry as described previously. Briefly, lung samples were disaggregated with collagenase IV, and red blood cells were lysed with ACK buffer (NH 4 Cl 0.15 M, KHCO 3 0.01 M, Na 2 EDTA 0.1 mM; pH 7.2–7.4). Then, lung samples were stained with a viability dye diluted in PBS buffer and flow cytometry antibodies in PBS-BSA (0.5%)-EDTA (2 mM) buffer (; ) and acquired using a BD FACSDiscover S8 Cell Sorter (BD Biosciences). Analyses were performed using FlowJo software version 10.10.7 to quantify the percentage of neutrophils (CD45 + CD11b + CD11c − Ly6G + ) and activated and effector T cells (CD45 + CD3 + CD4 + CD44 + and CD45 + CD3 + CD4 + CD69 + , respectively) relative to total CD45 + cells for neutrophils and to total CD4 + cells for activated and effector T cells.

Total anti-N-RSV antibodies were evaluated 3 days post-infection in serum samples using an in-house indirect ELISA, as described previously. Briefly, serum samples were diluted from a 20-fold dilution to a 2,560-fold dilution in PBS with the addition of 5% nonfat dry milk and incubated on a 96-well plate previously coated with 100 ng of recombinant RSV nucleoprotein (GenScript) per well. A goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) HRP-linked secondary antibody (ThermoFisher), diluted 1:2,000, was then used. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm after the addition of H 2 SO 4 using an 800 TM TS Absorbance Reader (BioTek).

Results are shown as the mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical significance was determined by Ordinary One-Way ANOVA and Two-Way ANOVA, followed by Dunnett’s and Tukey’s post-hoc tests, respectively, using GraphPad Prism 10 software (GraphPad Software, Inc.); a p -value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sample sizes are described in , including PBS/Mock, PBS/RSV, rBCG-N-RSV GMP/RSV, and BCG WT/RSV groups.
sections.results:
The manufacturing process of the drug substance (DS) began with the preparation of the master cell bank (MCB), followed by the working cell bank (WCB), both of which were produced under stringent GMP conditions. These processes were conducted in controlled and aseptic conditions to ensure microbiological purity and consistency. Subsequently, the DS was utilized to prepare the drug product (DP), the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine in vials. The manufacturer initially performed quality controls in 2010 for the MCB, WCB, and DS, and in 2013 for the DP. After these initial quality control assessments, the HPI in Athens, Greece, conducted a second round of GLP quality control testing on the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine in 2024. This evaluation aimed to assess the current quality conditions of the cell banks, DS, and vaccines in vials, gene characterization through PCR using specific primers (), protein expression, safety and immunogenicity of the vaccine.

For the MCB, the formulated bulk material pre-freeze underwent sterility tests using tryptic soy broth (TSB) and fluid thioglycollate medium (FTM), showing no microbial growth. Similarly, the bacteriostasis tests confirmed the absence of growth, proving the sterility of this intermediate ().

Additionally, potency testing for CFUs yielded 1.04 × 10 9 CFU/mL, which complies with the approval criteria (). Post-freeze analysis of the final vial material indicated no microbial contamination in sterility tests across samples at the storage rack’s beginning, middle, and end (). Potency tests revealed CFU values of 4.34 × 10 8 , 3.21 × 10 8 , and 7.78 × 10 8 CFU/mL, respectively, with bacterial purity demonstrated by colonies exhibiting a homogeneous appearance, confirming the MCB’s bacterial purity and potency ().

PCR was used to analyze the MCB’s genome, confirming the presence of intact DNA cassettes in all colonies. This, in turn, confirmed the presence of the recombinant plasmid carrying the N-RSV sequence (). Antigen expression matched that of the reference material, proving the subsequent expression of the RSV N protein. Furthermore, the material complied with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for freedom from virulent mycobacteria and excessive dermal reactivity in guinea pigs, proving its BCG identity ().

For the WCB, the formulated bulk pre-freeze material underwent sterility testing, with no microbial growth observed. Bacteriostasis tests similarly showed no growth, and potency tests measured 7.43 × 10 8 CFU/mL, which is within the expected range (). Final vial post-freeze sterility tests showed no growth across vials from the storage rack’s beginning, middle, and end (). Potency results were 7.56 × 10 8 , 9.32 × 10 8 , and 7.56 × 10 8 , CFU/mL, respectively, passing the acceptance criteria for this assay (). Furthermore, the WCB was tested for its bacterial purity, resulting in a uniform colony appearance. PCR identity tests verified the presence of intact DNA cassettes, indicating the presence of the recombinant plasmid carrying the N-RSV sequence (). Antigen expression remained equivalent to that of the accession bank material, confirming the expression of RSV N protein. The antibiotic sensitivity tests also confirmed susceptibility to first-line tuberculosis (TB) antibiotics, verifying the WCB’s BCG identity ().

For the bulk drug substance (BDS), the concentrated bulk pre-freeze material sterility tests yielded no growth, and potency testing demonstrated a CFU count of 2.88 × 10 9 CFU/mL (). Furthermore, bacterial purity was maintained, as evidenced by consistent colony morphology, as expected (). Post-freeze DS material retained sterility across all samples, with potency results of 4.79 × 10 9 , 5.11 × 10 9 , and 3.83 × 10 9 CFU/mL for the beginning, middle, and end of the storage rack samples, respectively (). Colony morphology remained homogeneous in bacterial purity tests, thus confirming the sterility of the sample ().

According to international acceptance criteria for sterility, potency, and recombinant antigen expression, including absence of microbial contamination in sterility assays, acceptable CFU recovery ranges for potency, and detectable recombinant antigen expression, the MCB, WCB, BDS, and DS met the specified requirements for each measurement. , Consequently, these materials passed the manufacturer’s quality control.

The lyophilized vial product underwent rigorous quality control tests to ensure compliance with the specified requirements. Sterility testing using TSB and FTM on vials from the storage rack’s beginning, middle, and end revealed no microbial growth (). Potency testing was conducted at the same intervals, yielding CFU/mL results of 4.79 × 10 9 (initial), 5.11 × 10 9 (intermediate), and 3.83 × 10 9 (final). Bacterial purity assessments from CFU plates demonstrated colonies with a uniform appearance ().

Additionally, PCR identity testing confirmed that the colonies contained an intact DNA cassette, and antigen expression was equivalent to the MCB. This finding confirmed the presence of the recombinant plasmid carrying the N-RSV sequence and its subsequent viral nucleoprotein expression ().

Furthermore, endotoxin levels were tested in two vials and were significantly below the acceptable threshold, with results at <0.500 Endotoxin Units (EU)/mL (). The pH of eight vials was 7.02, and a visual inspection of the finished lot confirmed the absence of vial irregularities and a uniform lyophilized cake (). Lastly, vial moisture content was measured in ten vials, yielding a result of 0.91% moisture content relative to the total weight of the vial content ().

Overall, the product met all the acceptance criteria according to international specifications, indicating that the final DP, the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine vials, passed the manufacturer’s quality controls.

DNA samples were obtained from the rBCG-N-RSV MCB, WCB, and BDS. The samples were undiluted, and 1/10 dilutions were re-analyzed by PCR at the HPI to confirm the presence of specific genetic markers and the recombinant plasmid. Amplification of the 16S rRNA gene, a conserved bacterial marker, produced clear products at the expected size of around 100 bp in all samples (01–08), confirming the identity of Mycobacterium spp. in each colony analyzed (A). Similarly, amplification of the IS6110 DNA sequence, specific to the genomes of M. bovis BCG strains, yielded PCR products of the expected size, approximately 157 bp, in all samples, further validating the presence of the N-RSV sequence (B).

A specific set of primers was used to amplify a 1,518 bp fragment spanning the N-RSV insert and a portion of the pMV361 plasmid backbone to verify the presence of the recombinant plasmid carrying the N-RSV sequence within rBCG-N-RSV. PCR products of the expected size were observed in samples 01–06 and 08. At the same time, no amplification was detected in sample 07 (undiluted rBCG-N-RSV BDS), suggesting that the target DNA was not amplified, as the diluted DNA sample (number 06) yielded the expected PCR product (C). The robust amplification observed in the samples indicates effective plasmid integration and stability through the years in the GMP recombinant BCG. These results confirm the genetic integrity of the GMP recombinant BCG vials and validate their use in downstream protein expression assays. Although PCR analysis confirmed the presence of the RSV insert sequence, future studies, including complementary molecular approaches, will be important for further assessing the integrity and stability of the insert.

Western blot analyses were used to assess the expression of the recombinant RSV N protein in the MCB, WCB, BDS, and DP of rBCG-N-RSV. Each assay was performed in duplicate to ensure reproducibility and reliability. Protein transfer efficiency was first evaluated through Ponceau S staining, which revealed consistent protein transfer across all samples (01–08), confirming successful electrophoresis and transfer steps (A).

First, SDS-PAGE analysis was conducted to separate the total proteins from each sample. The protein migration profiles showed multiple bands for all samples, evidencing proper protein extraction and integrity (B). A protein signal at approximately 45 kDa, corresponding to the expected molecular weight of the RSV N protein (44.4 kDa), was observed in all lanes, except the negative control lane. The positive control, consisting of purified RSV N protein with a His-tag, also produced a signal at 44.4 kDa, serving as a reference for the molecular weight of this protein (C).

Overall, the western blot results confirm the proper expression of RSV N protein in all the rBCG-N-RSV products tested. The consistent results across replicates highlight the robustness of the expression system and confirm the potential of GMP recombinant BCG as a stable vaccine platform.

To further evaluate the integrity of rBCG-N-RSV GMP, potency and sterility of the vaccine were retested. The samples evaluated are listed in . The results validate the sterility of the vials, as no bacterial growth was observed on the inoculated LB plates. The kanamycin stock used was confirmed to be functional, as the BCG-WT Danish strain seeded in 7H10 medium supplemented with kanamycin showed no growth. Additionally, the correct growth conditions were corroborated by the successful growth of M. smegmatis on 7H10 plates, confirming the reliability of the assay.

The CFU counts for the separar vaccine on day 21 showed an average count of 2.47 × 10 6 CFU/mL, calculated from countable plates at a 1/1,000 dilution. The standard deviations were 4.24 × 10 5 CFU/mL, and the log (CFU/mL) average was 6.40 (). These values align with the established reference value of ≥1.00 × 10 6 CFU/mL ().

Overall, these data confirm that the potency, stability, and sterility of the GMP rBCG-N-RSV vials have been maintained within the required specifications over time.

The quality control evaluation of rBCG-N-RSV and its intermediates confirmed compliance with all predefined specifications of pH, bacterial endotoxin test, vacuum leak test, and vial moisture (). For the MCB (lot 10-45M-001), the pH was 6.8, and endotoxin levels were <1.0 EU/mL, within the required ranges of pH 6–8 and <10.0 EU/mL, respectively (). Similarly, the WCB (lot 10-45W-001) displayed a pH of 6.66 and endotoxin levels <1.0 EU/mL, meeting the determined specifications (). The bulk DS (lot 10-45C-003) had a pH of 6.44 and endotoxin levels <1.0 EU/mL, passing quality control criteria (). The final lyophilized product in vials, rBCG N-RSV (reconstituted DP, lot 13-603F-001), also complied with all standards, with a pH of 6.44, vial moisture between 0.0% and 0.2% (specification: 0.0%–2%), no leaks under pressure, and endotoxin levels <1.0 EU/mL (). These results confirm the consistency and quality of the vaccine and its intermediates throughout the manufacturing process and storage conditions.

To evaluate the safety of the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine, mice were inoculated with the vaccine and monitored several times post-immunization for body weight loss, appearance, behavior, fever, and adverse effects at the injection site area. No altered clinical parameters were observed in rBCG-N-RSV-vaccinated mice until day 3 post-immunization, similar to the WT and placebo groups (data not shown). Efficacy was evaluated using an in vivo RSV challenge in immunized mice (). Infected mice vaccinated with rBCG-N-RSV GMP showed a significant reduction ( p < 0.0001) in the clinical score at 2 and 3 days post-infection (dpi) compared with the phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)/RSV group (A). Immunized mice with the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine lost significantly less weight compared with unimmunized mice at 3 dpi (). Moreover, the respiratory capacity, as measured by the enhanced paused (Penh) value, of the rBCG-N-RSV GMP/RSV group was significantly lower at days 2 and 3 dpi ( p < 0.0001) compared with the PBS/RSV group. Although the BCG-WT/RSV group did not show a significant improvement in respiratory capacity compared with PBS/RSV mice, a trend was observed (B). A similar protective effect of the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine was observed relative to the ratio of time to peak expiratory flow (Rpef) value, compared with the PBS/RSV group (C). This finding was accompanied by a significant reduction in lung viral load of these mice compared with the PBS/RSV group (D). Moreover, a significant increase in lung neutrophils was detected in the PBS/RSV group compared with uninfected mice at 3 dpi. At the same time, the rBCG-N-RSV GMP/RSV group exhibited significantly lower numbers of lung neutrophils compared with the PBS/RSV group (E). A non-significant decrease was also observed in the BCG-WT group for this parameter (E).

To evaluate cellular infiltration in the lungs associated with the adaptive immune response against RSV induced by vaccination, CD4 + T cell responses in the lungs were assessed by flow cytometry at 3 dpi. A significant increase of CD4 + T effector cells (A) and CD4 + CD69 + T activated cells was observed in rBCG-N-RSV GMP-immunized mice compared with PBS/RSV mice (B). No differences were observed in CD8 + T cells (). Moreover, total anti-N-RSV IgG levels in the serum were evaluated by the reciprocal value (base 10 logarithm) of total IgG at 3 dpi (C). Mice immunized with rBCG-N-RSV GMP exhibited significantly higher IgG titers compared with mice from the BCG-WT, PBS/RSV, and PBS/Mock groups (C).
sections.discussion:
The findings presented in this study underscore the significant stability of the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine, highlighting its potential as a considerable approach against RSV in newborns and infants. Our data demonstrate the successful integration of biotechnology development and rigorous quality control standards, offering a strong foundation for future vaccine development initiatives.

The rBCG-N-RSV vaccine has been shown to elicit robust antigen-specific CD4 + and CD8 + T cell responses in various animal models and humans, representing a promising and innovative solution for mitigating RSV-related disease during the winter season in the pediatric population. , The BCG platform, traditionally used to combat TB in several countries, was further enhanced through genetic engineering to express the RSV nucleoprotein, providing a cost-effective and scalable approach to address two global health challenges: TB and RSV infection.

Although rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccination did not completely abolish disease-associated parameters after RSV challenge, it significantly reduced viral burden, inflammatory cell infiltration, and lung pathology, indicating attenuated disease severity. This finding is relevant because protection against RSV may not necessarily require sterilizing immunity, but rather the prevention of severe lower respiratory tract disease. Nevertheless, the extent to which these reductions translate into clinically meaningful protection in humans remains to be determined in future clinical studies.

Notably, rBCG-N-RSV GMP is a lyophilized formulation, which significantly enhances its thermal stability during transportation and storage. This feature offers a significant advantage over other vaccines, such as inactivated or mRNA-based platforms, which typically require cold-chain logistics, thereby limiting their distribution in resource-constrained settings. , Compared with inactivated vaccines, which may elicit weaker cellular responses and often require multiple doses accompanied by adjuvants, rBCG-N-RSV GMP induces strong, robust antigen-specific CD4 + and CD8 + T cell responses, which are crucial for protection against RSV. , In contrast to mRNA vaccines, which can cause transient systemic adverse events, such as fever, fatigue, and myalgia, particularly in younger individuals, the rBCG-N-RSV GMP platform utilizes a live attenuated organism with a long-standing history of use in humans. This may result in a different reactogenicity and safety profile; however, further studies are needed to comprehensively evaluate these characteristics across age groups.

Notably, the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine offers several practical and immunological advantages, particularly for the pediatric population. First, it is designed as a single-dose intervention, which is particularly valuable in infant immunization schedules where minimizing clinic visits and simplifying logistics are essential. Second, the long history of BCG use in neonates, including in low- and middle-income countries, provides a well-established framework for integrating it into existing immunization programs. Additionally, the vaccine’s ability to induce both humoral immunity and cellular responses early in life may offer protection during the most vulnerable months of infancy, when RSV-related morbidity and mortality are highest. , , ,

A fundamental outcome of this study is the comprehensive validation of the vaccine’s quality and safety through adherence to GMP standards. The meticulous characterization of vaccine batches, including pH, residual moisture, vial integrity, and endotoxin levels, illustrates the importance of implementing stringent quality controls. Such guidelines, established by organizations such as the WHO, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the European Medicines Agency (EMA), provide the foundation for rigorous assessments of critical quality attributes to investigational medicinal products. For example, validated assays, such as the limulus amebocyte lysate (LAL) test, confirmed endotoxin levels well below the acceptable threshold, ensuring safety and compliance with international standards. Furthermore, the stability assessments conducted on the vaccine over the past decade reaffirm the formulation’s long-term viability, particularly critical for lyophilized formulations. Notably, the study’s use of advanced technologies aligns with International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) Q8 and Q9 guidelines, further enhancing batch-to-batch consistency.

Additionally, one of the most relevant results was the vaccine’s genetic stability. Over ten years of monitoring, no evidence of plasmid instability or loss of function was observed in the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vial samples, underscoring the robustness of rBCG-N-RSV GMP. This stability ensures consistent expression of the RSV nucleoprotein, an antigen previously associated with inducing cellular immune responses against RSV in animal models and humans. , Furthermore, the N protein is highly conserved across various circulating RSV strains, which enables this antigen to be highly immunogenic to the host, including cross-reactivity with the bRSV N protein. ,

Our preclinical safety and in vivo immunological efficacy results confirm that the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine, administered as a single dose of 1 × 10 5 CFU, is both safe and immunogenic. These results are consistent with those previously reported, including testing of the GMP vaccine in mice and newborn calves, and in a phase 1 clinical trial conducted in healthy adult male volunteers vaccinated with the same dose of rBCG-N-RSV. , , , , , Given the favorable safety and immunogenicity profiles observed with GMP rBCG-N-RSV, this vaccine is a promising candidate for further evaluation in pediatric populations.

Importantly, mice immunized with the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine exhibited lower clinical scores and less weight loss than the other groups after RSV challenge, as previously observed. , In addition, pulmonary function studies (measuring Penh and Rpef) conducted by whole-body plethysmography showed that rBCG-N-RSV-vaccinated mice exhibited less pulmonary damage after RSV challenge compared with unvaccinated mice. This finding, along with a lower lung viral burden, suggests that this vaccine decreases disease severity caused by RSV infection in mice.

Additionally, we observed a significant reduction in lung-recruited neutrophils in mice vaccinated with rBCG-N-RSV GMP compared with those in the PBS/RSV group. This outcome is relevant, given that RSV causes severe lung disease in humans, specifically in newborns, infants, and the elderly population. Moreover, the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine elicited effective cell-mediated immunity, characterized by the early recruitment of effector and activated CD4 + T cells in the lungs. Finally, we observed significantly higher anti-N-RSV IgG titers at the systemic level than in the other groups. These results suggest that the vaccine promotes a Th1-type cellular and humoral response against RSV infection in mice, consistent with previous reports from our research group. , , ,

The rBCG-N-RSV GMP preparations evaluated in this study are consistent and compliant with international regulatory standards. Furthermore, reproducible results across multiple preparations of rBCG-N-RSV GMP confirm the robustness of the manufacturing process and the vaccine’s stability, highlighting its quality, safety, immunogenicity, and reliability.

While the primary focus of the rBCG-N-RSV vaccine has been on the pediatric population due to RSV’s high burden in infants and young children, the favorable safety and immunogenicity profile observed in adult volunteers opens the possibility of studying this vaccine’s potential in other RSV-vulnerable populations, including pregnant women and the elderly. These characteristics may support a universal RSV vaccination strategy targeting multiple vulnerable groups.

The following steps involve conducting large-scale clinical trials to further evaluate the vaccine’s safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy across diverse populations and geographic regions. Regulatory alignment will be essential, particularly in countries targeted for future implementation. To this end, the formulation’s compliance with internationally recognized quality standards and its compatibility with immunization policies in low- and middle-income countries position rBCG-N-RSV GMP as a viable candidate for global RSV vaccination efforts.

This comprehensive validation underscores the potential of the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine for public health applications, particularly in regions with high RSV incidence and limited cold-chain infrastructure, thereby supporting its inclusion in national immunization programs.
sections.methods:
The rBCG-N-RSV Master Cell Bank (MCB) was generated in 2010 from a characterized recombinant Mycobacterium bovis BCG Danish 1331 clone expressing the RSV N protein, manufactured by IDT-Biologika (formerly the AERAS TB Vaccine Foundation, Rockville, MD, USA) under GMP conditions. The Working Cell Bank (WCB) was subsequently expanded from the MCB under GMP conditions. Bulk Drug Substance (BDS) was produced by large-scale expansion of the WCB, and the final Drug Product (DP) consisted of lyophilized vaccine vials formulated for storage and administration. The vaccine product (vials) was manufactured under GMP conditions in 2013. The following quality control tests, similar to the initial quality controls carried out at IDT-Biologika, were performed according to the manufacturer’s internal Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs): sterility, potency, bacterial purity, PCR identity, antigen expression, pH measurement, bacterial endotoxin, residual moisture, and inspection of vials and lyophilized cakes. MCB, WCB, and BDS are currently stored at −140 to −200 °C, and DP at −15 to - 25°C.

DNA was extracted from 5 μL of the rBCG-N-RSV MCB, WCB, and BDS vial stocks using the RBC BioSciences automated extractor MagCore. The RBC BioSciences 101 DNA extraction protocol was applied using the MagCore Genomic DNA Whole Blood Kit. To assess assay reproducibility and evaluate the potential presence of PCR inhibitors associated with high DNA concentrations or residual extraction components, 10 −1 dilutions of each original DNA template were prepared and analyzed under identical experimental conditions. Consistent amplification profiles between undiluted and diluted samples were considered indicative of the absence of inhibition.

Specific Mycobacterium and RSV genes were detected in rBCG-N-RSV DNA samples (undiluted and 1/10 diluted) by Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). The presence of 16S, IS6110, and pMV361-derived DNA sequences was detected with specific primers detailed in . Primers were resuspended to reach a concentration of 10 μM. The reaction included a positive control (rBCG-N-RSV vaccine DNA) and a negative control (genetic material from a human nasopharyngeal swab), to exclude potential buffer contamination with PCR templates and nonspecific amplification. The reaction mix was prepared using 1X PCRBIO HS Taq DNA polymerase Mix, 400 nM of each primer (forward and reverse), and nuclease-free water, following the manufacturer’s recommendations (PCRBIO HS Taq DNA Polymerase Protocol, PB10.21). DNA samples were added at a final concentration of 100 ng per reaction.

Proteins were extracted from rBCG-N-RSV GMP samples (BDS (Lot 10-45C-003), rBCG-N-RSV WCB (Lot 10-45W-001), rBCG-N-RSV MCB (Lot 10-45M-001), and DP rBCG-N-RSV (Lot 13-603F-001). Each vaccine vial was resuspended in 1 mL of PBS-Tween 80 0.05%, centrifuged at maximum speed for 15 min at 4°C, and washed with PBS-Tween 80 0.05% and sterile PBS 1X. The pellet was resuspended in protein extraction buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 5 mM EDTA, 0.6% SDS) containing one tablet of protease inhibitor (#11697498001, cOmplete protease inhibitor cocktail, Roche) and sonicated for 6 pulses at 18–20 kHz. After sonication and centrifugation, supernatants were recovered and stored at −80°C. Extracted proteins were quantified by Micro BCA Protein Assay Kit (#23235, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for Western Blot analyses. Extracted proteins from the wild-type BCG strain Danish (nonrecombinant) (BCG-WT) were used as a negative control, and RSV N recombinant purified protein was used as a positive control (#40823-V07E, Sino Biological Europe GmbH). The Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile facilitated negative and positive controls for HPI (BCG-WT protein concentration: 500 ng/μL; volume: 100 μL; N-RSV protein concentration: 1.78 mg/mL; volume: 20 μL). Furthermore, purified recombinant RSV nucleoprotein (His-Tag) (#40823-V07E, Sino Biological Europe GmbH) was also tested in western blot assays as a positive control. Reconstitution of the RSV N protein was done following the manufacturer’s recommendations. One RSV N protein (Sino Biological) vial was resuspended in 400 μL of sterile water to prepare a stock solution of 0.25 mg/mL. Aliquots of 20 μL were stored at −80 °C until use.

A total of 20 μL of each sample at 1.5 mg/mL concentration was loaded on SDS-PAGE gels (including loading buffer). The positive control was loaded in a volume of 20 μL at a concentration of 0.3 mg/mL. After sample loading, gels were run at 90 V for 30 min, followed by 120 V for 60 min in a running buffer. After the run, the resolved gels were transferred to Immobilon PVDF membranes (Merck Millipore) using the conventional wet transfer technique. The damp transfer involved soaking the PVDF membrane in methanol and transfer buffer before sandwiching it with the gel and then performing an electric transfer for 90 min at 300 mA at 4°C to minimize the heat generated by the electrodes. PVDF membranes were stained with Ponceau Staining (0.1% w/v) to confirm appropriate protein transfer. Membranes were blocked with 10% skim milk in PBS-Tween 20, 0.1% for 1 h and subsequently incubated with primary murine antibody anti-N-RSV clone 1E9/D1 (1:500 dilution) in 3% PBS-BSA overnight at 4°C. Membranes were then washed three times with PBS-Tween 20 0.1% to remove unbound antibodies and incubated with Peroxidase AffiniPure Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (H + L) (#115-035-003, Jackson Immuno Research) as the secondary antibody (1:10,000 dilution) in 3% PBS-BSA for 1 h at room temperature. Afterward, the membranes were rinsed three times in PBS-Tween 20 (0.1%) and then developed using chemiluminescent reagents (ECL Plus, Amersham Bioscience, Buckinghamshire, UK). Protein bands were visualized and captured using an imaging system (ChemiDoc MP System, Bio-Rad, Los Angeles, CA, USA).

The lyophilized rBCG-N-RSV vials were resuspended in 1 mL of PBS containing 0.05% Tyloxapol (PBS-Tyloxapol) using a 1 mL insulin syringe. Serial dilutions (1:10, 1:100, and 1:1,000) were prepared from the resuspended stock in PBS-Tyloxapol, with each dilution vortexed for 10 s to ensure homogeneity. 450 μL of PBS-Tyloxapol was added to each microtube to prepare the dilutions. For the 1/10 dilution, 50 μL from the resuspended stock was transferred to the microtube and vortexed for 10 s. For the 1/100 dilution, 50 μL from the 1/10 dilution was transferred to the respective microtube and vortexed for 10 s. For the 1/1,000 dilution, 50 μL from the 1/100 dilution was transferred to the respective microtube and vortexed for 10 s. The prepared microtubes were maintained on ice until they were plated for analysis. For each dilution (1/10, 1/100, and 1/1,000), 50 μL was plated in triplicate onto supplemented 7H10 agar (BD) or LB plates. Plates were incubated at 37°C and were examined after 48 h to assess potential contamination. After 21 days of incubation, colony counts were performed. The colony-forming unit (CFU) count was calculated using the following , in which a volume correction factor was used to extrapolate the colony count to the volume used.

The CFU count per dilution was averaged from triplicate samples, and the results were reported as CFU per milliliter (CFU/mL).

Bacterial endotoxin testing (BET) was performed using the Endosafe Portable Testing System (PTS), based on kinetic chromogenic detection of pyrogens using the kinetic D turbidimetric method. To begin, the operator entered the username and password, cartridge lot number, and calibration code. The sample ID, lot number, and corresponding dilution factor were then recorded. The diluted sample was loaded into the four reservoirs of the cartridge, where the reader mixed the sample with the Limulus Amebocyte Lysate (LAL) reagent in the sample wells and with the positive control in the Spike wells. The mixture was incubated at 37°C inside the reader, and after incubation, a chromogenic substrate was added to initiate the reaction. The optical density of the wells was measured and analyzed against a previously archived standard curve in the system. Assays were performed in duplicate, and results were averaged. The following acceptance criteria were established to validate the results: compensation coefficient of the archived curve > −0.980, coefficient of variation <25%, and peak recovery between 50% and 200%. LAL with a 1–0.01 EU/mL sensitivity was used to perform the analyses in two sample dilutions (1:100 and 1:1,000).

Using the vacuum leak test method, a container-closure integrity test was performed on rBCG-N-RSV GMP vials. First, a sample was placed in a tight evacuation test chamber with an external vacuum source. A suitable pump can quickly achieve a vacuum level between 50 and 100 microns. The vacuum system is isolated with the appropriate tools and allowed to stand for 15 to 30 min. The evacuation is considered complete if the micron level does not exceed 500 microns. If the container’s integrity under test has been compromised (i.e., leaking), pressure will be increased within the chamber. This may result in a) a coarse leak if the vacuum does not reach the preset level, b) a medium leak if the vacuum level drops below the preset level during the test, or c) a decay leak or microscopic leak if the vacuum level exceeds the decay limit during the test time.

The vials were allowed to reach room temperature before the process began. First, the pH meter was calibrated using buffer solutions with pH values of 7.00, 4.01, 10.01, and again 7.00. The sample was diluted to 1/100 and 1/1000 concentrations using water for injection. The vaccine and the dilution factor are transferred to Falcon vials. No vortex was used for mixing, but the tubes were gently shaken by hand. The electrode was dipped into the sample and gently shaken inside the tube to measure and record the pH value.

Moisture analysis was performed using a moisture analyzer based on the thermogravimetric principle. First, the instrument determines the initial weight of the sample. The sample is then subjected to rapid heating by the integral halogen drying unit, which causes the vaporization of the moisture present in the sample. During the drying process, the analyzer continuously measures the sample’s weight and displays the result in terms of percentage moisture content (%MC). Before starting the measurement, the samples were allowed to stand until they reached room temperature. The sample pan was placed flat on the stand, and the analyzer lid was closed, automatically setting the equipment to zero. The fiberglass pan was moistened with the sample, and the lid was closed again. The analyzer automatically initiated the drying and measurement process, reporting the moisture content as a percentage (%MC).

Six-to eight-week-old female and male BALB/c mice were evenly distributed across all experimental groups: PBS, BCG-WT, and rBCG-N-RSV GMP. Mice were housed in a BSL-2 climate-controlled environment animal facility at the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. rBCG-N-RSV vaccine produced under Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) standards, and commercial WT BCG vaccine for human use (Serum Institute of India), were used in in vivo assays. Lyophilized vials of both vaccines were reconstituted in sterile saline solution (sterile 0.9% sodium chloride). Mice were subcutaneously (s.c.) vaccinated in a conscious state with a single dose of vaccine in the interscapular region with 100 μL containing 1 × 10 5 CFU of rBCG-N-RSV GMP. As a control, a group was vaccinated in the same manner with BCG-WT. The vehicle used for all formulations was sterile saline solution, of which 100 μL was also administered only in the placebo group.

To evaluate the safety of the rBCG-N-RSV GMP vaccine, mice were monitored 30 min post-immunization and at 24, 48, and 72 h post-inoculation. A clinical score considering body weight loss, appearance, behavior, and adverse effects in the injection site was generated according to the physiological parameters of Mus musculus (), with zero related to typical clinical signs and higher than zero scores corresponding to altered clinical signs, with a maximum final score of 13.

To evaluate the clinical and immunological efficacy of the vaccine, mice were anesthetized in an isoflurane (Baxter; cat#218-082) chamber with 5% oxygen and intranasally challenged at 28 days post-vaccination with 1 × 10 6 PFU of RSV Long strain harvested from infected HEp-2 cells as previously described. , A non-infectious supernatant was used as a control and referred to as Mock. During the infection, mice were monitored daily, and visual disease parameters, including body weight loss, appearance, and behavioral alterations, were quantified and consolidated into a clinical score (). The sum of the infection-related clinical scores ranged from 0 (normal) to 10 (altered clinical signs) (). Additionally, whole-body plethysmography was performed to obtain the values of Enhanced Pause (Penh) and Ratio of time to peak expiratory time (Rpef). Finally, at 3 days post-infection, the mice were euthanized by lethal injection with ketamine (Richmond Vet Pharma; cat #144B) and xylazine (CENTROVET; cat #XI-49052201) (80 mg/kg and 4 mg/kg, respectively), and blood and lung samples were collected for the determination of immunogenicity and lung viral burden.

title: Introduction to Respiratory Syncytial Virus.
abstract: Human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a significant human pathogen in infants, young children, older adults, and the immunocompromised. Over the last decade, many important mechanisms contributing to RSV infection, replication, and disease pathogenesis have been revealed, and a body of information has accumulated regarding how RSV proteins modulate molecular signaling and immune responses to infection. In this chapter, we briefly introduce RSV replication and pathogenesis and summarize the state of the RSV vaccine and antiviral compounds in the clinical stages of development. This chapter frames the features of this book and the molecular methods used for understanding RSV interaction with the host.

title: Targeting RSV-neutralizing B cell receptors with anti-idiotypic antibodies.
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes lower respiratory tract infections with significant morbidity and mortality at the extremes of age. Vaccines based on the viral fusion protein are approved for adults over 60, but infant protection relies on passive immunity via antibody transfer or maternal vaccination. An infant vaccine that rapidly elicits protective antibodies would fulfill a critical unmet need. Antibodies arising from the VH3-21/VL1-40 gene pairing can neutralize RSV without the need for affinity maturation, making them attractive to target through vaccination. Here, we develop an anti-idiotypic monoclonal antibody (ai-mAb) immunogen that is specific for unmutated VH3-21/VL1-40 B cell receptors (BCRs). The ai-mAb efficiently engages B cells with bona fide target BCRs and does not activate off-target non-neutralizing B cells, unlike recombinant pre-fusion (preF) protein used in current RSV vaccines. These results establish proof of concept for using an ai-mAb-derived vaccine to target B cells hardwired to produce RSV-neutralizing antibodies.

sections.other:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common seasonal pathogen that generally causes mild respiratory symptoms in adults but can cause serious lower respiratory tract infection in infants and the elderly. RSV is responsible for ∼60,000 recorded in-hospital deaths annually in children under 5 , and accounts for a substantial hospitalization burden in infants as well as aged adults. , , In 2023, two RSV vaccines, AREXVY (GSK) and ABRYSVO (Pfizer), were approved for use in adults over 60 years of age. Both are protein subunit vaccines based on the viral fusion protein (F). F can adopt a metastable pre-fusion (preF) state and a highly stable post-fusion state (postF). Most neutralizing antibodies in the serum of infected individuals map to preF, highlighting its importance for vaccine design. , Epitope mapping of anti-F monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) has identified distinct antigenic sites termed Ø–V. Some sites, such as Ø, III, and V, are only present on preF, while the others are present on both conformations. , , , , , , , , Advances in antigen engineering have led to the development of stabilized preF immunogens, which form the basis for AREXVY and ABRYSVO.

Despite these important advances in RSV vaccine development, a vaccine for use in infants remains a critical unmet need. Prophylaxis for infants currently relies on passive immunity. Since 1998, the site II-directed mAb palivizumab, under the commercial name of SYNAGIS (Sobi), has been available for high-risk infants. , More recently, the extended half-life site Ø-specific mAb nirsevimab, under the commercial name Beyfortus (Sanofi), has been approved for all infants under 8 months of age entering their first RSV season. ,

As an alternative prophylactic strategy, ABRYSVO is approved for use in pregnant individuals in the final month of gestation with the goal of protecting infants from birth through the first 6 months of age through transplacental transfer of protective antibodies. , Prophylactic strategies afford transient protection against lower respiratory tract disease in infants but are imperfect solutions because protection wanes as these antibodies are cleared. ABRYSVO is only administered after 32 weeks of gestation, providing a short window for implementation, and this timing may not be congruent with the seasonal pattern of RSV transmission. High costs prohibit the widespread use of passively transferred mAbs, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. While these prophylactic strategies are welcome tools for the prevention of RSV in the infant population, the development of an active vaccine that can rapidly establish durable protection in infants and toddlers could overcome the limitations of passive immunity.

Prevention of severe RSV infection in infants with palivizumab and nirsevimab suggests that neutralizing antibodies targeting F are important for protection against RSV-mediated disease in infants and indicates that a vaccine should seek to elicit high neutralizing antibody titers. However, raising protective antibodies in infants has historically been fraught with challenges. The earliest RSV vaccine was based on formalin-inactivated whole virus in which F preferentially adopted the postF conformation. Unfortunately, this vaccine formulation led to enhanced respiratory disease in infants that required hospitalization and, in some cases, led to death. This manifestation has been attributed in part to non-neutralizing anti-F antibodies. , , Due to this failure, infant RSV vaccine research has proceeded cautiously.

In addition to issues with formulation, infant vaccination faces unique immunological challenges. For example, the infant immune system is inefficient at generating somatically mutated antibodies, , which are often required for high-affinity binding and/or neutralizing potency. Moreover, maternal antibodies can interfere with de novo immune responses in infants. Maternal antibodies can bind to vaccine antigens and suppress the infant response to immunization, which can further complicate vaccination strategies. , Indeed, infants tend to elicit higher neutralizing titers following RSV infection when maternal antibody levels are low. ,

Characterization of mAbs elicited by RSV infection in infants has provided critical insight into their humoral responses. The isolation of F-reactive mAbs from infected infants has identified a class of potently neutralizing mAbs derived from the same antibody variable heavy (VH)- and variable light (VL)-chain genes: VH3-21 and VL1-40. These VH3-21/VL1-40 mAbs mapped to an epitope on antigenic site III present only on preF , and remarkably, were able to potently neutralize RSV without undergoing affinity maturation.

The crystal structure of an unmutated neutralizing VH3-21/VL1-40 mAb in complex with preF revealed that the heavy-chain (HC) contacts are primarily made with complementarity-determining HC region 1 (CDRH1) and CDRH2, which are chromosomally encoded by VH3-21. Similarly, the light chain (LC) contacts are made by complementarity-determining LC region 1 (CDRL1) and CDRL2 encoded by the VL1-40 gene. In addition to infected infants, B cells expressing F-reactive VH3-21/VL1-40 B cell receptors (BCRs) were also found in cord blood and in naive B cells from healthy adults. Collectively these data indicate that unmutated VH3-21/VL1-40-derived antibodies are a public clonotype that is pre-configured to bind to and neutralize RSV, establishing them as an attractive, ubiquitous vaccine target.

We have demonstrated previously that vaccine antigens derived from anti-idiotypic mAbs (ai-mAbs) raised against unmutated precursor versions of neutralizing antibodies against HIV-1 and influenza could activate B cells in vitro and generate robust on-target B cell and serum responses using knockin mice in vivo . , , , , Given that germline-encoded VH3-21/VL1-40 antibodies are preconfigured to neutralize RSV without the need for somatic mutation, we reasoned that they may be readily elicited by an anti-idiotype vaccine. To this end, we raised ai-mAbs by immunizing mice with preF-reactive, unmutated VH3-21/VL1-40 RSV-neutralizing mAbs. By integrating binding, B cell sorting, and structural analysis, we identified two ai-mAb candidates. One bound to VH3-21 HCs, and the other bound to VL1-40 LCs, both with high affinity and specificity. From these, we developed a bispecific ai-mAb that combined the binding properties of both. The bispecific ai-mAb was able to select for B cells capable of producing RSV-neutralizing antibodies from a diverse pool of naive B cells ex vivo and activate B cells engineered to express relevant target BCRs in vitro. These results provide proof of concept that an anti-idiotype vaccine has the potential to elicit RSV-neutralizing antibodies by specifically targeting and activating B cells expressing VH3-21/VL1-40 BCRs that are hardwired to neutralize RSV.

PBMC were collected from adults without HIV who were recruited at the Seattle HIV Vaccine Trials Unit (Seattle, Washington, USA) as part of the study “Establishing Immunologic Assays for Determining HIV-1 Prevention and Control”, also referred to as Seattle Assay Control (SAC) Cohort. All participants signed informed consent, and the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (Seattle, Washington, USA) Institutional Review Board approved the SAC protocol (FHIRB0005567) prior to study initiation. Donors were selected randomly and no considerations were made for age or sex.

All cell lines were incubated at 37°C in the presence of 5% CO 2 and were not tested for mycoplasma contamination. 293-6E cells (human female) and suspension adapted 293T cells (human female) were maintained in Freestyle 293 media (ThermoFisher Cat# 12338018) with gentle shaking. DG-75 cells (human male) were maintained in RPMI (Corning Cat# 15-040-CV) + 10% FBS, 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (cRPMI). HEp-2 (human male) and Vero cells (African green monkey) were maintained in DMEM (Gibco Cat#11965-092) + 10% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin (cDMEM).
