sections.methods:
Monoribonucleotides were obtained from Trilink Biotechnologies or Sigma-Aldrich. Synthetic oligonucleotides and genes were synthesized by Sigma-Aldrich and GenScript Biotech, respectively. GpppA, GpppG, and m 7 GpppG were obtained from New England Biolabs. Guanosine(5′)tetraphospho(5′)guanosine (GppppG) was purchased from BIOLOG Life Science Institute (Germany). [α- 32 P]GTP and [α- 32 P]CTP (3000 Ci/mmol) were from PerkinElmer/Revvity. [α- 32 P]GDP was prepared from [α- 32 P]GTP with the nucleoside 5′-triphosphatase (NTPase) activity of the vaccinia virus capping enzyme (Cellscript) as described previously []. 5′-Triphosphorylated oligo-RNAs were synthesized with T7 RNA polymerase from partially double-stranded oligo DNA templates essentially as described previously [, ]. 5′-Diphosphorylated oligo-RNAs were prepared from 5′-triphosphorylated oligo-RNAs with the RNA 5′-triphosphatase (RTPase) activity of the vaccinia virus capping enzyme as described previously []. Capped RNAs were generated with the vaccinia virus capping enzyme in the presence or absence of VP39 (2′- O -MTase) (Cellscript) using [α- 32 P]GTP and 5′-pppGGGAC as substrates as described previously []. 32 P-Labeled 5′-hydroxyl ApC and GpC were generated as described previously [].

JNJ-8003 [], AVG-233 [], and PC786 [] were purchased from MedChemExpress. BI-D [] (CAS number, 851658–10-1; RSV L-protein-IN-1) was synthesized by MedChemExpress. All the compounds were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).

The codon-optimized genes (GenScript Biotech) for the expression of P and L (GenBank accession numbers: AAX23990 and AAX23996 , respectively) of HRSV (strain Long) in insect cells were subcloned into the pFastBac-1 vector (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and its derivative (encoding a C-terminal GT SEPEA sequence, C-tag [] underlined), respectively, for the Bac-to-Bac baculovirus expression system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Site-directed mutagenesis was carried out using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase and KLD Enzyme Mix (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Recombinant baculoviruses were generated using the pFastBac plasmids according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific). ExpiSf9 cells (1.5–2.5 × 10 8 cells; Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a 125 ml flask containing 30 ml of ExpiSf CD Medium with ExpiSf Enhancer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were co-infected with baculoviruses expressing C-tagged L [wild-type (WT) or mutant] and non-tagged P, each at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1, and cultured at 27°C with shaking at 130 rpm for 3 days. The infected cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and then lysed in 5 packed cell volumes of buffer A [50 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.5), 1 mM 1,4-dithiothreitol (DTT), 10% glycerol] containing 150 mM NaCl, 1% (w/v) Triton X-100, and 1 × Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on ice for 10 min. The lysate was centrifuged at 15 000 × g for 10 min, and the resulting supernatant was recovered. After adding NaCl to the clarified lysates to a final concentration of 300 mM, they were incubated with ∼10 µl of CaptureSelect C-tagXL resin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 4 h at 4°C with rotation. After washing the resin with 500 µl of buffer A containing 1 M NaCl and 0.05% Triton X-100 three times, the L–P complexes were eluted from the resin with 10 µl of buffer A containing 2 M MgCl 2 four times. The eluates were combined and dialyzed against buffer B [20 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8.0), 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM MgCl 2 , 1 mM DTT, 10% glycerol] twice. After centrifugation of the dialysates at 15 000 × g for 5 min, the resulting supernatants were collected and stored in small aliquots at −80°C. Protein concentrations were determined by a Bradford protein assay (Bio-Rad) using bovine γ-globulin as a standard. Proteins were analyzed by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) followed by staining with One-Step Blue (Biotium).

In vitro capping was carried out with partially purified L–P complexes (0.2 µg), 0.25 µM [α- 32 P]GDP or [α- 32 P]GTP (5 × 10 2 cpm/fmol), and 5 µM pppGGGAC (or other RNAs shown in figures) in 10 µl of a capping buffer [25 mM 2-( N -morpholino)ethanesulfonic acid-NaOH (pH 5.8), 0.5 mM MnCl 2 , 2 mM DTT, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 0.1 mg/ml bovine serum albumin (BSA)] [] for 2 h at 30°C. RNA substrates were preheated at 65°C for 2 min and then immediately chilled on ice prior to the assays. After the capping reactions, the reaction mixtures were treated with calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase (CIAP, Thermo Fisher Scientific) as described previously []. RNA products were extracted from the reaction mixtures, precipitated with ethanol, and digested with nuclease (Nase) P1 (Sigma-Aldrich) as described previously []. When indicated, the products were digested with Nase P1 and Cap-Clip acid pyrophosphatase (Cellscript) followed by CIAP as described previously [, ]. The resulting digests were analyzed along with external and/or internal standards by thin layer chromatography (TLC) on a polyethyleneimine (PEI) cellulose plate (Millipore Sigma) followed by autoradiography as described previously []. The 32 P radioactivity in excised regions of the TLC plate corresponding to the migration positions of the cap structures ( e.g . GpppG, GppppG, and GpppA) was measured by liquid scintillation counting. The radioactivity value obtained from the enzyme-minus control, which represents the background signal, was subtracted from that of each sample. The amounts of the cap structures formed during the reactions were calculated based on specific radioactivities of [α- 32 P]GDP or [α- 32 P]GTP as described previously []. All the experiments were repeated three times. Graphs were prepared using the GraphPad Prism software (version 11). Statistical analyses were performed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using the GraphPad Prism software. When the effects of compounds on RNA capping were examined, all the reaction mixtures included DMSO at a final concentration of 2%. Absolute 50% inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) values were determined by fitting experimental data to the four-parameter logistic equation. The data represent the means and standard deviations of three independent experiments.

Partially purified L–P complexes (0.3 µg) were incubated with pppGGGAC (<1.5 × 10 4 cpm/pmol, labeled with [α- 32 P]CMP) in the capping buffer at 30°C for 15 min. Putative L–pRNA intermediates were analyzed by 7.5% SDS-PAGE followed by autoradiography as described previously [].

In vitro transcription was performed with partially purified L–P complexes (0.1 µg), containing the WT or mutant L, 2 mM ATP or GTP, 20 µM [α- 32 P]CTP (AC synthesis, 0.7–1 × 10 3 cpm/pmol; GC synthesis, 35–50 cpm/pmol), and 1 µM oligo-RNA template [ Le (−)1–10, 5′- UUU UUC GCG U, Tr (+)1–10, 5′- UUU UUC UCG U, or other RNAs shown in figures] in 25 µl of a transcription buffer [50 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8.0), 5 mM MgCl 2 , 40 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT, 0.2 mg/ml BSA] for 1 h at 30°C. RNA products were extracted from the reaction mixtures, precipitated with ethanol, treated with CIAP, and analyzed by 20% urea-PAGE followed by autoradiography as described previously [].

In vitro cap methylation was performed with partially purified L–P complexes (0.15 µg), 0.1 mM SAM, and 2 nM 32 P-labeled GpppGGGAC or m 7 GpppGGGAC (1–2 × 10 2 cpm/fmol) in 10 µl of a methylation buffer [50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.9), 2 mM DTT, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 0.1 mg/ml BSA] for 2 h or the indicated periods at 30°C. RNA substrates were preheated as described above. After the methylation reactions, RNA products were extracted from the reaction mixtures, precipitated with ethanol, and digested with Nase P1 as described previously []. The digests were analyzed by PEI-cellulose TLC followed by autoradiography [].

Western blotting was performed using the SuperSignal West Dura Extended Duration Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) as essentially described by Ogino et al . []. C-tagged L was detected using CaptureSelect HRP anti-C-tag conjugate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 7 303 072 100, 1:1 000 dilution). P was detected using mouse anti-respiratory syncytial virus phosphoprotein antibody (Abcam, ab94965, 1:1 000 dilution) and horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 32 430). Immunoblots were imaged using the Azure Sapphire Biomolecular Imager.
sections.results:
HRSV mRNAs transcribed from internal genes are capped with the cap 1 structure, whereas the anti-genomic RNA and the leader RNA, synthesized from positions 1 and 3, respectively, at the 3′-terminal Le region [], are considered to be uncapped (Fig. ). By analogy with the rhabdoviral PRNTase domain, we hypothesized that the putative PRNTase domain of HRSV L preferentially caps 5′-triphosphorylated pre-mRNAs in a sequence-specific manner. To design RNA substrates for the putative HRSV PRNTase domain, we first analyzed the 5′-end sequences of 10 HRSV mRNAs. The mRNA-start sequences share a consensus motif: 5′-GGGRCAAA (R = G/A) (Fig. ), with nine of them beginning with 5′-GGGGCAAA. However, to reduce the number of tandem G residues—which may form G-quadruplex structures—in the substrates, we synthesized a 5′-triphosphorylated oligo-RNA containing the HRSV L -mRNA-start sequence (GGGAC).

In rhabdoviruses, separately expressed L and P can be purified and reconstituted into transcriptionally active RdRp complexes [, , ]. In contrast, HRSV L requires its cognate P for its efficient expression and/or stability []. Thus, HRSV L tagged with the C-tag was co-expressed with non-tagged P in insect cells co-infected with baculoviruses containing respective codon-optimized genes, and their complex was affinity-purified using CaptureSelect C-tagXL resin (Fig. ). Western blotting with anti-C-tag antibody detected full-length L (∼250 kDa) and its degradation products in the purified sample (Fig. ). Furthermore, Western blotting using anti-P antibody identified the 35-kDa protein copurified with L as P (Fig. ).

We performed oligo-RNA capping with the purified L–P complex using [α- 32 P]GDP as a pRNA acceptor under the conditions for VSV L [] (Fig. , left). The resulting capped RNA products were digested with Nase P1 and their digests were analyzed by PEI-cellulose TLC followed by autoradiography. The L–P complex generated a Nase P1-resistant product, which co-migrated with GpppG, when incubated with pppGGGAC (Fig. , right, lane 2), but not with ppGGGAC (lane 3). On the other hand, the enzyme produced a product, which co-migrated with GppppG, when incubated with [α- 32 P]GTP and pppGGGAC (lane 4). Both the former (Fig. , lane 2) and latter (lane 7) Nase P1-resistant products were resistant to CIAP (lanes 3 and 8, respectively), whereas they were similarly digested with Cap-Clip acid pyrophosphatase into GMP (lanes 4 and 9, respectively). Furthermore, their digestion with Cap-Clip and CIAP generated inorganic phosphate (P i ) (lanes 5 and 10). Therefore, we concluded that the HRSV L–P complex produced GpppG and GppppG caps on the RNA using GDP and GTP as pRNA acceptors, respectively. Consistent with this observation, the HRSV L–P complex exhibited significantly lower GTPase activity—required to produce GDP—than VSV L under the capping conditions (). These results therefore indicate that HRSV L efficiently transfers pRNA to GTP without hydrolyzing it. In contrast, VSV L preferentially uses GDP (generated from GTP) rather than GTP as the pRNA acceptor and produces GpppA and GppppA as the major and minor products, respectively, when incubated with [α- 32 P]GTP and pppAACAG (the VSV mRNA-start sequence) [].

To demonstrate that the putative PRNTase domain in HRSV L is responsible for the capping activity, we generated various single-point mutants of L complexed with P (). As expected, the capping activity was abolished by a single-point mutation in the putative active site of the PRNTase domain (H1338R; Fig. , lane 4), but not by mutations in the RdRp (D811A; lane 3) or 2′- O -MTase active site (K1973R; lane 5). We also investigated the RNA substrate specificity of the HRSV PRNTase domain in RNA capping. Unexpectedly, in addition to pppGGGAC (Fig. , lane 2), HRSV L capped pppRNAs with various sequences, including pppGCGAC (lane 4), pppGGCAC (lane 5), pppGCGAA (lane 9, the HRSV leader RNA-start sequence from position 3), and pppAACAG (lane 10). Although pppGGGGC (lane 3, the HRSV major mRNA-start sequence), pppGGGCC (lane 6), pppGGGCA (lane 7), and pppACGCG (lane 8, the HRSV anti-genome-start sequence from position 1) exhibited little or no substrate activity, they may potentially form duplex structures that prevent access to the PRNTase active site. Therefore, in contrast to rhabdovirus PRNTase domains [, ], the HRSV PRNTase appears to use non-structured RNAs initiated with a 5′-triphosphorylated purine nucleoside as pRNA donors, with no strict sequence specificity.

We examined whether HRSV L forms a covalent enzyme–pRNA (L–pRNA) intermediate for the unconventional RNA capping reaction as reported for rhabdovirus Ls [–]. When the HRSV L–P complex was incubated with pppGGGAC labeled with [α- 32 P]CMP, an SDS-resistant 32 P-labeled 250-kDa band comigrating with L was generated (Fig. , lane 2). In contrast, such a high-molecular weight protein band was not observed when incubated with 32 P-labeled ppGGGAC (lane 3) or [α- 32 P]CTP (lane 4). Furthermore, the H1338R mutation (Fig. , lane 4), but not the D811A mutation (lane 3), diminished the formation of the 32 P-labeled product with pppGGGAC. We confirmed that the purity of these mutant L–P complexes was similar to that of the WT complex (Fig. ). These results strongly suggest that L forms a putative L–pRNA intermediate for capping using the H1338 residue as a nucleophile.

We also established in vitro RNA synthesis initiation (first phosphodiester bond formation) assays for the HRSV L–P complex using an oligo-RNA containing the 3′-terminal 10 residues of the genomic Le region [ Le (−)1–10] (Fig. ). In vitro transcription was performed with [α- 32 P]CTP in the presence of either ATP or GTP as the initiator nucleotide to synthesize AC (Fig. , lane 2) or GC(G) (Fig. , lane 2), respectively. As described for the VSV initiation assay [], transcripts and remaining substrates were digested with CIAP prior to 20% urea-PAGE, which can separate 5′-hydroxyl dinucleotides labeled with [α- 32 P]CMP at their 3′-ends from 32 P-labeled P i derived from [α- 32 P]CTP. The HRSV L–P complex generated GC and GCG potentially using the C3-G4-C5 sequence in Le (−)1–10 as the template region. Note that 5′-hydroxyl trinucleotides migrate faster than 5′-hydroxyl dinucleotides [].

Unexpectedly, the U1A (Fig. , lane 3) or G2A (lane 4) mutation in Le (−)1–10 moderately reduced AC synthesis activity, whereas the C3A (lane 5) or G4A (lane 6) mutation significantly diminished it. In addition, Le (−)1–10 containing the U1A/C3A double mutation retained weak template activity (lane 8), whereas the G2A/G4A template was inert (lane 9). On the other hand, the U1A (Fig. , lane 3) or G2A (lane 4) mutation in Le (−)1–10 exhibited little effect on GC(G) synthesis, whereas either the C3A (lane 5) or G4A (lane 6) mutation abolished it. The C5A mutant template produced only the GC product (lane 7), suggesting that the C5 residue is required as part of the template for GCG trinucleotide synthesis. These results suggest that AC is synthesized more efficiently from the internal C3-G4 sequence than from the terminal U1-G2 sequence, even though the C3 residue in the template mismatches the first A residue of the dinucleotide transcript (Fig. , left and middle). On the other hand, GC(G) is suggested to be synthesized exclusively from the internal C3-G4(-C5) sequence (right). As expected, the D811A RdRp mutation in L completely abolished both AC (Fig. , lane 3) and GC(G) (Fig. , lane 3) synthesis, whereas neither the H1338R nor K1973R mutation did (Fig. and E, lanes 4 and 5).

We performed site-directed mutagenesis of HRSV L to investigate whether PRNTase motifs A–E (Fig. ) [] are required for RNA capping. In addition to the previously mentioned H1338R mutation, single mutations (H1338A, R1339H, and R1339A; Fig. , lanes 3–5) and a double mutation (H1338R and R1339H, referred to as HR-RH; lane 6) in motif D impaired the RNA capping activity of L. However, some of these mutations ( e.g . H1338A, R1339H, and R1339A) also reduced the RNA synthesis initiation activities [AC and GC(G) synthesis] of L (Fig. and D, lanes 3–5). In contrast, the G1218A mutation in motif A completely abrogated both the PRNTase and RdRp activities (Fig. , lane 3), suggesting that this mutation may affect the structural integrity of the RdRp-PRNTase superdomain. Unexpectedly, neither the G1264 nor T1267 residue in motif B was required for the capping activity or RNA synthesis initiation activities (lanes 4 and 5), although the G1264A mutation markedly reduced AC synthesis activity (Fig. , lane 4). The W1297A mutation in motif C and the F1385A mutation in motif E abolished RNA capping activity and also reduced RNA synthesis initiation activities (Fig. , lanes 6 and 8). Remarkably, the Q1386A mutation in motif E impaired RNA capping but had little effect on RNA synthesis initiation (lane 9). Thus, the H1338R, HR-RH, and Q1386A mutations are ideal for specifically abolishing the PRNTase activity.

In alpharhabdoviruses such as VSV, a large loop structure—referred to as the priming-capping loop and flanked by PRNTase motif B (Fig. )—extends into the RdRp active site cavity [] and governs both terminal de novo initiation at the genomic Le promoter and capping during the intermediate formation step []. The tryptophan residue (W1167 in VSV) and the TxΨ motif (T1161-x-I1163 in VSV), both conserved in the alpharhabdoviral priming-capping loop, are critical for terminal de novo initiation and capping, respectively [] (Fig. , upper). In contrast, the HRSV counterpart of the VSV priming-capping loop is located near the PRNTase active site in the apo structure of L [] (Fig. ). Notably, the consensus amino acid sequence of the pneumovirus counterparts is entirely distinct from that of the alpharhabdoviral priming-capping loops (Fig. , lower). However, the functional role of the pneumovirus counterpart remains incompletely understood.

A previous study [] showed that alanine substitutions at P1261 and W1262—rather than at Y1276, which was originally proposed as the HRSV counterpart of VSV W1167 due to its aromatic nature []—reduce RNA synthesis initiation at both terminal and internal initiation sites. We validated the effects of these mutations on capping and RNA synthesis initiation using our assay systems (Fig. ). The P1261A mutation reduced both AC (Fig. , lane 4) and GC(G) (Fig. , lane 4) synthesis, but not capping (Fig. , lane 4). In VSV, Y1152 in PRNTase motif B is thought to play a structural role, as an alanine substitution at this residue abolishes both transcription and capping []. Consistently, an alanine substitution at W1262—the HRSV counterpart of VSV Y1152—diminished all these activities (Fig. , lane 5), suggesting that it may affect the folding of the entire RdRp-PRNTase superdomain. On the other hand, the Y1276A mutation moderately affected all these activities (lane 6). Remarkably, valine could functionally substitute for P1261 almost completely in capping (Fig. , lane 3) and GC(G) synthesis (Fig. , lane 3), and partially in AC synthesis (Fig. , lane 3), suggesting that the nonpolar hydrophobic nature—rather than the non-aromatic cyclic structure—of the side chain of P1261 is important for these activities. The W1262Y mutation rather enhanced capping activity (Fig. , lane 4) but exhibited AC (Fig. , lane 4) and GC(G) (Fig. , lane 4) synthesis activities comparable to those of the WT enzyme (Fig. and I, lane 2), suggesting that the aromatic nature of W1262 is structurally important for both capping and RNA synthesis initiation. Notably, the P1261V and W1262Y L mutants partially and almost fully supported gene expression from a mini-genome in cultured cells (, see Supplementary results). We also investigated the effects of alanine substitutions at each residue within the pneumovirus-specific QEKK sequence (residues 1268–1271), located immediately downstream of motif B (Fig. , lower), on capping and RNA synthesis initiation (Fig. ). The Q1268A mutation had little or no effect on either activity (Fig. , lane 3). On the other hand, the E1269A, K1270A, and K1271A mutations significantly and moderately reduced capping (Fig. , lanes 4–6) and AC synthesis (Fig. , lanes 4–6) activities, respectively, but had little effect on GC(G) synthesis (Fig. , lanes 4–6). Unexpectedly, none of the pneumovirus-specific residues in the HRSV counterpart of the rhabdovirus priming-capping loop are critical for capping and RNA synthesis initiation at the genomic Le and anti-genomic Tr (, see Supplementary results) promoters, although E1269, K1270, and K1271 appear to play supportive roles in capping.

We examined the effects of HRSV L inhibitors, AVG-233 [], BI-D [], JNJ-8003 [], and PC786 [], on RNA capping by HRSV L (Fig. and B). Among these compounds, JNJ-8003 strongly inhibited capping at IC 50 of 32 ± 9 nM. However, as the dissociation constant for the L–JNJ-8003 complex was reported to be 0.84 nM [], the IC 50 of JNJ-8003 was suggested to be close to half the concentration of enzymatically active L in the capping reaction. On the other hand, BI-D inhibited capping at IC 50 of 15 ± 6 µM, whereas the other two compounds exhibited weak inhibitory effects on the reaction (IC 50 : >100 µM). We found that 1 µM JNJ-8003 (Fig. , lane 3), but not BI-D (lane 4), inhibits the formation of the putative L–pRNA intermediate in capping. Consistent with these results, JNJ-8003 is known to directly binds the PRNTase active site of HRSV L [] (Fig. ). We confirmed that all the compounds used in this study have anti-HRSV activities (average IC 50 values calculated from three independent experiments: AVG-233, 0.73 ± 0.14 µM; BI-D, 0.68 ± 0.21 µM; JNJ-8003, 1.8 ± 0.4 nM; PC786, 7.6 ± 1.3 nM) when HRSV-induced cytopathic effect assay was used (A and B). In addition, we verified that JNJ-8003 inhibits HRSV gene expression and syncytium formation at 10 nM in infected cells (C–F).

To elucidate the mechanism of cap methylation by HRSV L, we established an in vitro cap methylation assay for the HRSV L–P complex (Fig. and ) by adapting a method previously developed for SeV L—the first assay used to demonstrate guanine- N 7 -MTase activity in NNS RNA viruses []. The GGGAC oligo-RNA was capped in the presence of [α- 32 P]GTP by the vaccinia virus capping enzyme, and the resulting G p ppGGGAC ( 32 P-labeled phosphate underlined) and SAM were used as a methyl acceptor and donor, respectively, for the MTase reactions with HRSV L (Fig. , left). After digestion of the products with Nase P1, the cap structures were analyzed by PEI-cellulose TLC. When the capped RNA was incubated with the HRSV L–P complex (WT) in the presence of 100 µM SAM (Fig. , right, lane 3), but not in the absence of SAM (lane 2), for 2 h, two methylated cap structures, m 7 GpppG (cap 0) and m 7 GpppGm (cap 1), were produced. To investigate whether these methylation reactions are catalyzed by the MTase domain of L, we examined the effects of three key mutations within this domain on the reactions. The E1854A mutation in the glycine-rich SAM binding motif G[−]GxG (where [−] denotes a negatively charged residue; G1853-E1854-G1855-x-G1857) significantly reduced guanine- N 7 -methylation (lane 4). The E1854A mutant generated a small amount of cap 0, but not cap 1. On the other hand, the D1936A (lane 5) and K1973R (lane 6) mutations in the 2′- O -MTase motif (K–D–K–E tetrad, K1831–D1936–K1973–E2004) [] abrogated cap methylation at both the guanine- N 7 - and 2′- O positions. In contrast, the transcription-defective D811A (lane 7) and capping-defective H1338R (lane 8) mutations had little effect on their guanine- N 7 - and 2′- O -methylation activities. If guanine- N 7 -methylation of the cap structure is a prerequisite for 2′- O -methylation, mutations affecting the former reaction are likely to indirectly impact the latter reaction. However, even if m 7 GpppGGGAC was used as a substrate (Fig. , left), the E1854A (right, lane 3), D1936A (lane 4), and K1973R (lane 5) mutations abolished 2′- O -methylation of the cap 0 structure.

In a time-course experiment, single cap methylation at the guanine- N 7 position, generating cap 0, occurred during the earlier incubation periods ( e.g . 15 min; Fig. , lane 2), while 2′- O -methylation of cap 0 to form cap 1 occurred more slowly over the 4-h incubation period in a time-dependent manner (lanes 3–6). Furthermore, single guanine- N 7 -methylation was observed at lower SAM concentrations (0.1–1 µM; Fig. , lanes 3 and 4), whereas 2′- O -methylation of cap 0 was observed at higher SAM concentrations (10–100 µM, lanes 5 and 6). However, single 2′- O -methylation of the cap core was not observed during the time course (Fig. ) or at any SAM concentrations examined (Fig. ). In addition, the RNA with the 2′- O -methylated cap structure (GpppGmGGAC) was found to be a significantly poorer substrate for guanine- N 7 -methylation (Fig. , lane 4) than GpppGGGAC (lane 2). Thus, as observed during in vitro transcription with native HRSV RNPs [, ], the cap core on the GGGAC RNA was methylated first at the guanine- N 7 position, followed by the 2′- O position, to generate the cap 1 structure during in vitro cap methylation with the HRSV L–P complex. Taken together, these results indicate that our recombinant HRSV L–P complex is active in the formation of the cap 1 structure on the externally added RNA substrates.
sections.discussion:
The mechanism of HRSV mRNA capping had remained unresolved for three decades since the formation of the cap structure on in vitro synthesized HRSV mRNAs with viral RNPs in the presence of cell extracts was initially demonstrated []. However, the inability to develop an in vitro assay for RNA capping with purified HRSV L, independently of transcription, has hampered progress toward characterizing the enzymatic properties of the putative PRNTase domain present in HRSV L, directly identifying amino acid residues within the PRNTase domain as essential for capping, and investigating the effects of antiviral compounds, which target HRSV L, on capping. Furthermore, the lack of efficient cap methylation assays with full-length HRSV L impeded further studies on the roles of its MTase domain in the cap 1 formation. In this study, we established in vitro capping and cap methylation assays for the HRSV RdRp complex using 5′-triphosphorylated and 5′-capped oligo-RNAs with the 5′-GGGAC L -mRNA-start sequence, respectively, as RNA substrates. Using these assays, we demonstrated that HRSV L catalyzes the polyribonucleotidyl transfer to GDP to generate the cap core structure and the methyl transfer to the cap core structure at the guanine- N 7 and ribose-2′- O positions to yield the cap 1 structure.

Similar to the report by Braun et al . [], our attempts to detect the PRNTase activity using oligo-RNA substrates initiated with 5′-pppGGGGC—the major HRSV mRNA-start sequence—were unsuccessful, possibly due to the formation of intermolecular G-quadruplex structures with the four G stretch. Thus, the successful detection of the PRNTase activity of HRSV L was initially thought to result from using the 5′-pppGGGAC L -mRNA-start sequence containing the three G stretch as the HRSV PRNTase substrate, although the specific activity of the HRSV L–P complex in capping using pppGGGAC as a pRNA donor (4.9 ± 0.5 fmol GpppG/µg protein/2 h, Fig. ) was approximately 1000-fold lower than that of VSV L using pppAACAG []. However, to our surprise, the PRNTase domain of HRSV L formed the cap core structure on pppRNAs in a sequence-independent manner, as 5′-pppAACAG—the VSV mRNA-start sequence—also serves as an efficient pRNA donor. This property of the HRSV L PRNTase domain is inconsistent with that of the VSV L PRNTase domain, which specifically recognizes its mRNA-start sequences to form the L–pRNA intermediate [, ]. The HRSV PRNTase may recognize only a 5′-triphosphorylated first purine (G or A) nucleoside of non-structured RNAs when externally added to the capping reactions. Interestingly, pppGCGAA (the HRSV leader RNA-start sequence from position 3) serves as a relatively good substrate for the HRSV PRNTase, although the HRSV leader RNA is considered to be uncapped. Unfortunately, the significantly low efficiency of the putative L–pRNA intermediate formation by HRSV L precluded further detailed analyses of the intermediate formation and subsequent pRNA transfer reactions. However, by analogy with the VSV capping reaction [, ], we speculate that the PRNTase domain of HRSV L recognizes the 5′-triphosphorylated pre-mRNAs containing the 5′-GGGRC sequence to form the covalent L–pRNA intermediate and subsequently transfers pRNA to GDP to yield the GpppG cap structure on pre-mRNAs (Fig. ). Currently, it remains unclear how GDP is efficiently generated from GTP prior to the pRNA transfer reaction during transcription, because the HRSV L–P complex generated only the unusual GppppG cap structure by the direct transfer of pRNA to GTP under the capping conditions. As the GppppG-capped RNA did not serve as a substrate for the guanine- N 7 -methylation reaction with HRSV L (D), the production of GDP from GTP by guanosine 5′-triphosphatase (GTPase) activity is suggested to be a key step to produce properly capped mRNAs with the HRSV transcription machinery.

We demonstrated that the key residues in the PRNTase motifs, except for motif B, of HRSV L are structurally or catalytically critical for its RNA capping activity (Figs. and ). Notably, the mutations of H1338 (motif D), the HRSV counterpart of the VSV L H1227, on the catalytic loop were found to abolish RNA capping at the step of the putative L–pRNA intermediate formation (Fig. ), but not RNA synthesis initiation (Fig. ) or cap methylation (Fig. ). Furthermore, this study shows that both the HRSV counterparts (G1264 and T1267) of the VSV G1154 and T1157 residues in motif B are dispensable for the PRNTase activity of HRSV L (Fig. ). Consistent with these results, the G1264A and T1267A mutants of HRSV L seem likely to produce capped mRNAs from an HRSV mini-genome in cultured cells, although to a lesser extent than WT L []. Liang et al . [] claimed that the G1154 and T1157 residues in motif B (referred to as GxxT) of the VSV PRNTase domain accommodates GDP during capping, despite being unsupported by any experimental evidence. In contrast, based on our mutagenesis analysis [], we have suggested that G1154 and T1157 of VSV L are required for the structural maintenance of the PRNTase domain and the L–pRNA intermediate formation in capping, respectively, rather than GDP binding. However, the claim by Liang et al . [] has been largely preferred in the field [, –] over the proposed roles of the GxxT sequence based on our experimental results []. Here, given the dispensability of the GxxT sequence in HRSV RNA capping, we conclude that this sequence does not play a common role, such as GDP binding, in mRNA capping among NNS RNA viruses. In HRSV, G1264 and T1267 rather play an important role in replication at an early stage of elongation []. Furthermore, in contrast to rhabdoviruses [] and BoDV-1 [], motif B-flanking residues on the HRSV counterpart of the rhabdovirus priming-capping loop seem unlikely to be essential for RNA synthesis initiation (Fig. and , see Supplementary discussion).

This study also provides direct evidence that JNJ-8003, anti-HRSV compound, strongly inhibits RNA capping mediated by HRSV L at the step of the L–pRNA intermediate formation (Fig. ). Remarkably, JNJ-8003 was reported to interact with a cleft formed between motifs D and E in the HRSV PRNTase domain [] (Fig. ). Our previous in silico docking study of the VSV PRNTase domain with a GpppA cap analogue [] suggested that the aromatic side chain of the conserved phenylalanine in motif E has the potential to π-stack with its adenine ring fitting within the similar cleft adjacent to motifs D and E. Combining our previous findings on the essential roles of motifs D and E in the L–pRNA intermediate formation [, ], we suggest that this cleft play a critical common role in binding of the 5′-triphosphorylated first-nucleotide (HRSV, pppG-; VSV, pppA-) of pre-mRNA and subsequent nucleophilic attack from the histidine residue in motif D to the α-phosphorus in the 5′-triphosphate group of pre-mRNA to form the capping intermediate. It is noteworthy that MRK-1, a compound analogous to JNJ-8003, binds to the same cleft in the PRNTase domain []. Both the compounds were found to allosterically inhibit RNA synthesis mediated by the RdRp domain [, ]. Therefore, drug binding to the cleft formed between motifs D and E has the potential to exert dual inhibitory effects on both enzymatic activities catalyzed by the RdRp-PRNTase superdomain of HRSV L, thereby strongly inhibiting virus replication.

On the other hand, although BI-D was originally suggested to inhibit capping and thereby trigger premature termination of mRNA synthesis [], its concentrations required for capping inhibition in vitro (Fig. ) were 10–100-fold higher than those reported to inhibit in vitro transcription and virus replication in infected cells (B) [, ]. Although BI-D resistance mutations (E1269D, I1381S, and L1421F) have been mapped within the PRNTase domain of HRSV L [], it is not known whether these sites directly contribute to BI-D binding. Notably, at sub-micromolar concentrations, BI-D stimulates RNA synthesis initiation from position 3 in the Le promoter but inhibits RNA synthesis initiation from the NS1 gene-start sequence, resulting in the generation of larger amounts of potential read-through products terminated around 50–300 nt []. Furthermore, BI-D inhibits replication by repressing initiation at position 1 of the genome at sub-micromolar concentrations []. Thus, the major antiviral effect of BI-D at sub-micromolar concentrations is suggested to be inhibition of accurate stop-start transcription and replication rather than pre-mRNA capping.

In this study, we also demonstrate that the MTase domain of HRSV L in the L-P RdRp complex methylates the cap core structure (GpppG) into cap 1 (m 7 GpppGm) in the following order: (i) guanine- N 7 -methylation → (ii) guanosine-2′- O -methylation. A similar recombinant HRSV L–P complex produced in insect cells was reported to be unable to methylate the cap core or cap 0 structure at the 2′- O position during a 6-h incubation []. It was also unclear whether the products of overnight reactions with their HRSV L–P complex included cap 1 (m 7 GpppGm) [], because the reaction products appeared to include ³²P-labeled inorganic phosphate—a degradation product of the ³²P-labeled cap structure and/or contaminated [α-³²P]GMP, [α-³²P]GDP, and/or [α-³²P]GTP—which is known to co-migrate with m 7 GpppGm on PEI-cellulose plates under their TLC conditions, and because the experiments lacked an SAM-minus negative control. Strikingly, the optimal pH for the MTase activities of the C-terminal fragment of HRSV L ( N 7 , pH 7–7.5; 2′- O , pH 7–8) [] are different from that of our L–P complex ( N 7 , pH 5–6; 2′- O , pH 5.5–6) (A). The latter optimum pH is remarkably similar to that of the guanine- N 7 -MTase activity of recombinant SeV L as well as native SeV RNPs []. The HRSV L–P complex specifically methylated the cap structure on the HRSV L -mRNA-start sequence (GGGAC) to produce the cap 1 structure (B and C, see Supplementary discussion).

Under the conditions similar to those used for the HRSV L–P complex, recombinant SeV L (3–10 ng protein) as well as native SeV RNPs (4 µg protein) could methylate the cap structure on the SeV mRNA-start sequence (AGGGU) at the guanine- N 7 position, but not the 2′- O position [], although in vitro mRNAs synthesized by native SeV RNPs possess the fully methylated cap 1 structure []. In contrast to a previous report [], recombinant VSV L as well as native VSV L–P complexes, highly purified in our laboratory, is unable to methylate externally added VSV pre-mRNAs (80–200 nt) or capped oligo-RNAs containing the VSV mRNA-start sequence ( e.g . AACAG, AACAGUAAUC), although they are enzymatically fully active in co-transcriptional cap 1 formation when transcription elongation complexes were reconstituted with P and N-RNA template []. Therefore, these Ls from different NNS RNA viruses exhibit divergent enzymatic properties in in vitro methylation reactions and display distinct dependencies on transcription.

In summary, using newly established in vitro assay systems, we demonstrate that HRSV L catalyzes PRNTase, guanine- N 7 -MTase, and 2′- O -MTase activities that are critical for the formation of the cap 1 structure on pre-mRNAs. In particular, the PRNTase assay for the HRSV L–P complex could be useful for identifying amino acid residues required for the PRNTase activity of L, thereby uncovering functional similarities and differences among pneumoviruses and rhabdoviruses. Furthermore, the assay enables direct evaluation of the effects of antiviral compounds on RNA capping catalyzed by HRSV L. Currently, it is not known how the HRSV transcription machinery efficiently produces GDP as the pRNA acceptor for the formation of the cap core structure. Further studies on the mechanisms of co-transcriptional capping and cap methylation are essential to enhance our understanding of the pathway of mRNA maturation by the HRSV transcription machinery.

title: [Expert consensus on key issues in prevention and control of human respiratory syncytial virus infection in the older population in China].
abstract: Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) is one of the most common pathogens causing acute lower respiratory infections in children globally and poses a significant burden of severe respiratory disease among elderly and adults with underlying conditions. Several immunization products are currently available to prevent severe HRSV disease in infants and elderly adults. To guide and standardize HRSV control and prevention among the elderly population, School of Population Medicine and Public Health, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College established a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop this expert consensus. Based on domestic and global research progress, evidence, and prevention/control experience, this expert consensus focuses on key technical issues including HRSV disease burden, surveillance, prevention/control strategies, vaccine application and recommendations. The consensus particularly emphasizes identifying critical technical questions from a policy perspective and consolidating expert consensus, aiming to provide healthcare professionals with reference for HRSV prevention and control in elderly populations.

title: Proposal for Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus Nomenclature below the Species Level.
abstract: Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) is the leading viral cause of serious pediatric respiratory disease, and lifelong reinfections are common. Its 2 major subgroups, A and B, exhibit some antigenic variability, enabling HRSV to circulate annually. Globally, research has increased the number of HRSV genomic sequences available. To ensure accurate molecular epidemiology analyses, we propose a uniform nomenclature for HRSV-positive samples and isolates, and HRSV sequences, namely: HRSV/subgroup identifier/geographic identifier/unique sequence identifier/year of sampling. We also propose a template for submitting associated metadata. Universal nomenclature would help researchers retrieve and analyze sequence data to better understand the evolution of this virus.

sections.other:
Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) is the leading cause of severe respiratory illness in children <5 years of age and is associated with substantial illness from lower respiratory tract infections in industrialized countries and substantial illness and death in low- and middle-income countries ( – ). HRSV also causes severe disease among elderly and high-risk adults ().

In 2016, HRSV was reclassified by the International Committee on Virus Taxonomy (ICTV) into a new family, Pneumoviridae , genus, Orthopneumovirus , and species, Human orthopneumovirus . (). The wider availability of viral sequencing technologies has increased submissions of HRSV sequences to databases (), a trend we anticipate will continue. Although ICTV provides nomenclature standards for virus taxa, there is currently no standardized format for HRSV nomenclature below the species level. Given the current interest in both HRSV and database submissions, a standard nomenclature is needed to simplify studies of the genomic diversity of HRSV strains and variants below the species level. ICTV’s taxonomic reassignment provides us a timely opportunity to propose a universal naming convention for HRSV strains, sequences, and isolates, including a framework for database submissions that are rich in contextual information and associated metadata.

Several large laboratory HRSV surveillance and epidemiology studies are currently in progress. These studies include the World Health Organization’s Global Respiratory Syncytial Virus (WHO RSV) Surveillance Project ( https://www.who.int/influenza/rsv ), which conducts large-scale testing for HRSV and extensive sequencing of HRSV-positive clinical specimens from >20 countries worldwide. Focused molecular analyses have helped elucidate HRSV household () and local () transmission dynamics and may guide development of strategies for the control of HRSV transmission. For example, molecular analysis showed that HRSV in healthcare facilities can be acquired from sources within the facility or introduced from the community ( , ).

In temperate climates, annual HRSV epidemics usually occur in winter months; it remains to be seen how social distancing measures and nonpharmaceutical interventions due to the current coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic will affect global HRSV circulation patterns. One of the 2 major genetic and antigenic HRSV subgroups, A or B, usually predominates in alternating years, but both subgroups can also co-circulate in the same season. Early research has shown that subgroup A HRSV is associated with slightly greater clinical severity than subgroup B (). Disease severity has been correlated with specific strains, genotypes, or clades, but to date, no consistent association has been established between strains ( – ), genotypes, or clades ( – ) and virulence. Thus, a possible role of different HRSV strains in disease severity remains to be elucidated. The lack of standard nomenclature and the scarcity of rich metadata in databases currently limit and complicate such studies.

Reliable and concise nomenclature systems below the species level are available for measles virus, influenza virus, rotavirus, filovirus isolates ( – ), and many other human viral pathogens. A similar nomenclature system tailored to HRSV and its pathology would support the requirements of researchers and the public health community by minimizing information errors when handling, storing, and shipping HRSV samples and when submitting, searching, and displaying sequencing data and associated metadata. Moreover, consistent nomenclature would improve the ability of researchers to pool and analyze data and associated information from different sources. To fill this need, an international group of researchers, in conjunction with the WHO RSV Global Surveillance Project, proposes a concise nomenclature system for HRSV below the species level.
sections.results:
HRSV has a single-stranded nonsegmented negative-sense RNA genome ≈15,191–15,277 nt long (, panel A) (). The HRSV genome contains 10 genes, each encoding a separate mRNA with a single open reading frame (ORF) (, panel A; ), except for the M2 mRNA, which contains 2 overlapping ORFs. The 11 HRSV proteins are 2 nonstructural proteins (NS1 and NS2), nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), small hydrophobic envelope protein (SH), attachment glycoprotein (G), fusion glycoprotein (F), the transcription processivity factor (M2–1), RNA regulatory factor (M2–2), and large RNA polymerase protein (L) () ( , ). The F glycoprotein is the major viral neutralization and protective antigen, followed by the G glycoprotein ().

HRSV subgroups A and B exhibit genomewide nucleotide and amino acid divergence (, panel A) ( , ). The reference sequences for the 2 subgroups are derived from strains HRSV A2 ( – ; GenBank accession number M74568.1 ; RefSeq accession number NC_038235 ) and HRSV B1 (; GenBank accession number AF013254.1 ; RefSeq accession number NC_001781.1 ; , panel B). F glycoprotein sequences between the 2 subgroups are well conserved (89% aa identity), whereas the G glycoproteins are the most divergent (53% aa identity between the subgroups) among the HRSV proteins (, panel A) and undergo continuous molecular evolution. The ectodomain of the G glycoproteins of both subgroups contains a conserved central domain, representing an important antigenic site, flanked by 2 hypervariable domains (). Except for the central conserved region, the antigenic cross-reactivity between G glycoproteins of the 2 subgroups is low ().

Because the G ORF exhibits the greatest degree of genetic variability between isolates, it is most commonly used for studies on the molecular evolution of HRSV. The genetic variability of HRSV strains over time has been commonly determined by sequencing the distal C-terminal third of the G ORF, which includes the second hypervariable domain. The variability in the G ORF is characterized by a high rate of nonsynonymous nucleotide changes, suggesting that evolution may be driven by immune pressure, even though this factor may be partially antibody independent (). It is likely that variability in the G protein contributes to the capacity of HRSV to cause yearly outbreaks in the community ( – ). The nomenclature proposal outlined herein will be useful for the sequence analyses required to follow the molecular evolution of HRSV.

In a parallel effort, several research groups are working together on a genotyping proposal to provide a consensus on uniform genotype designations (,). As virus evolution continues, we expect new genotypes to emerge and older genotypes to become extinct. HRSV genotyping designations will need to capture present molecular evolutionary status and be adaptable to changes and will need to be reevaluated periodically by a global consortium.

For molecular epidemiology studies, a concise standard for short identifiers of specific HRSV sequences, suitable for the short definition lines that give context to a sample and its derived sequence, would be useful. Ideally, concise standardized identifiers should convey key information about each individual sequence in an alignment or phylogram, including source, date, and type, if known. Here, we aim to define this type of common naming convention for HRSV samples and isolates. We also propose using standard names and appropriate annotations for HRSV genes, provide examples to guide the annotation of sequence data during the sequence submission process, and suggest how to submit metadata associated with the source materials of HRSV sequences.

GenBank records available through the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) are identified by 2 elements: a unique alphanumeric accession number and a definition line. The definition line is the portion of the identifier commonly associated with GenBank records shown in BLAST results and other searches. Definition lines are generated by the submitter during the sequence submission process and include the species and isolate name (e.g., Human orthopneumovirus isolate HRSV/A/USA/001/2011, complete genome [proposed]). (). We propose a standardized format to capture 5 sample-specific parameters of HRSV-positive clinical samples or isolates to be included in sequence definition lines compatible with database naming requirements (), in this specific order: [virus name abbreviation]/[HRSV subgroup]/[geographic identifier]/[unique sequence identifier]/[year of sampling].

ICTV’s species name, Human orthopneumovirus (), will be reflected as HRSV in the NCBI definition line. During submission to databases, the organism name can be entered as either Human orthopneumovirus or human respiratory syncytial virus. The abbreviation HRSV should be used in the definition line regardless of which organism name is provided.

If not specified by a research network, the ISO 3166–1 α-3 letter country code ( https://www.iso.org/iso-3166-country-codes.html ) should be used to indicate the country of sampling (XXX, if unknown). We strongly suggest that submitters provide any more specific geographic information on the sampling location (e.g., city or state) in metadata fields rather than in the definition line. The WHO Global RSV Surveillance Project plans to use just the simple English-language name for the country. Individual national studies may require a state, province, or city designation, in addition to the mandatory country name. If required, a period should be used to set off the country name ([state/province/city].[country name]).

This field must be restricted to 8 alphanumeric characters. Underscores are permitted, but neither other special characters (e.g., /, %, $, @) nor spaces can be used. Controversial names or phrases, names of prominent people, and trademarked names or phrases cannot be used. To prevent duplication of sample or isolate identifiers by different groups, we recommend inserting a lettercode identifying a study or institute before the sample number. For example, unique isolate identifiers for samples from the INFORM-RSV study might use “INF” followed by a number (e.g., INF001 in HRSV/A/COUNTRY/INF001/2019).

HRSV/A/USA/001/2011 HRSV/B/Denver.USA/14617/1985 HRSV/A/IRN/001/2017 HRSV/A/Iran/001/2017 HRSV/X/IRN/001/2017 (subgroup unknown) HRSV/B/New_Zealand/FR123/2020

Our nomenclature proposal prioritizes a short, concise definition line that will be easy to use in the laboratory, easily readable, and be a uniform system for HRSV in public databases. Additional host, virus, location or temporal information if desired could be submitted in metadata fields, which would allow researchers, epidemiologists, and database users to apply specific metadata filters, as needed for data retrieval and specific applications, analyses, or for displaying designations, such as in dendrograms.

To support efficient data analysis, uniform designations must be used at the database submission stage. Commonly accepted names for HRSV genes and proteins are shown in the table. An HRSV gene comprises a gene start signal GGGGCAAAT(A/G), an ORF with adjacent noncoding regions, if present, and the gene end signal through the last adenosine residue [AGT(T/A)A(T/A/G)(A/T)(A/T)(A/T)A n ] (; 41 ). Each HRSV gene contains a single ORF, except for the M2 gene, which has 2 overlapping ORFs, M2–1 and M2–2. Nucleotide annotations of genes and ORFs for the HRSV A2 () and HRSV B1 reference sequences are shown in the table.

What is the most pertinent host data will depend on the interests and objectives of individual study groups. For example, when studying HRSV in a pediatric setting, prematurity may be of interest, but when studying HRSV in an adult setting, researchers may be more interested in whether participants are immunocompromised. We suggest information that could be included in metadata fields for HRSV:

Viral RNA can be extracted directly from a clinical sample, from an isolate grown in cell culture, or possibly from a cDNA-derived recombinant virus. The sources of sequences from isolated viruses can be identified by the following designations: wt: wild-type; sequences derived from RNA extracted directly from clinical specimens tc: tissue culture; sequences derived from RNA extracted from HRSV isolates propagated in tissue culture rec: recombinant; sequences of cDNA-derived recombinant virus (including vaccine strain)

If >6 months of age, birthweight and gestational age at birth. Significant pediatric co-morbidities, including prematurity, congenital cardiac disease, and broncho-pulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Twin? (Y/N) Exposed to specific HRSV therapeutic, vaccine, antibody, or antiviral? (Y/N) Viral or bacterial co-infections, if known; pathogen species should be spelled out. Adult underlying conditions, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or asthma, or altered immune status (e.g., immunocompromised, bone marrow transplant recipient). Disease outcomes. Five grades are distinguished: No medical care. Outpatient or emergency room. Hospital admission. ICU admission. Death.

For NCBI submissions, data can be entered through the web interface, or uploaded as tab-delimited text files. Sequences can be uploaded in FASTA format ( https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov ; ), with associated metadata provided in a plain text, tab-delimited, source modifier table ( Table 1) and gene or protein annotations provided in a plain text, tab-delimited, 5-column feature table ( Table 2).

Molecular surveillance has revealed that multiple HRSV genotypes circulate simultaneously in communities. Circulating genotypes often vary between communities, and circulation patterns within a community can change from year to year. Extended monitoring of circulating viruses is necessary to better understand transmission and molecular evolution (). As HRSV vaccine candidates and antivirals are being developed, molecular epidemiology studies may reveal potential effects of prevention strategies on viral evolution and possible antibody-escape variants. Timely sharing of HRSV data worldwide through the use of public databases is essential. We propose that sequence data be uploaded to publicly accessible databases, such as NCBI (). Although NCBI is the most complete repository for HRSV sequence information, studies may require that sequences first be submitted to other databases, such as GISAID ( https://www.gisaid.org ).

Public access will provide useful availability for investigators to submit, query, and analyze HRSV sequence data, enabling the evolutionary analysis of sequence diversity within or between HRSV genotypes. The utility of public access has been clearly demonstrated with the emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and the critical role that genetic sequence analysis has played. Notably, a nomenclature model for SARS-CoV-2 similar to what we have proposed for HRSV has been adopted, although some differences remain between databases (e.g., NCBI, SARS-CoV-2/human/USA/COVID20–1096/2020; GISAID, hCoV-19/Australia/VIC12/2020). When an HRSV vaccine becomes available, high-quality, geographically representative, country-specific data on circulating strains and rich datasets of well-curated, standardized, and parsable data will be required to monitor and trace possible evolutionary changes in response to vaccine-induced selective pressure ( , ). This proposal will profit from strong support by members of the International RSV Society, a special interest group of the International Society for Influenza and other Respiratory Virus Diseases ( https://isirv.org ), members of the WHO Global RSV Surveillance Project, and the HRSV research community.

title: A potently neutralizing and protective human antibody targeting antigenic site V on RSV and hMPV fusion glycoprotein.
abstract: Human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) are frequent drivers of morbidity and mortality in susceptible populations. The primary target of neutralizing antibodies is the fusion (F) glycoprotein on the surface of the RSV and hMPV virion. As a result of the structural conservation between RSV and hMPV F, three antigenic regions are known to induce cross-neutralizing responses: sites III, IV, and V. Leveraging LIBRA-seq, we identify five RSV/hMPV cross-reactive human antibodies. One antibody, RM 5-1, potently neutralizes all tested viruses from the major subgroups of RSV and hMPV and provides protection against RSV and hMPV in a mouse challenge model. Structural analysis reveals that RM 5-1 utilizes an uncommon genetic signature to bind an epitope that spans sites Ø, II, and V. These findings highlight the molecular and structural elements influencing RSV and hMPV cross-reactivity as well as the potential of antibody RM 5-1 for translational development.

sections.other:
Human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV) are worldwide, endemic respiratory pathogens of the Pneumoviridae family. Representing non-segmented negative-strand RNA viruses, RSV and hMPV induce severe and lethal bronchiolitis and pneumonia among particularly susceptible populations, most notably infantile, geriatric, and immunocompromised, , with RSV being a leading cause of lower respiratory-tract-infection-associated hospitalization and mortality in children under 5 years of age. , Similar to RSV, infants younger than 1 year have disproportionately high risks of severe hMPV infection, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, making hMPV an important pathogen in the first year of life. A turbulent history of disease enhancement following RSV vaccination has only recently been met with clinical success in the advancement of effective prophylactic strategies leveraging structure-based vaccine design , , and neutralizing antibodies with extended half-lives. , Currently there are no approved therapeutic or prophylactic options against hMPV infection.

The major target of neutralizing antibodies in human sera against RSV and hMPV infection is the fusion (F) glycoprotein on the surface of the virion. , , , RSV/hMPV F is a trimeric type I transmembrane fusion protein responsible for mediating viral entry into host cells of the airway epithelium. Substantial conformational changes occur in F, as it transitions from the metastable prefusion form to the stable postfusion form, and understanding of these structural rearrangements has enabled engineering of prefusion-stabilized F antigens. , , , , Stabilization of RSV and hMPV F in the prefusion state induces high neutralizing titers in experimentally inoculated animals, and prefusion-stabilized RSV F serves as the backbone of the recently approved human RSV vaccines. Importantly, differential glycosylation patterns on the apex of RSV and hMPV F result in conformationally specific contributions toward the induction of neutralizing responses: RSV prefusion F epitopes are exceptionally immunogenic and invoke potently neutralizing antibodies, , whereas pre- and postfusion hMPV F stimulate comparable neutralizing responses. , Antibody isolation and characterization efforts against RSV and hMPV have enabled extensive definition of the antigenic landscapes of RSV and hMPV F. The antigenic topology of RSV and hMPV F follows a synonymous nomenclature, with the major sites represented as site Ø through site V, as well as the more recently described site VI on RSV F. Antigenic sites Ø, V, and VI are preserved exclusively on the prefusion conformations of the proteins, , , whereas sites I, II, III, and IV are exposed on the pre- and postfusion conformations.

Broadly reactive and neutralizing antibodies that recognize both RSV and hMPV have been described with varied breadth and potency of virus neutralization. , , , , , , , , The frequency of such cross-reactive B cells in human repertoires is extremely low and nearly undetectable, suggesting natural infection does not efficiently elicit B cells of this phenotype. However, due to the structural homology between RSV and hMPV F glycoproteins, three shared epitopes on F, sites III, IV, and V, can induce cross-reactive antibody responses, despite low overall amino acid sequence identity between RSV and hMPV F monomers (∼35%). Residues within site III are relatively conserved between both viruses and a common target of cross-neutralizing antibodies encoded by IGHV3-11/IGHV3-21: IGLV1-40 , , , , a germline gene pairing reported to be enriched in infant and adult anti-RSV antibody repertoires recognizing site III. Low- and high-resolution structural analyses of site III and IV cross-reactive antibodies provide evidence that binding pose may influence cross-reactivity; however, the mode of antigenic recognition of a site V cross-neutralizing antibody remains unknown.

Leveraging LIBRA-seq (linking B cell receptor sequence to antigen specificity by sequencing), we identified from human peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples five RSV/hMPV cross-reactive antibodies that showed high neutralization potencies against both RSV and hMPV that were comparable to virus-specific (RSV- or hMPV-only) as well as cross-reactive antibodies in the literature, with one monoclonal antibody (mAb) RM 5-1 potently neutralizing the major subgroups of RSV and hMPV. We determined the epitope of RM 5-1 by single-particle cryo-EM using a prefusion-stabilized hMPV F with inter- and intra-protomer disulfide bonds and found that the binding site of RM 5-1 spans antigenic sites Ø, II, and V on an individual protomer. Analysis of the interface identified residues that are important for RSV and hMPV cross-neutralization. Finally, RM 5-1 showed robust protection in a mouse challenge model against both RSV and hMPV, therefore establishing this antibody as a prime candidate for further translational development.
