title: Molecular Surveillance Reveals F-Gene Mutations and Constrained G-Gene Evolution in Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus: Implications for Vaccine Efficacy in Saudi Arabia.
abstract: Background/objectivesHuman Respiratory Syncytial Virus (HRSV) is a major global cause of acute lower respiratory infections in children. With recent approval of pre-fusion F protein-based vaccines and monoclonal antibodies, ongoing molecular surveillance is critical. This study examined HRSV molecular epidemiology and evolution in Riyadh, focusing on mutations in the attachment (G) and fusion (F) glycoproteins and their potential impact on vaccine efficacy.MethodsNasopharyngeal aspirates (NPAs) (200 samples) were collected from pediatric patients. HRSV-positive samples were typed, and the G gene hypervariable region and F gene were sequenced. Sequence and phylogenetic analyses were performed to identify circulating genotypes and amino acid substitutions.ResultsHRSV was detected in 15% of samples, with HRSV-B slightly predominant over HRSV-A. Infants aged 2-5 months had the highest incidence rate of infection. The ON1 subgenotype remained dominant. The duplicated region of the G gene showed constrained evolution, with 18 variable and 6 conserved residues over 13 years. In the F protein, HRSV-A isolates exhibited high conservation, with only three amino acid substitutions in antigenic sites (Ø and II). Sites III, IV, and V remained fully conserved. In contrast, HRSV-B isolates displayed eight substitutions in antigenic sites, including six in site II (palivizumab-binding epitope).ConclusionsGiven the highly effective HRSV prophylactics, including the approved vaccines and monoclonal antibodies, these mutations raise critical concerns regarding vaccine efficacy against HRSV-B. These findings underscore the necessity of sustained, seasonal molecular surveillance to monitor the emergence of variants and provide a molecular basis for further clinical studies.

sections.other:
Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus (HRSV), also referred to as Human Orthopneumovirus (HOPV), is one of the leading causes of acute lower respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in infants, children, immunocompromised individuals, and elderly individuals [,]. Because long-lasting immunity cannot be established, recurrent HRSV infections are common, which impedes the development of viable vaccine candidates []. HRSV infections are associated with a significant rate of morbidity and mortality across the globe. According to recent estimates, HRSV infections are associated with 33 million confirmed cases of acute RTI worldwide. In addition, it was reported that HRSV infection is associated with nearly 3.6 million hospitalizations and 26,300 hospital deaths. It is estimated that HRSV infection causes more than 100,000 deaths in children younger than five years [].

HRSV is classified within the Pneumovirus genus of the Pneumoviridae family. It is a single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus with a genomic size ranging from 15,191 to 15,226 nts long that encodes eleven structural and nonstructural proteins, including the major glycoproteins on its surface and the fusion envelope (F) and attachment (G) proteins []. The G and F proteins play critical roles in viral infection, as G facilitates virion attachment to the host cell membrane, whereas F mediates the fusion step []. HRSV is classified into two main groups, A and B, based on genetic variations in the G glycoprotein. HRSV-A currently comprises at least 14 genotypes (GA1–GA7, SAA1, NA1–NA4, ON1, CB-A, etc.), whereas HRSV-B includes more than 30 genotypes [,].

The F protein is primarily synthesized as the F0 precursor (574 amino acids). It undergoes cleavage by a furin-like host protease to yield two subunits (F1 and F2) and pep27 polypeptides []. The resulting mature F protein is a homotrimer, with F1 being essential for membrane fusion []. Structurally, the protein is known to transition between a metastable, ‘lollipop’-shaped prefusion conformation found on the virion membrane and a stable, cone-shaped postfusion form characterized by a 6-helix bundle []. Due to its high sequence conservation, the F protein is a critical target for both cytotoxic T lymphocytes [] and for neutralizing antibody and vaccine development. Six antigenic sites named Ø, I, II, III, IV, and V have been mapped within the F protein []. The antigenic site Ø is exclusively found in the prefusion state []. The antigenic site II, located between amino acids 262 and 275, serves as the binding domain for the therapeutic neutralizing antibodies such as palivizumab and motavizumab, where mutations can lead to drug resistance [].

HRSV is characterized by a high mutation rate, leading to the continuous emergence of new genotypes with distinct clinical manifestations in infected individuals []. The most recent example of this is the HRSV-A genotype ON1, with a duplication of 72 nucleotides (nt) in the second hypervariable region of the G gene, which first appeared in Ontario, Canada, in 2010. Since then, multiple studies have reported the emergence of this genotype in many countries [,,]. In Saudi Arabia, our group previously reported that most HRSV infections during the winter seasons of 2007/08 and 2008/09 in Saudi Arabia belonged to the HRSV-A group, and we observed a genotype shift from NA1 to ON1 [].

The history of HRSV prevention is characterized by a significant early setback with the formalin-inactivated respiratory syncytial virus (FI-RSV) vaccine in the 1960s, which led to vaccine-enhanced respiratory disease and suspended vaccine development for decades []. For over twenty years, the primary prophylactic tool was the monoclonal antibody palivizumab (Synagis), which provides passive immunity by targeting conserved antigenic site II on the F protein in high-risk infants []. However, the landscape of HRSV prevention has been fundamentally changed by the recent approval of stabilized prefusion F protein-based vaccines, Arexvy (GSK) and Abrysvo (Pfizer) [,]. These vaccines, approved in 2023, represent a major scientific breakthrough, with Arexvy being the first to gain approval for older adults and Abrysvo being approved both for older adults and for maternal immunization to protect infants []. The efficacy of these F protein-targeting prophylactics, including the recent long-acting monoclonal antibody, nirsevimab, is directly dependent on the antigenic stability of the circulating strains. Although the F protein is considerably conserved among different HRSV types, a single amino acid change, particularly within the antigenic sites, can interfere with the efficacy of monoclonal antibodies and vaccine effectiveness []. Continuous molecular surveillance is therefore essential to detect emerging variants that could compromise the effectiveness of these newly introduced prophylactics.

Despite the worldwide rollout of HRSV F-based vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapeutics, comprehensive data on the long-term molecular epidemiology of HRSV-A in Saudi Arabia remain inadequate. The evolutionary kinetics behind the sustained dominance of the ON1 genotype and the antigenic evolution of the F protein have not been systematically investigated in Saudi Arabia. Therefore, the current study aimed to (i) describe the molecular epidemiology and circulation pattern of HRSV-A in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, over multiple seasons, (ii) elucidate the genetic factors contributing to the continued predominance of the ON1 genotype, and (iii) examine the antigenic stability of the F protein in contemporary Saudi HRSV isolates in the context of the recently approved vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapeutics. To achieve these objectives, NPAs were collected from hospitalized children and screened for HRSV. The G and F genes of HRSV-A strains were amplified and sequenced for sequence and phylogenetic analysis.

After the parents of the children provided a written informed consent form and the Research Ethics Committee (RES) at King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, approved the study (Ethics Reference No. E-141326/IRB), 200 NPA samples of children at King Khalid University Hospital who had symptoms of respiratory tract infection were collected during the winter of 2022–2023. The Virology Research Laboratory (VRG) at King Saud University’s College of Science collected the samples, combined them with two milliliters of the viral transport medium, and sent them right away in cooling boxes. After that, the samples were divided into smaller portions and stored at −80 °C until analysis.

A QIAamp Viral RNA Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) was used to extract viral RNA from clinical samples. A One-Step RT-PCR Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and the following primer set were used: HRSV-U-F (5′-GGA ACA AGT TGT TGA GGT TTA TGA ATA TGC-3′) and HRSV-U-R (5′-CTT CTG CTG TCA AGT CTA GTA CAC TGT AGT-3′). PCR typing was attempted via the same PCR kit and the following primer sets: HRSV-A [HRSVA-F (5′-GAT GTT ACG GTG GGG AGT CT-3′) and HRSV-A-R (5′-GTACACTGTAGTTAATCACA-3′)] and HRSV-B [HRSV B-F (5′-AATGCTAAGATGGGGAGTT-3′) and HRSV B-R (5′-GAAATTG AGTTAATGACAG-3′)] []. The PCR program included reverse transcription for 30 min at 50 °C, initial denaturation at 95 °C for 15 min, 35 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 30 s, annealing at 52 °C for 30 s, and extension at 72 °C for 2 min, followed by a final extension step at 72 °C for 10 min. The reaction was carried out in a GeneAmp 9700 thermal cycler (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The amplified products were compared to a 100 bp DNA ladder (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and visualized on an agarose gel stained with 1% ethidium bromide.

The G ectodomain encompassing the two HVRs and the full-length F gene was amplified via the One-Step Ahead RT-PCR Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), which was carried out in a GeneAmp 9700 thermal cycler. The following two primer sets were used for the G gene [HRSVA-G-F1 (5′-CTC GAG TCA ACA CAT AGC ATTC-3′), HRSVA-G-F1 (5′-GTT GGA TTG TTG CTG CAT ATG-3′), HRSVA-G-F2 (5′-CAAGATGCAACAAGCCAGATC-3′), and HRSV-G-R2 (5′-ACTG CAC TGC ATG TTG ATT G-3′)]. Three primer sets were used to amplify the whole F gene [HRSVA-F-F1 (5′-GGC AAA TAA CAA TGG AGT TG-3′); HRSV-F-R1 (5′-CTC CAT TTG ATA AGC TGA CTAC-3′); HRSVA-F-F2 (5′-GTT AGG TGT TGG ATC TGC AATC-3′); HRSV-F-R2 (5′-CAT AGC ATG ACA CAA TGG CTC-3′); and HRSVA-F-F3 (5′-GAG GAT GGT ACT GTG ACA ATG-3′) and HRSV-F-R3 (5′-GCA AGG ATT CCT TCG TGAC-3′)]. DNA bands corresponding to the expected size were retrieved from the gel via the Illustra™ GFX PCR DNA and Gel Band Purification Kit (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA). The amplified fragments were sequenced on both strands via Macrogen, Inc. (Seoul, Republic of Korea). Raw sequence data were edited via the BioEdit program, version 7.0 (Ibis Biosciences, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and assembled via the Edit sequence tool of the MegAlign program, Lasergene software, version 3.18 (DNAStar, Madison, WI, USA). Only 9 sequences were selected for sequence and phylogenetic analysis on the basis of their sequence heterogeneity. The final assembled sequences were added to the GenBank database with accession numbers [G: PP454562–PP454570 ) and (F: PP454571–PP454579 )].

To understand the evolution and diversity of HRSV-A in Riyadh over time, the 9 sequences of the G gene from the winter season of 2022/23 were aligned with Riyadh strains from 6 previous winter seasons: 2007/08 ( n = 4), 2008/09 ( n = 5), 2014/15 ( n = 6), 2015/16 ( n = 5), 2019/20 ( n = 4) and 2021/22 ( n = 3). A total of 61 international strains used for phylogenetic analysis were retrieved from GenBank databases based on the following criteria: (i) a broad range of geographical regions and collection years; (ii) representative strains from all genotypes to ensure a comprehensive evolutionary context; (iii) representative of the ON1 sequences that described in the earliest reports; and (iv) prototypes as reference strains ( AF065257 , M17212 , KT992094 , AF233917 , and KU316106 ). Both the nucleotide and deduced amino acid sequences were aligned via ClustalW, the MegAlign program of Lasergene software, version 3.18 (DNAStar, Madison, WI, USA). Changes in protein length, sequence gaps, insertions and deletions, and synonymous and nonsynonymous mutations were considered in the analysis. In addition, genotype-specific amino acids were determined. Similarly, the nucleotide and deduced amino acid sequences of the full-length F gene (seasons: 2008/09 and 2022/23) were aligned against 43 international strains retrieved from Gene bank database. These strains were selected to cover a broad range of temporal and geographical regions. Crucially, the F gene of the HRSV-B type was included in the study to assess the potential vaccine efficacy against this subtype. Furthermore, 4 reference strains ( AF065257 , M17212 , KT992094 , and AF233917 ), which are the most used in vaccine design, were incorporated into the comparison. The F gene of strain A2, widely used for vaccine design, was set as the consensus sequence. Mutations at both the nucleotide and amino acid levels were determined, and amino acid changes within the five antigenic sites of the F protein were recorded.

The strains detailed in the previous section were utilized to generate two phylogenetic trees. The first tree included a total of 101 sequences (61 international + 40 local) and was constructed based on the 2nd HVR of the G gene. The second tree included 55 strains (43 international + 12 local) and was constructed based on the full-length F gene. Both trees were inferred using the Maximum Likelihood method via MEGA 6.0 (Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA). The accuracy of the tree topology was evaluated by performing 1000 bootstrap replicates.

Deduced amino acid sequences (Riyadh and international strains) of both the G and F proteins were used to determine potential O- and N-glycosylation sites via Net-N-glyc 1.0 and Net-O-glyc 3.1, respectively [,]. Conserved and new potential sites for N- and O-glycosylation were identified.
sections.results:
Among the 200 NPAs tested for HRSV, 30 (15%) were positive; 14 (7%) were HRSV-A, and 16 (8%) were HRSV-B (). The screening results indicated a slight predominance of HRSV-B over HRSV-A. Age-group analysis revealed that the prevalence of HRSV-A was considerably greater (6.74%) ( p < 0.05) in the 2–5-month age group. The sex-based analysis revealed that male-infected children had a greater incidence of HRSV-A infections (7.69%) than female-infected children (6%).

The kinetics of HRSV-A evolution were analyzed over 7 winter seasons: 2007/08, 2008/09, 2015/16, 2016/17, 2019/20, 2021/22, and 2022/23. The analysis was based mainly on the two HVRs of the attachment G gene, which ranged in length from 615 nt (genotypes GA-1 to GA7 and SAA1) to 687 nt (subgenotype ON1). Nucleotide sequence analysis was performed by aligning the two HVRs of the Saudi strains from the winter season (2022/23) and the 6 previous winter seasons with their international counterparts available in the GenBank database. An overview of the nucleotide sequence alignment report revealed no sequence abnormalities or sequence gaps. The subgenotype ON1 possesses a unique sequence feature that distinguishes it from the other genotypes, which is the insertion of a duplicate region of 72 nucleotides at the C-terminus of the second HVR. This insertion resulted in an increase in the length of the G gene from 894 to 966 nucleotides. This feature is shared by all ON1 strains circulating worldwide. No year-specific mutations among the different HRSV-A genotypes were recorded. The overall sequence heterogeneity between Saudi ON1 strains (winter season: 2022/23) ranged from 0.4 to 8.6% and from 2.7% to 10.6% at the nucleotide and amino acid levels, respectively. However, the degree of sequence heterology between the Riyadh ON1 and GA2 strains ranged from 7.4% to 13.9% and from 5.1% to 16.3% at the nucleotide and amino acid levels, respectively.

The Saudi ON1 strains of the winter season (2022/23) presented a total of 130-point mutations, which represented 19% of the sequenced fragment. Among these mutations, 66 mutations were nonsynonymous and resulted in changes in their corresponding amino acid residues. Intensive amino acid analysis of the 2nd HVR revealed several genetic characteristics of the HRSV genotypes. In addition to the duplicate region (), a total of 16 (18.6%) amino acid residues were conserved among the different genotypes. Some amino acids were specific to individual genotypes, including 233E, 258 L, 262 M, 265F, 280S, 290S and 293P for genotype GA1; 222Q and 250T for genotype GA3; and 225A for genotype GA5. All ON1 strains, including the Riyadh strains, presented an insertion of 24 amino acids between residues 283 and 284, of which 23 amino acids were duplicated, as highlighted in . In addition, ON1 strains have two specific amino acids: 232G and 253K. The GA2 genotype strains, including ON1, share one common specific amino acid at position 269T (). The Saudi ON1 strains presented the following specific amino acids: 230T for Riyadh-01-2023, 243S for Riyadh-03-2023, 219I and 227I for Riyadh-04-2023, and 213 N for Riyadh-08-2023.

The duplicated region (nts: 811–882) of Saudi ON1 strains (5 winter seasons) has been aligned against 100 international ON1 strains since 2011. The ON1 prototype, ON138-0111A (accession number: JN257694 ), was set as the consensus sequence. The duplicate regions of the 9 Riyadh ON1 strains (winter season 2022/23) presented 18 amino acid substitutions. However, the Riyadh ON1 strains (winter season 2019/20, 2020/21) presented 17 amino acid changes and 14 amino acid changes in the Riyadh ON1 strains in the winter seasons of 2014/15 and 2015/16. The duplicated region of all ON1 strains had 6 amino acids (285Q, 288T, 292T, 295E, 302Q, and 306T) that remained unchanged across 13 years. This constrained evolution suggests a strong functional requirement for the conserved residues, while the variable sites are under intense immune pressure ().

The nucleotide and deduced amino acid sequences of the HRSV-A and HRSV-B F protein were aligned against the reference strains (USA-Long-1956, Strain A2), which are the most commonly used for vaccine design. This comparative analysis was specifically conducted to identify mutations within the five major antigenic sites to assess the potential impact of these amino acid changes on viral antigenicity and the effectiveness of current or future vaccine candidates. At the nucleotide sequence level, in comparison with the consensus strain, 112 nucleotide mutations were reported in HRSV-A strains, and 309 were reported in HRSV-B strains. Analysis of the deduced amino acid sequences of the HRSV-A and HRSV-B F protein (A,B) from Riyadh isolates revealed distinct patterns of variation across the five major antigenic sites in the prefusion F protein (Ø, II, III, IV, V). The HRSV-A isolates displayed a total of 24 amino acid changes, with only three substitutions mapping to the defined antigenic sites: two at Site Ø (K65R and R213S) and one at Site II (N276S). Notably, the three antigenic sites III, IV, and V showed no amino acid changes in the HRSV-A strains, indicating a high degree of conservation in these regions, a finding consistent with the visual stability observed in the global HRSV-A lineage.

In contrast to HRSV-A, the HRSV-B subgroup, which visually exhibits greater overall sequence diversity, presented a significantly greater number of total amino acid changes ( n = 63) in the Riyadh isolates. Eight of these changes are located within the antigenic sites, with six changes specifically reported in antigenic site II (the palivizumab-binding epitope): D200N, K201N, K209Q, K209R, S211N, and N276S. The HRSV-B isolates also presented a significantly greater number of total amino acid changes ( n = 63). Eight of these changes are located within the antigenic sites (N67T, D200N, K201N, I206M, K209Q, K209R, S211N, and N276S). Due to the overlapping of these antigenic sites, reported amino acid changes may affect more than one site. The remaining two changes are N67T (Site Ø) and I206M (Site II). Due to the overlapping nature of these antigenic sites, some reported amino acid changes may affect more than one site. Notably, both HRSV-A and HRSV-B isolates were completely conserved across antigenic sites III and IV, suggesting these regions are under strong functional or structural constraint. The observed accumulation of mutations in the HRSV-B antigenic sites, particularly Site II, highlights a significant difference in the evolutionary dynamics between the two subgroups and suggests a potential mechanism for immune evasion, a conclusion supported by the visual evidence of increased substitution frequency in the global HRSV-B strains (A,B).

Amino acid substitutions in both HRSV-A and HRSV-B strains are concentrated near key antigenic sites, suggesting potential impacts on immune recognition. In HRSV-A strains, specific changes were reported near antigenic site II (L171S/P and R213S) and site IV (R213S). The HRSV-B strains displayed a broader mutational profile, with several substitutions clustered across multiple sites: S190N, K191R, and S211N were observed near site Ø; S169N and I206M were found near site II; L305I, P311H, and T326I were observed near site III; and S190N, K191R, and I206M were identified near site V.

Phylogenetic analysis of the 2nd HVR G gene resulted in the clustering of the HRSV-A strains into 8 genotypes: GA1–GA7 and SAA1. The GA1 clade includes the extinct strains identified early in the USA. The GA2 clade is divided into two subclades: the ON1 subclade with four cluster groups (ON1A to ON1D) and the other GA2 strains subclades (A). The Saudi strains identified in the 2 winter seasons of 2007/08 and 2008/09 were clustered into the GA2 genotype, whereas strains of the 5 winter seasons of 2014/15, 2016/17, 2019/20, 2021/22, and 2022/23 were clustered within the ON1 genotype with no special preference for distinct subgenotypes (A). The strains are scattered and clustered within genotypes on the basis of their genetic relatedness, with no effect on the period.

The phylogenetic analysis of the full-length F gene (B) clearly demonstrated the evolutionary relationships of the isolates. The significant sequence heterogeneity between the two major subgroups results in the robust separation of all strains into two distinct clades: HRSV-A and HRSV-B. The historical reference/vaccine strains, OK649668 , M11486 and FJ614814 (strain A2), are positioned at the base of the HRSV-A clade, confirming their ancestral status within this subgroup. The nine HRSV-A isolates from Riyadh form a distinct, highly supported monophyletic cluster (99% bootstrap value) that is nested within the larger HRSV-A clade, demonstrating a close evolutionary relationship with the reference strains and other contemporary global HRSV-A isolates. This clustering indicates that while the Riyadh HRSV-A strains constitute a locally evolving lineage, they share a common ancestor with the M11486 vaccine strain. In contrast, the single HRSV-B isolate from Riyadh is located in a separate HRSV-B clade, confirming the genetic distance between the two subgroups.

The deduced amino acids (229 aa for ON1 strains and 205 aa for the other genotypes) were analyzed for possible sites for O- and N-glycosylation. For the GA1 strains, 5 sites (103, 135, 237, 251, and 294) were predicted as potential sites for N-linked glycosylation. The GA2 genotype has the same N-linked glycosylation sites as GA-1 does. However, some GA2 strains, such as Brazil-STA839-2010, lack site 237 because of the N237D mutation. Some Saudi GA2 strains from the winter seasons of 2007/08 and 2008/09, such as Riyadh-27-2008, presented six potential N-glycosylation sites. The 9 Saudi ON1 strains from the winter season (2022/23) presented variable numbers of N-linked glycosylation sites, ranging from 2 in Riyadh-06-2023 and -07-2023 to 4 in Riyadh-08-2023. In addition, these strains have two conserved N-glycosylation sites at 103 NLSG and 237 NTTK compared with three conserved N-glycosylation sites (103 NLSG, 135 NTT, and 237 NTTK) in the winter seasons of 2014/15 and 2016/17.

Saudi ON1 strains harvested in the winter of 2021–2022 presented 3–5 sites for N-glycosylation. However, ON1 strains from the winter seasons of 2007/08 and 2008/09 presented 3 conserved N-glycosylation sites at residues 103, 135, and 237. The number of these sites in international ON1 strains ranged from 3 sites in the Philippines-99071-2019 to 5 sites in Novosibirsk-7.69Hl-2022. Site 251, the most common N-glycosylation site in HRSV genotypes, is lacking in ON1 strains because of the mutation T253K, a characteristic mutation of this subgenotype (). For the GA5 and GA7 genotypes, 5 potential N-glycosylation sites were recorded (103, 135, 237, 250 (GA5)/251 (GA7), 294).

The G protein is rich in serine and threonine residues, which range from ~33S/58T in GA2-7 to 37S/64T in the ON1 subgenotype and represent 30.5% and 31% of the whole G protein length, respectively. In the analyzed fragment, the number of potential O-linked glycosylation sites generally ranged from 56 in Panama-PAN22A-2011 to 77 in Austria-MUW1515402-2022. The number slightly increased to 78 sites in Riyadh-05-2023. In general, the number of O-linked glycosylation sites increased in ON1 strains (82 sites in some strains; G score 0.5–0.99) due to the insertion of 24 aa, the duplicate region (). In contrast to the G protein, the F protein of all strains, including Saudi strains, presented 5 conserved sites (27, 70, 116, 126, and 500) for N-linked glycosylation (), with few exceptions, with only 4 sites, such as UK-440104002-2021 and Riyadh-RSVAF44-2023. In addition, no O-linked glycosylation sites were predicted in the F protein in most of the strains, including Saudi strains. Only a few strains displayed one or more potential sites for O-glycosylation: USA-RSV-A-human-OR-S24493-2023 (1 site), Riyadh-91-2009 (3 sites), Spain-SE01A-0064-V02-2018 (3 sites), USA-strain long-1956 (3 sites), and USA-A2-1995 (3 sites).
sections.discussion:
HRSV has long been recognized as a common cause of lower respiratory tract infections in humans of different age groups. Disease severity and mortality are common in neonates, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients. Since its discovery more than 6 decades ago, no fully protective vaccine has been developed. In the present study, HRSV was detected in 30 (15%) of the 200 NPA samples collected during the two winter seasons of 2021–22 and 2022–23. In terms of age group, the incidence rate was high (25%) in infants (<2 months), followed by 15.38% (≥12 months), 13.33% (6–11 months), and 11.24% in infants aged 2–5 months. These findings are consistent with our previous studies in Riyadh [,,], reports from other parts of Saudi Arabia [,,,], nearby countries [,,,], and worldwide records [,,,]. The high incidence rates in neonates and younger infants could be attributed to the immature immune response and waning levels of maternal antibodies [,]. In the study group, HRSV-B slightly predominated over HRSV-A. This finding was reported in several studies where both types alternately predominated during epidemics [,,].

Recurrent infections, even with the same genotype, are common [,]. This could be because the virus continually produces new genotypes and variants to evade preexisting immunity [,]. Therefore, monitoring virus evolution and linking disease severity to circulating genotypes are priorities for alleviating disease symptoms and reducing mortality rates. During epidemics, several genotypes of HRSV-A circulate concurrently, and dynamic replacement of the existing genotypes has been reported between epidemics on a spatial and temporal basis.

The two HVRs of the G gene were used for nucleotide and deduced amino acid analysis. However, the 2nd HVR region was used for phylogenetic analysis, which is reliable and has been reported in several studies for both types (A and B) of HRSV worldwide [,,]. The evolutionary dynamics of HRSV witness the extinction, replacement and co-circulation of different genotypes. For example, the GA1 genotype became extinct approximately 44 years ago []. The predominant genotypes until 2007 were GA2 and GA5 [,], and within 7 years, GA2 replaced GA5 []. The GA2 genotype continues to generate new subgenotypes (e.g., NA-1, NA-2, and CB-A), which spread to all countries worldwide []. Among these subgenotypes, NA-1 and NA-2 were replaced within 2 to 4 years by the subgenotype ON1. ON1 was first reported in Ontario, Canada [], and subsequently reported in many countries worldwide [,,].

In Saudi Arabia, our previous studies identified the subgenotype NA2 (genotype GA2) as the dominant strain in the winter seasons of 2007/08 and 2008/09 []. However, we reported a shift in the circulating subgenotype from NA2 to ON1 in the winter seasons of 2014/15 and 2015/16 []. The same genotype, ON1, was also detected in the winter seasons of 2019/20 and 2021/22 []. In the present study, we identified the ON1 subgenotype in the winter season of 2022/23. The rapid shift to ON1 and its stability over 13 years without the emergence of new genotypes/subgenotypes may be explained by the acquisition of novel antigenic features, particularly the duplicated region in the 2nd HVR of the G protein. The insertion of a duplicate region (60 nt/20 aa) was also reported in HRSV-B identified in Saudi Arabia in our previous studies [,]. This may help to resolve the HRSV to generate new genotypes and variants to cope with the host immune response. Further classification of ON1 into 4 lineages has been reported in several studies [,] and a fifth lineage has also been proposed []. In the current study, Saudi strains of the 5 winter seasons, 2014/15, 2015/16, 2019/20, 2021/22, and 2022/23, are scattered into 4 lineages (ON1-A to ON-D).

To understand the evolution and stability of the ON1 subgenotype, extensive analysis of the 2nd HVR, including the duplicated region (72 nt/24 aa), was performed. The ON1 strain in the present study presented 130 point mutations and 66 amino acid substitutions, whereas the ON1 strain in the winter seasons of 2014/15 and 2015/16 presented 112 mutations and 36 amino acid substitutions []. Among the 66 amino acid substitutions, 5 aa were changed to threonine, and 13 aa were substituted with serine, which consequently affected the glycosylation profile of the G protein. In the duplicated region alone, 18 amino acid substitutions were reported, and 6 amino acids (285Q, 288T, 292T, 295E, 302Q, and 306T) seemed to be unchanged across 13 years. In addition, Saudi ON1 strains have 3 specific amino acid residues at E232G, T253K, and 314 L, which distinguish them from other GA2 strains. Three specific sites were also observed in strains from China and Italy [,].

For the Riyadh strains from the winter season (2022/23), the duplicated region included 10 additional new O-linked glycosylation sites (288T, 291S, 292T, 293T, 294S, 299S, 301S, 305T, 306T, and 307S). The addition of such new glycosylation sites increased the number of potential O-glycosylation sites (67–82) in ON1 strains compared with other subgenotypes (56–77). The duplicated region does not affect the number of N-linked glycosylation sites; however, it results in a shift of N-glycosylation site 294 to position 318. Few N-linked glycosylation events have been reported in Riyadh strains (season 2022/23), which is slightly lower than those reported in the winter seasons of 2007/08, 2008/09, 2014/15, and 2015/16. Such variation in the N- and O-glycosylation sites combined with the change in protein length (imposed by the duplicated region) may increase the ability of the ON1 strains to escape preexisting immunity and cause recurrent infections [,,,]. Viral protein glycosylation reportedly has several functions, such as protein transportation, stability, the ability to mediate virus binding to cellular receptors, and the ability to hinder antibody binding []. Therefore, the increased number of O-glycosylation sites in the G protein of ON1 strains may explain the high incidence rate and increased risk of hospitalization [,,].

The considerable mutation rate observed in the fusion (F) protein of HRSV-B strains, particularly within major antigenic sites, raises significant concerns about the effectiveness of vaccines based on the prototype HRSV A2 strain. The F protein is a primary target for neutralizing antibodies and, therefore, a primary candidate for vaccine development []. Its prefusion conformation is especially important, as it presents the most potent neutralizing antibody targets []. While the F protein is generally considered more conserved than the G protein, recent studies highlight the convergent evolution of mutations in the HRSV-B F protein, with key substitutions such as K191R, I206M, and Q209R becoming predominant in circulating strains since 2020 []. These mutations are located in or flanking major antigenic sites, including Ø, I, and V, suggesting a potential mechanism for immune evasion [].

A comparative analysis of Riyadh isolates against the reference strain A2, which is commonly used for vaccine design, was conducted to identify mutations within the five major antigenic sites. At the nucleotide level, HRSV-A strains had 112 mutations, while HRSV-B strains showed a much higher number with 309 mutations. This significant difference in mutational load between the subgroups is consistent with previous findings of greater genetic variability in HRSV-B strains []. In the HRSV-A isolates, only 24 amino acid changes were found, with only three located in antigenic sites: two in Site Ø (K65R and R213S) and one in Site II (N276S). Notably, antigenic sites III, IV, and V were completely conserved in HRSV-A strains, indicating a high degree of stability, which is a favorable characteristic for vaccine targets.

These structural changes could alter the protein conformation enough to reduce the binding affinity of vaccine-induced antibodies, thereby diminishing the vaccine’s protective efficacy. HRSV-B isolates from Riyadh have 63 amino acid changes, with eight of these located within antigenic sites. Six of these mutations were found in antigenic site II, the palivizumab-binding epitope (D200N, K201N, K209Q, K209R, S211N, and N276S), with other changes including N67T (Site Ø) and I206M (Site II). This accumulation of mutations in HRSV-B antigenic sites, particularly Site II, highlights a significant difference in the evolutionary dynamics between the two subgroups and suggests a potential mechanism for immune evasion. The observation of multiple changes within the palivizumab-binding site (Site II) is of particular concern, as it suggests a potential for reduced efficacy of this prophylactic monoclonal antibody, a finding that warrants further investigation into contemporary circulating strains [].

Since the current vaccine strategies depend mainly on the F protein from the A2 strain, the substantial genetic divergence of HRSV-B strains is a major challenge. While some studies have shown that vaccines based on the HRSV-A F protein can induce cross-protective immunity against HRSV-B, the level of protection may not be complete or equivalent []. For example, HRSV A-based monovalent Ad26/preF protein vaccine induced cross-neutralizing antibodies against both subtypes; however, the overall protective efficacy against HRSV-B was not always equivalent to that against HRSV-A []. This difference is likely due to the significant sequence divergence between the two subtypes []. Therefore, the accumulation of mutations in the F protein of circulating HRSV-B strains could indeed compromise the effectiveness of a monovalent vaccine based on the A2 strain, potentially leading to breakthrough infections and reduced overall vaccine impact in populations where HRSV-B is prevalent. This highlights the potential need for bivalent vaccines that include antigens from both HRSV-A and HRSV-B to ensure broad and robust protection [].

This study provides comprehensive molecular surveillance of HRSV-A circulation in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, confirming the sustained dominance of the ON1 genotype over multiple seasons, driven by constrained evolution in the duplicated region of the G gene and alterations in glycosylation profiles that likely enhance immune evasion. Critically, the F protein of contemporary HRSV-A isolates demonstrated remarkable antigenic stability, with only three amino acid substitutions mapped to antigenic sites Ø (K65R, R213S) and II (N276S), while sites III, IV, and V remained fully conserved. This high degree of conservation relative to prototype strains used in vaccine design (e.g., A2) supports the anticipated efficacy of recently approved prefusion F-based vaccines (Arexvy, Abrysvo) and the long-acting monoclonal antibody nirsevimab against HRSV-A in this population. In contrast, HRSV-B isolates exhibited substantially greater F protein variability, including multiple substitutions within the palivizumab-binding site II, raising concerns about reduced efficacy of this prophylactic agent and potentially incomplete cross-protection from HRSV-A-based vaccines. These findings underscore the importance of continued genomic monitoring to detect emerging variants that could compromise prophylactic interventions and highlight the potential value of bivalent vaccine strategies for broader protection. Overall, the preserved antigenic profile of circulating HRSV-A strains is encouraging for the implementation of current F-targeted preventives in Saudi Arabia.

title: P-2181. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Infection After High-Inoculum RSV Human Challenge: Analysis of a Randomized Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial of EDP-323, an Oral, Non-Nucleoside Polymerase Inhibitor Antiviral
abstract:
RSV causes high secondary transmission rates in families, hospitals, nursing homes and other settings. Breakthrough RSV infections occur despite RSV vaccination or monoclonal antibody injection. Certain patients at great risk of severe RSV do not respond to RSV vaccination. No effective RSV treatments exist. EDP-323, a first in class, potent, oral, non-nucleoside small molecule RSV polymerase (L-protein) inhibitor rapidly reduces viral load and disease severity when treatment is started after an active RSV infection is identified 1 . The efficacy of RSV antivirals used for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is unknown.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo (PBO)-controlled study ( NCT06170242 ) evaluated the efficacy, antiviral activity and safety, of EDP-323. Healthy volunteers received large intranasal exposures of a low-passage clinical strain of RSV-A (Memphis-37, 4 Log 10

plaque forming units) 2 on Day (D)0. RSV RT-PCR was performed on nasal washes collected twice daily on D2-12. title: Meta-analysis of the efficacy of palivizumab versus nirsevimab at preventing medically attended respiratory syncytial virus infections in non-hospitalized preterm infants.
abstract: Palivizumab has >27 y of proven effectiveness in the prevention of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in high-risk infants. However, there remains limited data on its efficacy at preventing medically attended, non-hospitalized RSV infections (MARI). A systematic literature review was undertaken to identify randomized, placebo-controlled studies of prophylactic interventions against MARI and RSV-related hospitalization in healthy infants born ≤35 weeks' gestational age (wGA). The findings informed a meta-analysis of three studies (N = 2,464) that found palivizumab significantly reduced MARI by 70.5% compared with placebo in 29-35 wGA infants, with broadly similar efficacy to nirsevimab.

sections.other:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of respiratory infections in young children and contributes to substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly in high-risk infants who are born preterm. Palivizumab prophylaxis has been proven effective at reducing the risk of RSV hospitalization (RSVH) in high-risk infants who are ≤35 weeks’ gestational age (wGA) and those with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) and hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease (HS-CHD), as evidenced in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) , and over 27 y of real-world use. Despite the development of newer RSV preventives, including nirsevimab, clesrovimab and the maternal RSVpreF vaccine, uptake of these agents continues to be limited in many low- and middle-income countries, with palivizumab being the only available option (currently available in 93 countries worldwide; AstraZeneca, personal communication, March 10, 2026). It is increasingly recognized that medically attended RSV infection not requiring hospitalization (MARI) can make a substantial contribution to the acute burden of RSV illness. , Although more recent studies of newer RSV preventive agents include MARI as a specific outcome, this was not the case for the earlier pivotal RCTs of palivizumab. , This meta-analysis was primarily aimed to assess the efficacy of palivizumab in the prevention of MARI in healthy, preterm infants born at ≤35 wGA, including an assessment of its relative efficacy compared to nirsevimab.

The authors thank Oana Coban, PhD, of Violicom Medical Communications for editorial support.

Notable work includes being part of an international expert group that developed and validated the International Risk Scoring Tool for identifying infants born 32–35 weeks’ gestational age at greatest risk of RSV hospitalization. Barry was also one of the investigators on the EROS study that assessed the burden to parents of having a child hospitalized with RSV. Barry is a member of the PROUD Taskforce of 24 RSV global experts assembled to help identify solutions to the burden of RSV in low- and middle-income countries.

sections.methods:
To support the meta-analysis, a systematic literature review was undertaken to identify randomized controlled studies (RCTs) of prophylactic interventions (monoclonals and maternal vaccine) versus placebo in the prevention of MARI and RSVH in infants ≤35 wGA without comorbidities (e.g. BPD, HS-CHD). A brief description of the systematic literature review is provided below with the full protocol registered in PROSPERO (ID: CRD42025638486; Supplementary Appendix Table 1).

Literature searches were conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library databases, from January 1, 1998 to December 31, 2024 using the following search terms: RSV OR “respiratory syncytial virus” OR bronchiolitis OR “lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI)” OR “acute respiratory tract infection (ARTI)” OR “lower respiratory infection (LRI)” OR “acute respiratory infection (ARI)” OR “acute lower respiratory infection (ALRI)” OR human respiratory syncytial virus [MeSH/ESH]; (preterm OR prematur*) OR ((“29” OR “30” OR “31” OR “32” OR “33” OR “34” OR “35” OR “36”) AND (gestational age OR weeks’ gestational age OR wGA)); palivizumab OR Synagis OR nirsevimab OR Beyfortus OR motavizumab OR Numax OR suptavumab OR clesrovimab OR RSV vaccine OR Abrysvo OR prophylaxis OR immunoprophylaxis OR monoclonal antibod* OR mAb OR monoclonal antibodies [MeSH/ESH] (see Supplementary Appendix Table 1 for more details). Using a standardized template, two reviewers (BRG and NW) screened titles and abstracts and full-text articles to select and extract data from relevant RCTs meeting the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes, and Study (PICOS) inclusion criteria. Grey literature sources (e.g. conference proceedings) and bibliographies of included papers were also searched to identify any relevant studies not indexed in the database searches. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration Risk of Bias tool. All authors approved the final list of studies to be included in the meta-analysis.

A Bayesian network meta-analysis was undertaken linking available study data on RSVH and MARI rates in a logical block diagram versus placebo as the common comparator. Bayesian inferential output (10,000 Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo [MCMC] iterations) was used to derive the median ratio of the MARI rate (i.e. the rate of non-hospitalized RSV infection) for palivizumab versus placebo. Using this ratio, the MARI rate in the palivizumab group was estimated from the base rate in the placebo group and the relative risk reduction (RRR) of prophylaxis calculated. Since palivizumab and nirsevimab target different sites on the RSV prefusion F protein (site II vs site Ø, respectively), , and have differing half-lives (~20 d vs ~71 d), , and preclinical activity against RSV has been reported to be >50 fold greater for the latter over the former, we explored whether these differences translate into a potential difference in efficacy between the two monoclonals. Assuming that the relative efficacy of RSV preventives against RSVH and MARI rates will run parallel and proportionately, palivizumab efficacy at preventing MARI was compared to that of nirsevimab by assessing the difference between the median ratios ( versus placebo) in pairwise comparisons, with a probability of >0.05 indicating similar effectiveness. No heterogeneity tests across studies were undertaken as Bayesian meta-analysis accounts for such testing by enabling prior probability component variables to comply with their unique distributions through Gibbs sampling (MCMC) while generating posterior probabilities. WinBUGS version 1.4.3 was used for the Bayesian meta-analysis, with the validity of the results for the relative efficacy of palivizumab versus nirsevimab supported by non-stochastic linear manipulation of the same data in EXCEL 365.
sections.results:
The systematic literature review assessed 234 citations, of which six research articles covering five RCTs met the eligibility criteria (Supplementary Appendix Table 2 & Supplementary Appendix Figure 1). ,, Two of the studies were on palivizumab (IMpact and MAKI, , reporting on RSVH and RSVH/MARI, respectively), two on nirsevimab (Griffin et al. and Domachowske et al., both reporting RSVH/MARI), and one on suptavumab (Simoes et al., RSVH/MARI). The risk of bias for all five RCTs was assessed as low. Two studies were subsequently excluded from the meta-analysis. One was excluded due to insufficient data (Domachowske et al. reported no RSVH or MARI cases in the placebo arm). The other study was excluded because suptavumab did not reduce overall RSVH/MARI rates ( versus placebo) and its clinical development was halted. Since the three remaining studies spanned different gestational age ranges and follow-up periods (IMpact: ≤35 wGA, 150 d; MAKI: ≥33 to ≤35 wGA, median 10 months; Griffin et al.: ≥29 to ≤35 wGA, 150 d), the data from the IMpact trial used in the meta-analysis was aligned with Griffin et al. at 29–35 wGA. ,, In total, the meta-analysis included data from 2,464 infants across three studies (Supplementary Appendix Figure 2).

The median ratio of the MARI rate for palivizumab versus placebo was 1:3.43, with the 95% credible interval not spanning zero (CrI, 1.75–6.17), indicating statistical significance (). , This ratio translated into a 70.5% RRR in MARI for palivizumab over placebo (2.8% vs 9.5%, respectively). The difference between median ratios of the MARI rates for palivizumab versus placebo and nirsevimab versus placebo was 0.27, with the 95% CrI (−2.20–2.37) indicating no significant difference in efficacy between the two preventives (). ,
sections.discussion:
RSVH typically accounts for the majority of direct medical costs associated with RSV in infants due to high individual case costs. However, it is increasingly recognized that the economic burden posed by MARI should also be considered, as, despite the individual case costs being lower, incidence rates may be twice as high as for RSVH. , In a Canadian health economic assessment of palivizumab in infants born 32–35 wGA, MARI represented approximately 5% of hospital-related healthcare costs related to RSV infection, and this proportion would have been even greater, if the burden on primary care was also captured. The importance of the contribution of MARI to the burden of RSV infection is reflected in clinical trial endpoints assessing the efficacy of RSV preventives that have evolved over time from considering only hospitalization in the IMpact study to including the effect on both outcomes (alone and in combination) in recent trials. , This meta-analysis found palivizumab prophylaxis to be associated with a statistically significant 70.5% RRR in MARI versus placebo, demonstrating broadly comparable efficacy to nirsevimab. ,

The main limitations of the meta-analysis were that no MARI data were available for infants born <29 wGA and that the MAKI study included a narrower gestational age range of 33–35 weeks compared to the data reported in the IMpact and Griffin et al. studies. ,,, The study populations also varied in terms of geographical location and the time the studies were conducted: USA, Canada and UK from 1996 to 1997 (IMpact-RSV , ); the Netherlands from 2008 to 2010 (MAKI ); and 23 countries from 2016 to 2017 (Griffin et al. ). An important aspect of the effectiveness of RSV preventives is their duration of protection, and this may extend for up to 12 months for nirsevimab. The duration of efficacy against MARI could not be assessed specifically in our analysis due to the limited number of studies available for inclusion. The follow-up period was 150 d in the IMpact (palivizumab) and Griffin et al. (nirsevimab) studies and a median of 10 months in the MAKI trial (palivizumab). ,,, Of note, limitations in the number and sample size of the studies included in the analyses are reflected in the credible intervals reported for the outputs and the strength of the conclusions that have been drawn from them. Our study is based upon a network meta-analysis in which the efficacy of each preventative – whether derived from either RSVH or MARI rates – is calculated as a probabilistic outcome based on Gibbs sampling and Bayesian inference, drawn directly from the patient numbers reported in each source publication. An analogous process was then utilized to combine the individual rates, around an element common to the source publications, to provide a probabilistically derived efficacy projection. It is intrinsic to the methodology that the stochastic spread of the output of such analyses (posterior probability) is directly affected by the size of the studies used as input (priors). Predicated on these results and in the absence of any head-to-head comparative data, we feel that it is reasonable to conclude that the efficacy at preventing MARI is broadly similar for palivizumab and nirsevimab. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the reported efficacy for palivizumab and nirsevimab at preventing RSVH in the registrational studies was 78% (in otherwise healthy infants born ≤35 wGA) and 78.4% (in otherwise healthy 29–35 wGA infants), respectively. ,, Finally, we acknowledge that the definition of what constitutes MARI varies between studies, which complicates cross-trial comparisons. A clear and standardized definition for MARI (and RSVH) is needed that can be applied in diverse healthcare settings to support informed decision-making about their clinical- and cost-effective deployment.

MARI is now an essential clinical outcome employed to evaluate the overall burden of RSV and the effectiveness of emerging preventives. While palivizumab has well-established efficacy and effectiveness against RSVH in high-risk children, including preterm infants, data on its impact on MARI are more limited. This is the first meta-analysis on the efficacy of palivizumab in the prevention of MARI in otherwise healthy preterm infants, which lends further robustness to the preexisting evidence of its effectiveness in the reduction of RSVH.

title: Epidemiology and genetic diversity of human respiratory syncytial virus in Belgium between 2011 and 2019.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) is worldwide one of the leading causes of acute respiratory tract infections in young children and the elderly population. Two distinct subtypes of HRSV (A and B) and a multitude of genotypes have been described. The laboratory of Clinical and Epidemiological Virology (KU Leuven/University Hospitals Leuven) has a long-standing history of HRSV surveillance in Belgium. METHODS: In this study, the seasonal circulation of HRSV in Belgium was monitored during 8 consecutive seasons prior to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic (2011-2012 until 2018-2019). By use of a multiplex quantitative real time PCR panel, 27,386 respiratory samples were tested for HRSV. Further subtyping and sequencing of the HRSV positive samples was performed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. The prevalence and positivity rate were estimated in 4 distinct age groups and the circulating strains of each subtype were situated in a global context and in reference to the described genotypes in literature. RESULTS: HRSV circulated in Belgium in a yearly re-occurring pattern during the winter months and both HRSV subtypes co-circulated simultaneously. All HRSV-B strains contained the 60 nt duplication in the HVR2 region of the G gene. Strains of subtype HRSV-A with a 72 nt duplication in the HVR2 region were first observed during the 2011-2012 season and replaced all other circulating strains from 2014 to 2015 onwards.

sections.other:
Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) is the leading viral cause of acute respiratory tract infections in infants and children under the age of 5 years throughout the world []. Especially in low- and middle-income countries, HRSV is responsible for a high morbidity and mortality in young children and in the elderly population []. Recent global estimates attribute 5.2% of deaths among children under the age of 5 to lower respiratory tract infections caused by HRSV []. Regions with a temperate climate, such as Belgium, experience an annual re-occurring HRSV epidemic during the winter season [, ]. In tropical climates, the HRSV epidemic peak occurs during the rainy season [].

Under its species name Orthopneumovirus hominis , HRSV is classified as a member of the Pneumoviridae family []. Two distinct subtypes of HRSV (A and B) and a multitude of genotypes have been described, currently without consistency in genotype definition or nomenclature []. Though, efforts are currently being made by a group of experts in the field to reach a consensus on genotyping. A manuscript is under preparation. A consensus on HRSV nomenclature has been published, namely: namely: HRSV/subgroup identifier/geographic identifier/unique sequence identifier/year of sampling [, ]. The negative sense, single stranded RNA genome has a length of 15.2 kb and is composed of 10 genes, which code for 11 proteins []. The most variable part of the genome is located at the five-prime end of the G gene, more specifically in the ectodomain []. The ectodomain comprises a central conserved domain with 4 cysteine residues, flanked by 2 hypervariable regions (HVR1 and HVR2) (11) (Table ). In both HRSV subtypes, duplication events have occurred in the HVR2 region of the G gene, creating new strains that rapidly became the dominant circulating strains worldwide [–].

Within the framework of its activities as an associated laboratory to the National Reference Centre (NRC) for respiratory pathogens (Antwerp University Hospitals), the laboratory of Clinical and Epidemiological Virology (KU Leuven/University Hospitals Leuven) has a long-standing history of HRSV surveillance in Belgium [–]. Over the course of 27 epidemic seasons (1984–1985 until 2010–2011), the circulating HRSV-A strains in Belgium could be classified in 5 different genotypes: GA1, GA2, GA4, GA5 and BE/A1, with the first description of a new genotype BE/A1 during the 1986–1987 season. The number of simultaneously circulating HRSV-A genotypes has declined with time from 5 between seasons 1984–1985 and 2001–2002 [], to 2 between seasons 1996–1997 and 2010–2011 [, ], indicating that the genetic variability of HRSV-A strains has decreased. In line with circulation patterns observed globally, the variability of the circulating HRSV-B strains in Belgium also decreased with time []. Between the epidemic seasons of 1982–1983 and 2010–2011, the circulating HRSV-B strains clustered in 13 different lineages (genotypes GB1 to GB13), of which several newly described genotypes (GB5 to GB13) [, ]. Whereas multiple genotypes co-circulated in the first years of the HRSV surveillance in Belgium, genotype GB13 with a 60 nt duplication in the HVR2 region, became the dominant genotype over time for subtype HRSV-B []. In this study, the seasonal circulation of HRSV in Belgium was monitored during 8 consecutive seasons (2011–2012 until 2018–2019). The prevalence and positivity rate were estimated per age category and the circulating strains of each subtype were situated in a global context and in reference to the described genotypes in literature.

sections.methods:
The data used in this study were obtained from patients presenting with a respiratory infection at the University Hospitals of Leuven (UZL) during 8 consecutive epidemic seasons (2011–2012 until 2018–2019), where they were tested for infection with HRSV. Samples that tested positive for HRSV, using lab developed duplex or multiplex real time PCR assays at the UZL Centre for Molecular Diagnostics (CEMOL), were further subtyped by subtype-specific real-time PCR assays. For phylogenetic analyses, the sample set from UZL (N = 1462) was supplemented with a sample set from AZ St. Jan Bruges (N = 184). Both hospitals are located in the region of Flanders, at a distance of 130 km from each other.

Viral RNA was extracted from 140 µl of patient sample, using the QIAmp viral RNA mini kit (Qiagen, The Netherlands) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples were subtyped using a multiplex quantitative real time PCR (qRT-PCR) based on subtype-specific primer/probe sets for conserved regions within the F gene (HRSV-A) and N gene (HRSV-B) as described previously []. The carboxyterminal region of the attachment protein (G) was amplified as described previously []. The amplicon was purified, using the InnuPREP PCRpure kit (Analytik Jena, Germany), followed by ethanol precipitation and Sanger sequencing using the ABI3130xl Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, USA) (seasons 2011–2012 until 2015–2016). From the 2016–2017 season onwards, amplicons were purified using Exosap/Exozap (Applied Biosystems, USA) and sent out for off-site Sanger sequencing (Macrogen Europe, The Netherlands).

Patient sample data from UZL were studied between 25/JUL/2011 and 21/JUL/2019, encompassing 8 consecutive respiratory seasons. Duplicate samples from the same patient, collected at the same time point were removed from the data set. Respiratory seasons were defined from week 30 until week 29 of the following year, according to the ISO week numbering system. The studied population was divided in 4 age groups: young children (under 6 years old); children and adolescents (6 to 17 years old); adults (18 to 64 years old) and elderly (over or equal to 65 years old). The onset of the HRSV season was defined as described earlier []. Figures and plots were generated, using the R package ggplot2 v.3.3 in RStudio v.1.1 [, ].

A global HRSV sequencing dataset was generated by downloading all GenBank HRSV G gene sequences published between 01/JAN/2011 and 22/DEC/2020, according to the following criteria: ((Human respiratory syncytial virus) AND G[Gene Name]) AND ("2011/01/01"[Publication Date]: "2020/12/22"[Publication Date]). The resulting 16,106 nucleotide sequences were confirmed as HRSV sequences and subtyped by parsing GenBank information and/or through nucleotide alignment, using MAFFT v.7 [], followed by manual distinction in Aliview v.1.23 []. Non-HRSV, synthetic, mutant and vaccine strains or strains without location or date identifiers were removed from the dataset.

Per HRSV subtype, nucleotide alignments of all Belgian strains, supplemented with the global sequence dataset were generated, using the default options of MAFFT v.7 []. The second hypervariable domain (HVR2) of the carboxyterminal region of the G gene, comprising a heparin binding domain and a mucin-like region, was obtained from the alignments, including the duplicated region (Table ). The resulting alignments were used for further phylogenetic analysis. Lists of GenBank accession numbers of all used strains can be found in Table S1 (HRSV-A) and Table S2 (HRSV-B).

The best-fitting nucleotide substitution model was identified by comparing 88 candidate models using jModeltest v.2.1.10 []. Phylogenetic trees were reconstructed by rapid bootstrap analysis by RAxML v.8.2.12 [], using the Generalised Time Reversible substitution model with a gamma model of rate heterogeneity and taking invariable sites into account (GTR + GAMMA + I). Branch support was evaluated by bootstrapping based on 1000 pseudo-replicates and only unique sequences were used for tree reconstruction. Trees were midpoint rooted using the R package phytools v.0.7 [] and rendered with increasing node order using the R package ape v.5.4 []. Tree visualisations were created using R packages ggplot2 [] and ggtree [, ].

Nucleotide alignments for HRSV-A and HRSV-B subtypes were generated including all Belgian strains isolated during the seasons 2011–2012 until 2018–2019, reference strains of all genotypes described in literature [], and GenBank reference sequences with accession numbers KT992094.1 (HRSV-A) and AF013254.1 (HRSV-B), using MAFFT v.7 []. The second hypervariable domain (HVR2) was obtained from the alignments (Table ). Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree reconstruction using RAxML v8.2.12 [] and tree visualisations using R, was done in similar fashion as for the global dataset.

Lists of GenBank accession numbers of all strains can be found in Table S1 (HRSV-A) and Table S2 (HRSV-B).
sections.results:
Between week 30 of 2011 and week 29 of 2019, 27,386 respiratory samples were tested for HRSV, in 2491 samples (9%) the presence of HRSV could be confirmed (Table ). Human respiratory syncytial virus circulated in Belgium in a yearly re-occurring pattern during the winter months (Fig. ).

An increase in the positivity rate of HRSV was noted during the late fall, with a median onset of the epidemic in week 45 (SD 2.0). The epidemic reached its peak on average in week 49 (SD 1.6) and came to an end on average in week 5 (SD 2.1) of the following calendar year during the late winter (Table ). During the 2016–2017 and 2017–2018 seasons, the total number of positive tests decreased, as did the positivity rate. The number of performed tests doubled in the following season 2018–2019. Although the positivity rate didn’t rise again, the number of positive tests increased to comparable numbers as the seasons preceding 2016–2017 (Table ).

While the number of performed HRSV tests remained stable over time in the age groups of children and adolescents (7–18 years old) and adults (18–64 years old), testing of young children (under the age of 6 years old) decreased and testing in the elderly population (65 years and older) increased due to changes in the Standard of Care (SOC) testing strategy of UZL. During the 2018–2019 season in particular, testing has almost doubled in comparison to the previous season, from which 43% of tests were performed in the elderly population (Fig. A, B). When compared to the total of positive samples, the number of positive tests has known an increasing trend in the adult and elderly population and a steep decreasing trend in the youngest age group. The percentage of positive samples in infants and young children dropped from 86% of the total number of positive samples during the season 2011–2012 to 29% of the total number of positive samples during the season 2018–2019 (Fig. C, D). While the increase in number of tests doesn’t influence the positivity rate over time in the adult and elderly population, reduced testing in the youngest age group leads to a decrease in the positivity rate from 25% during the 2011–2012 season to 12% during the 2018–2019 season in this group of the population. However, based on the positivity rate, young children remain the largest HRSV infection-affected group (Fig. E, F).

During the epidemic seasons of 2011–2012 until 2018–2019, both HRSV subtypes co-circulated simultaneously. However, HRSV-B dominated almost exclusively during season 2013–2014 and 2018–2019, while HRSV-A was the dominant subtype in season 2014–2015. We describe the following order in subtype dominance: B, A, B, A, A, B, A, B (Fig. A). During every season, infections with HRSV were more prevalent in males than in females (Fig. B), especially in the youngest age group (Fig. D), which is confirmed when subtypes were considered separately (Fig. E). Co-circulation of HRSV subtypes was observed in all age groups. Children were more often infected with subtype HRSV-A, while adults and elderly were more often infected with subtype HRSV-B, however observed merely as a slight trend (Fig. C).

To situate the Belgian circulating strains in the context of a global HRSV diversity, phylogenies were inferred for each subtype from nucleotide alignments of the HVR2 region of the G gene. Alignments of respectively 5539 sequences for HRSV-A and 3730 sequences for HRSV-B were first corrected for identical sequences, to comply with the standard criteria for phylogenetic inference in RAxML. Final alignments (N = 2623 for HRSV-A, N = 2160 for HRSV-B) were subsequently used for phylogenetic tree reconstruction.

The Belgian strains are well dispersed over the tree, demonstrating a temporal rather than geographical clustering of HRSV strains in both subtypes (Fig. ).

Phylogenies were inferred based on nucleotide alignments of the HVR2 region of the G gene, including the Belgian strains isolated between 2011 and 2019 and reference strains of all genotypes described in literature, with exception of HRSV-B genotype BA subclade V [] and genotype BA11 []. The fragment has a length of 411 nt (HRSV-A) or 402 nt (HRSV-B), including the duplicated region of 72 nt or 60 nt, respectively. Alignments counted 451 (HRSV-A) or 588 (HRSV-B) sequences. After correction for identical sequences, final alignments comprised 214 sequences (146 Belgian and 68 genotype reference sequences) for HRSV-A and 303 sequences (186 Belgian and 117 genotype reference sequences) for HRSV-B. In the HRSV-A alignment, 28 genotype reference sequences contained only the last 336 nt of the HVR2 region, missing the first 75 nt of the heparin binding domain. Similarly, 32 HRSV-B genotype reference sequences contain the last 324 nt of the HVR2 region, missing the first 78 nt of the heparin binding domain and 4 reference sequences of genotype BA13 (HRSV-B) are missing the first 96 nt of the heparin binding domain. Since the shorter sequences all contained the complete mucin-like region II of HVR2, inclusion in the final alignments was accepted.

The circulating HRSV strains in Belgium cluster together in a time-dependent manner; strains from the same epidemic season tend to be more closely related to each other than to strains of other seasons (Fig. A, B). During the 2011–2012 and 2012–2013 seasons, a higher genetic variability can be observed than during the later seasons. Belgian strains from the 2011–2012 season cluster together with reference sequences of genotypes GA5, NA1, NA3 and ON1. Belgian strains from the 2012–2013 season cluster with reference sequences of genotype NA3, NA1 and ON1 (Fig. C). During the 2011–2012 season, a duplication of 72 nt in the HVR2 region was introduced, which was present in 10% of the HRSV-A strains. This new strain quickly gained predominance with 69% of the circulating strains already containing this duplication during the following season 2012–2013. Season 2013–2014 was dominated by subtype HRSV-B, no HRSV-A strains were successfully sequenced. From season 2014–2015 onwards, all circulating HRSV-A strains in Belgium contained the 72 nt duplication in the HVR2 region. In the phylogeny of subtype HRSV-B, all Belgian strains cluster with several genotype reference sequences that refer to the “BA viruses”, which include a 60 nt duplication in the HVR2 region: BA10, BA13, BA9, BA2.1, BA-IV. Additionally, when taking the complete ectodomain of the Belgian HRSV-B strains into account, all Belgian sequences show a deletion of 6 nt “AAAACC” at nucleotide position 471–476 of the G gene. This corresponds to a deletion of AA positions 157–159 “KKP” of the G protein ORF in reference strain B2.
sections.discussion:
During the 8 epidemic seasons (2011 until 2019) investigated in this study, the epidemic season of HRSV started in late October or early November and ended in late January or early February of the following year. The Belgian HRSV circulation followed thus the typical pattern with winter-peak that is observed in temperate climates [, ].

Infants and young children are the most vulnerable group to suffer from an HRSV infection [, ]. During the seasons 2016–2017 until 2018–2019, we saw a decrease in the number of tests performed in the population under the age of 6 years old and an increase in the elderly population. The reasons for this shift in the tested population can be found in a change in SOC testing policy within UZL. As of week 15 of 2016, a lab developed panel of 12 multiplex real-time PCR assays for detection of respiratory pathogens has been made available. The panel tests for 28 respiratory pathogens, including 22 viruses, 5 bacteria and 1 fungus. The change in SOC testing strategy translates into an increase of the cost for the patient, which makes physicians more reluctant to inquire testing in case the clinical presentation corresponds to a typical HRSV infection. Young children with an HRSV infection often present with a characteristic wheezing, while clinical symptoms in elderly are not substantially different from an influenza infection [, ]. Therefore, a diagnostic test to distinguish an HRSV infection from other viral respiratory infection, such as Influenza A virus , is more beneficial in the elderly population []. The doubling of HRSV tested samples in the 2018–2019 season can be attributed to the introduction of another combined HRSV/influenza molecular test in October 2018, which is substantially less expensive than the full respiratory panel. Due to the changes in testing strategies, positivity rates in young children have dropped. This suggests that there might be an underestimation of the number of HRSV infections in this age group during the later seasons.

During 14 consecutive seasons in Belgium, a regular 3-yearly cyclic pattern of subtype dominance with 2 HRSV-A seasons alternating with 1 HRSV-B season between 1996 and 2006, has been replaced by a yearly alternating pattern between 2006 and 2010. The HRSV-A dominated season of 2010–2011 broke the yearly alternating pattern [, ]. In this study, co-circulation of both subtypes was seen in all seasons between 2011 and 2019, without a well-defined subtype dominance pattern. There were as many HRSV-A dominated seasons as HRSV-B dominated seasons. More males suffered from HRSV infection than females, a phenomenon that has been attributed to differences in immune response between sexes, making males more vulnerable for paediatric infectious disease [, ]. A trend could be observed that suggests an association between age and HRSV subtype. Children were overall more often infected by subtype HRSV-A and adults with subtype HRSV-B, though differences were mild and a subtype dominance based on age has, to the best of our knowledge, not been described in literature.

The number of different genotypes that co-circulated during an epidemic season has been decreasing in the past years, pointing towards a reduction in the genetic variability of HRSV strains in Belgium []. Since their introduction, HRSV strains with a duplication in the HVR2 region have replaced strains that lack these mutations. This finding is in accordance with other studies all over the world [–] and suggests a fitness advantage in comparison to other strains [, ]. For subtype HRSV-B, the replacement already took place in Belgium in 2003 after the first introduction of the 60 nt duplication during the 2001–2002 season []. All circulating HRSV-B strains between 2011 and 2019 contained the 60 nt duplication. For HRSV-A, the duplication of 72 nt was first introduced in Belgium during the 2011–2012 season and is present in all HRSV-A strains since the 2014–2015 season. During the 2013–2014 season, there has been a very limited circulation of subtype HRSV-A, which might have created a genetic bottleneck that subtype HRSV-A strains without the duplication didn’t manage to pass. In addition to selective pressure on the G protein as a consequence of being targeted by the neutralising antibody response, this bottleneck contributed to the exclusive circulation of HRSV-A strains with duplication in the Belgian population [, ].

A temporal clustering per season was observed in both HRSV-A and HRSV-B subtypes. Genotype definition and classification are currently under discussion [, ]. Therefore, in this analysis we compared the Belgian sequences to all suggested genotypes in literature without assigning a genotype classification. Belgian HRSV-A strains showed genetic similarity with reference strains of genotypes GA5 [], NA1 [], NA3 [] and ON1 [] during season 2011–2012; NA3, NA1 and ON1 during season 2012–2013; and ON1 from season 2014–2015 onwards. The HRSV-B strains cluster together with examples of several suggested genotype classification systems, all including the 60 nt duplication: BA9, BA10 [], BA13 [], BA2.1 [] and BA-IV []. The use of nucleotide alignments covering a larger portion of the HRSV genome would be beneficial in the understanding of the evolution and pathology of circulating strains [, ]. Additionally, including the F gene will be important to monitor the effect of immune pressure after the introduction of F-targeted vaccines []. The dataset in this study was explored retrospectively, the less optimal HVR2 region of the G gene was therefore used to infer phylogenies due to the lack of complete genome data from older samples.

Epidemiological data of the seasons 2019–2020 and 2020–2021 show a decrease in HRSV circulation during the season of 2020–2021, most likely as a consequence of the safety measures taken for the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, with a delayed upsurge in the spring/summer of 2021, and a recurrence of the typical winter peak only in 2022–2023 []. It will be interesting to study the effect of this reduced circulation on the genetic diversity of HRSV in the following years.

In this study, the epidemiology and genetic variability of circulating HRSV strains in Belgium was assessed during 8 consecutive seasons (2011–2019). We conclude that HRSV followed an annual re-occurring pattern during the winter months. The predominant strains of both subtypes have a duplication in the HVR2 region, and these strains have replaced other circulating strains over time. It is essential to be aware of the context in which testing was performed in order to draw conclusions on fluctuations in epidemiological data. Surveillance of HRSV circulation in Belgium is further continued as part of the NRC activities of our lab.

title: Genomic characteristics of human respiratory syncytial virus from children in China during 2017-2020.
abstract: Acute lower respiratory tract infections (ALRTIs) are a leading cause of mortality in young children worldwide due to human respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The aim of this study was to monitor genetic variations in RSV and provide genomic data support for RSV prevention and control. A total of 105 complete RSV genome sequences were determined during 2017-2020. Phylogenetic analysis showed that all of the RSVA sequences were of genotype ON1, and all of the RSVB sequences were of genotype BA9. Notably, a phylogenetic tree based on the whole genome had more branches than a tree based on the G gene. In comparison to the RSV prototype sequences, 71.43% (50/70) of the ON1 sequences had five amino acid substitutions (T113I, V131N, N178G, H258Q, and H266L) that occurred simultaneously, and 68.57% (24/35) of the BA9 genotype sequences had 12 amino acid substitutions, four of which (A131T, T137I, T288I, and T310I) occurred simultaneously. In the F gene, there were 19 amino acid substitutions, which were mainly located in the antigenic sites Ø, II, V, and VII. Other amino acid substitutions were found in the NS1, NS2, P, SH, and L proteins. No significant evidence of recombination was found in any of the sequences. These findings provide important data that will be useful for prevention, control, and vaccine development against RSV.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccination Strongly Induces RSVpreF-specific IgG and Neutralizing Activity in Immunocompromised Individuals.
abstract: BackgroundProtein-based respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prefusion F (RSVpreF) vaccines show promising immunogenicity in immunocompromised individuals. We have recently shown that RSV-specific CD4 T-cell responses and IgG antibodies were significantly induced, but data on functional humoral responses as well as associations between cellular and humoral immunological endpoints remain limited. We therefore extended our previous studies and performed a head-to-head assessment of vaccine-specific RSVpreF IgG and neutralizing antibody activity across different immunocompromised populations, including kidney and lung transplant recipients, patients on hemodialysis, and patients with CKD.MethodsConformation-specific RSVpreF-specific IgG levels and RSV-neutralizing plasma activity were assessed before and 13-18 d after RSV vaccination in 61 patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), 15 patients receiving hemodialysis, 46 kidney transplant (KTx) recipients, and 31 lung transplant (LuTx) recipients. RSVpreF-specific IgG was measured by ELISA and neutralizing activity using an RSV-pseudovirus assay. Furthermore, comprehensive correlation analyses were carried out to assess associations between vaccine-induced humoral immune parameters and cellular immunity.ResultsVaccination significantly increased RSVpreF-specific IgG (P ≤ 0.0001) and neutralizing activity in all groups (P = 0.002 to P P ConclusionsRSV vaccination induces robust functional humoral immunity in all tested immunocompromised patient groups, but responses are lowest in kidney transplant recipients. Among transplant recipients, responses were reduced within the first year after transplantation and in patients on MMF/MPA, supporting the need for optimized vaccination strategies in these patient groups.
